This type of bearing relies on the tapered surface of the inner hole to expand the inner ring radially to achieve preloading, so it is called radial preloading. As shown in Figure 8-6a, what measures the amount of preload is the difference Δ = (D1 - D2) between the roller envelope circle diameter D2 and the outer ring raceway diameter D1, which is called the radial preload amount or simply "preload amount", with the unit of μm. During assembly, the outer ring is installed into the housing hole, and D1 is measured. Without installing spacer 1 first, the inner ring is installed on the spindle, as shown in Figure 8-6b. Tighten nut 2, and use a special envelope circle measuring instrument to measure the envelope circle diameter of the rolling elements until it is greater than D1 by Δ, measure distance ε, and grind the thickness of the spacer according to the ε value. Install the spacer and tighten the nut to obtain the predetermined preload amount. ② Preloading of angular contact bearings. This type of bearing achieves preloading by causing axial displacement between the inner and outer rings under the action of axial force Fa0, as shown in Figure 9-6c. What measures the preload is the axial preload force Fa0, referred to as preload force, with the unit of N. Multi-unit angular contact ball bearings are assembled based on preload force; bearing factories specify three levels of preload: light, medium, and heavy, and the preload level can be specified when ordering. Based on the preload force, the bearing factory grinds away an amount σ from the end face of the inner ring (for back-to-back assembly, as shown in Figure 9-6d) or the outer ring (for face-to-face assembly, as shown in Figure 9-6e). When pressed tightly during assembly, the predetermined preload force can be obtained. If a certain distance is required between two bearings, inner and outer spacers of the same thickness can be added between the two bearings. Under the action of axial load, the rolling elements and the raceway of the unloaded side bearing must not separate from contact. The minimum preload force meeting this condition is 35% of the maximum axial load for a duplex configuration (approximately taken as 1/3), and 24% for a triplex configuration (approximately taken as 1/4). 3) Lubrication and sealing of spindle bearings. Good lubrication can reduce the operating temperature of bearings and prolong service life. Sealing not only prevents dust, chips, and cutting fluid from entering, but also prevents the leakage of lubricating oil. ① Lubrication of spindle bearings. On CNC machine tools, spindle bearing lubrication methods include grease lubrication, oil lubrication, oil mist lubrication, and oil-air lubrication. Grease lubrication is currently the most commonly used lubrication method for spindle bearings on CNC machine tools, especially for front support bearings. Of course, if there is no cooling lubricating oil system in the spindle box, the rear support bearings and other bearings generally use grease lubrication. The grease filling amount for spindle bearings is usually 10% of the bearing's spatial volume, and must not be filled arbitrarily, otherwise it will exacerbate spindle heating. When using grease lubrication, effective sealing measures must be taken to prevent cutting fluid or lubricating oil from entering the bearing. Oil lubrication is also one of the common lubrication methods in CNC. Figure 8-7 shows a constant temperature oil lubrication and cooling method. Constant temperature oil controlled by an automatic oil temperature control box enters the spindle box via a hydraulic pump, flows along the spiral groove on the outer ring of the spindle front support sleeve to take away the heat generated by the spindle bearing; another path injects constant temperature oil onto the transmission gears and transmission shaft support bearings via an oil distributor in the spindle box to take away the heat they generate. When using oil lubrication for angular contact ball bearings, attention should be paid to the pumping effect of angular contact, and oil needs to be injected from the small opening of the bearing. Oil mist lubrication is a method where oil is atomized by high-pressure gas and sprayed from a nozzle onto the parts requiring lubrication. Because it is mist-like, the oil has good heat absorption and no oil stirring effect, so it is often used for the lubrication of high-speed spindle bearings. However, oil mist is easily blown out and pollutes the environment. Oil-air lubrication is a new lubrication method developed for high-speed spindles. As shown in Figure 8-8, it feeds a very small amount of oil (8~16 min, about 0.03 cm³) into compressed air, and then blows it into the bearing clearance, thereby lubricating the bearing and suppressing bearing heat. The oil level switch in the oil tank and the pressure switch in the pipeline can automatically cut off the power supply of the main motor when there is no oil in the tank or insufficient pressure. ② Sealing of the spindle. Spindle sealing includes contact sealing and non-contact sealing. Figure 8-9 shows several forms of non-contact sealing. Figure 8-9a utilizes the clearance between the bearing cover and the shaft for sealing; grooving inside the bearing cover hole is to improve the sealing effect. Example 7: The spindle of an XK5040-1 could not rotate after starting up. Fault cause analysis and elimination: Checking the motor, the condition was good; the transmission key was not damaged. After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

8.2 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Feed Drive Components The feed drive component is the main part of the servo feed system, mainly composed of a transmission mechanism, motion conversion mechanism, guiding mechanism, and executing component. It is the actuator that provides the motion and power required to realize the forming machining motion. Since the feed motion of CNC machine tools is the direct object of digital control, the final positional accuracy and contour accuracy of the machined workpiece are related to the transmission accuracy, sensitivity, and stability of the feed motion. In order to ensure the transmission accuracy and working stability of the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, the following requirements should be noted when designing the mechanical transmission device: ① Improve transmission accuracy and rigidity. The accuracy of the CNC machine tool itself, especially the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the feed drive device, plays a key role in the machining accuracy of parts and is a characteristic indicator of CNC machine tools. Therefore, it is first necessary to ensure the machining accuracy of each transmission part

Structurally, issues such as tool clamping, bearing configuration, bearing clearance adjustment, lubrication, and sealing must be well resolved. (1) Spindle. The spindle is an important part of the spindle transmission structure. Its structural dimensions, shape, manufacturing accuracy, material, and heat treatment have a great impact on the working performance of the spindle component. Spindle structures come in various forms depending on the design requirements of the spindle transmission system. During design, a series of issues must be properly handled, such as the clamping of chucks or tools, spindle unloading, positioning and clearance adjustment of spindle bearings, and sealing and lubrication of spindle components. The main dimensional parameters of the spindle include: spindle diameter, inner hole diameter, overhang length, and support span. The basis for evaluating and considering the main dimensional parameters of the spindle is the rigidity of the spindle, structural manufacturability, and the process application range of the spindle assembly. (2) Spindle Bearings. Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

Spindle sealing includes contact sealing and non-contact sealing. Figure 8-9 shows several forms of non-contact sealing. Figure 8-9a utilizes the clearance between the bearing cover and the shaft for sealing; grooving inside the bearing cover hole is to improve the sealing effect. This seal is used in grease-lubricated areas with relatively clean working environments. Figure 8-9b cuts a sawtooth annular groove on the outer diameter of the nut. When oil flows outward, the centrifugal force of the spindle rotation throws the oil along the slope into the cavity of end cover 1, and the oil flows back into the box. Figure 8-9c is a labyrinth seal structure, which provides reliable sealing effects in working environments with many chips and heavy dust; this structure is suitable for sealing grease or oil lubrication. When using a non-contact seal, to prevent leakage, the smoothness of the oil return hole must be ensured so that the return oil can be drained as soon as possible. Contact sealing mainly includes felt ring and oil-resistant rubber seal ring sealing, as shown in Figure 8-10. (3) Adjustment of Spindle Accuracy. Figure 8-11 shows the spindle of a certain model of CNC lathe. Its rotation accuracy includes two items: radial runout and axial movement. Radial runout is guaranteed by a double-row radial short cylindrical roller bearing at the front end of the spindle and a radial thrust ball bearing at the rear end; axial movement is guaranteed by the radial thrust bearing at the rear end of the spindle. Normally, this accuracy is adjusted before leaving the factory and generally requires no adjustment. If tool holder collision with the workpiece or other reasons affect the spindle's accuracy, spindle accuracy adjustment must be performed. During adjustment, loosen the lock screw on nut 1 or nut 2 for adjustment. After adjustment, retighten the lock screw. If requirements are still not met, repeat the above steps. After adjustment, perform an idling test for a certain period of time (usually about 1 hour). 3. Other Auxiliary Components of the Spindle. (1) Hydraulic power chuck. In CNC lathes, the hydraulic power chuck is the most commonly used workpiece fixture. It is the connecting interface between the machine tool spindle and the workpiece; the speed, torque, and rotation accuracy of the machine tool spindle are transmitted to the workpiece through the power chuck. Hydraulic power chucks are very widely used in CNC machine tools and have become indispensable fundamental functional components for mid-to-high-speed CNC lathes, CNC grinders, and CNC turn-mill centers. Hydraulic power chucks mainly include self-centering chucks, floating chucks, crankshaft chucks, and indexing chucks. Among them, the linearly driven self-centering hydraulic power chuck shown in Figure 8-12a is highly versatile and widely used. The hydraulic power chuck is fixedly mounted on the front end of the spindle. The rotary hydraulic cylinder 1 is connected to the connector 5 with screws 7, and the connector 5 is connected to the rear end face of the spindle with screws, causing the rotary hydraulic cylinder to rotate together with the spindle. The clamping and unclamping of the chuck are driven by the rotary hydraulic cylinder through a hollow draw tube 2. The rear end of the draw tube is threaded to the piston 6 inside the hydraulic cylinder, and the threads on both ends of the connection sleeve 3 are connected to the draw tube 2 and the slide sleeve 4 respectively. Figure 8-12b shows a schematic diagram of the wedge mechanism inside the chuck. When the pressure oil in the hydraulic cylinder pushes piston 6 and draw tube 2 towards the chuck, slide sleeve 4 moves to the right. Due to the action of the wedge groove on the slide sleeve and the chuck body, jaw base 11 moves radially outwards with jaw 12, thereby loosening the chuck; conversely, when the pressure oil in the hydraulic cylinder pushes the piston and draw tube towards the rear end of the spindle, the chuck clamps the workpiece through the wedge mechanism. Chuck body 9 is fixed with screws 10 and installed on the front end of the spindle. Item 8 is the box body of the rotary hydraulic cylinder. The distribution plate of the rotary hydraulic cylinder is shown in Figure 8-13. Oil is supplied to the hydraulic cylinder 3 via distribution plate 2 and piston rod 4. The distribution plate is supported by rolling bearing 1. Hydraulic cylinder 3 and piston rod 4 rotate synchronously with the machine tool spindle, while distribution plate 2 remains stationary. The distribution plate uses an axial annular clearance seal. If the oil path is improved to supply oil from the hydraulic cylinder body to the pressure cavity, the distribution plate can avoid axial movement. The piston rod of the hollow rotary hydraulic cylinder has a center hole, while other aspects are the same as the solid hydraulic cylinder. High-speed distribution pairs generate serious heat; therefore, heat dissipation fins are often designed outside the distribution plate to cool it and improve the cooling effect. To improve the reliability of clamping and ensure that the workpiece can still be clamped if a fault occurs in the oil supply line, a hydraulic lock is usually integrated into the rotary hydraulic cylinder to realize cylinder self-locking. In addition, based on different transmission mechanisms, linearly driven power chuck bodies can also be divided into wedge-type power chucks, lever-type power chucks, helical rack power chucks, and wedge-lever power chucks. This situation may be caused by the screw shoulder being too deep, too shallow, or the bearing not being installed in place. ② If the perpendicularity between the positioning shoulder surface for installing the bearing on the screw and the axis of the locking thread profile is out of tolerance, or the parallelism between the lock nut surface and the bearing mounting surface is out of tolerance, it will cause the bearing to tilt. Therefore, the lock thread profile on the screw used to install the bearing must be processed simultaneously with the bearing positioning shoulder surface to ensure perpendicularity; grinding is even better, and precision specialized lock nuts should be selected. ③ If the perpendicularity of the internal cavity positioning surface of the bearing housing and the gland installation surface to the axis of the bearing hole is out of tolerance, it will also cause the bearing to tilt, and the internal cavity positioning surface is difficult to process and measure. 5) Parallelism or flatness of the support housing surface is out of tolerance Whether the mating component surface is ground or scraped, as long as its parallelism or flatness exceeds the tolerance range, it will affect the positioning accuracy when the worktable moves. Usually, adjusting can be achieved by adding shims between the support housing and the base body. (2) Unsmooth Movement 1) Foreign matter entering the steel ball track If the ball screw is not equipped with a wiper or has poor protection, the accumulation of debris or dust generated during assembly and processing enters the steel ball track, causing unsmooth movement, reduced accuracy, and reduced service life. 2) Overtravel Limit switch failure, overshooting, misoperation, or collision will cause damage, dents, or even fracture of the return pipe, resulting in unsmooth operation of the steel balls, or even complete failure to rotate. 3) Eccentricity If the nut housing and the bearing housing are not concentric, radial loads will be generated. When the eccentricity is too large, the screw will bend or even become eccentric; even if it does not cause obvious bending, abnormal wear will continue to occur and rapidly reduce the accuracy of the screw. The higher the pre-tension set for the nut, the higher the requirement for eccentric accuracy. (3) Temperature Rise Problems 1) The influence of lubrication The choice of lubricating oil directly affects the temperature rise of the ball screw. Poor lubrication of the ball screw will produce a larger temperature rise, which may cause steel balls to crack or be damaged, thereby damaging the nut or screw ball grooves. Therefore, the timely replenishment of lubricating oil must be considered during the design process. If an automatic lubrication system cannot be used, the replenishment cycle of lubricating oil (grease) must be included in the maintenance manual. Generally, it is recommended to use bearing lubricating oil for ball screw oil lubrication, and lithium-soap-based grease for grease lubrication. The viscosity of the oil should be selected based on operating speed, working temperature, and load conditions. For high speed and low load conditions, it is best to use low viscosity oil; for low speed and high load, high viscosity oil is recommended. When applied in high-speed, heavy-load situations, forced cooling must be used to lower the temperature, and hollow screws should be used to introduce cooling oil to achieve the cooling effect. 2) The influence of pre-tension Generally, ball screws require certain pre-tension to achieve the purposes of improving accuracy and rigidity, but applying pre-tensioning force to the nut will increase the friction torque and resistance of the raceway, raising the temperature during work. It is recommended that the pre-tension should not exceed 8% of the screw's dynamic load. 3) The influence of pre-stretching When the temperature of the ball screw rises, the thermal stress effect will cause a slight elongation of the screw, so the length of the screw becomes unstable. Pre-compensation measures are often used to make up for this. The target value for pre-stretching compensation is to give a negative compensation value in advance. It is generally recommended that the compensation value per 1000mm is 0.02~0.03mm. Excessive pre-stretching will burn out the support bearings. Therefore, it is recommended to use a pre-stretching value corresponding to less than 5°C. However, if the screw diameter exceeds 50mm, it is not suitable for pre-stretching. A large screw diameter requires a large pre-stretching force, which leads to overheating and burning of support bearings. It is recommended to use a temperature rise of about 3°C as the compensation value. 4) The influence of the dn value The dn value is the product of the screw pitch circle diameter and the maximum rotational speed. For example, if the pitch circle diameter is Φ40mm and the maximum speed is 2000r/min, its dn value is 80000. The dn value has a significant impact on the noise, working temperature, circulation system, and service life of the screw. It is generally recommended that the dn value not exceed 70000. The dn value can be controlled by increasing the lead or decreasing the rotational speed. If the dn value exceeds the normal range, the manufacturer should be contacted for

(4) Braking of Ball Screws The ball screw and nut pair has high transmission efficiency but cannot self-lock. A braking device needs to be provided (especially in vertical transmission or high-speed, large-inertia applications). The most common braking method is the electrical electromagnetic method, that is, the use of an electromagnetic brake, and this brake is located inside the motor. Figure 8-27 is a schematic diagram of the electromagnetic brake of a FANUC servo motor. When the machine tool is working, under the action of the electromagnetic force of the electromagnetic coil 7, the outer gear 8 disengages from the inner gear 9, and the spring is compressed; when stopping or during a power outage, the permanent magnet 5 loses power, and under the restoring force of the spring, gears 8 and 9 mesh, and the inner gear 9 becomes one with the motor end cover, thus braking the screw connected to the motor shaft. This electromagnetic brake is installed inside the motor housing, forming an integrated structure with the motor. (5) Elimination of Axial Clearance and Pre-tensioning of Ball Screw and Nut Pair Figure 8-27 Schematic diagram of servo motor electromagnetic brake 1—Resolver 2—Tachometer generator rotor 3—Tachometer generator stator 4—Brush 5—Permanent magnet 6—Servo motor rotor 7—Electromagnetic coil 8—Outer gear 9—Inner gear The ball screw and nut pair has strict requirements on axial clearance to ensure movement accuracy during reverse motion. The so-called axial clearance refers to the maximum axial movement between the screw and the nut when there is no relative rotation between them. In addition to the structural clearance itself, it also includes the movement caused by elastic deformation after an axial load is applied. Therefore, it is difficult to completely eliminate the axial clearance. The double-nut pre-tensioning method is usually used to control the elastic deformation to a minimum. Currently, there are three common structural forms for double-nut pre-tensioning: 1) Pre-tensioning with a lock nut Figure 8-28 shows a thread-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair. The left and right nuts of the ball screw are connected to the outer sleeve with flat keys. The extended end of the right nut has no flange and is threaded. Using two round nuts 1 and 2, the right nut can be moved axially relative to the screw, and then locked after eliminating the clearance. This adjustment method has the advantages of a compact structure and convenient adjustment, so it is widely used, but the displacement amount is not easily controlled precisely. Figure 8-28 Thread-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair 1—Round nut 2—Lock nut 2) Adjusting clearance by grinding a spacer As shown in Figure 8-29, by grinding and adjusting the thickness of the spacer, the left and right nuts of the ball screw generate axial displacement to achieve pre-tensioning. This method has a simple structure and good rigidity. When adjusting the clearance, the adjusting spacer needs to be removed for grinding. For the convenience of assembly and disassembly, it is best to make the adjusting spacer into a half-ring structure. Figure 8-29 Spacer-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair 3) Differential tooth adjustment Figure 8-30 shows a differential tooth clearance-adjusting ball screw and nut pair. External gears are machined on the ends of the left and right nuts, with the number of teeth being Z1 and Z2 respectively, and Z1 and Z2 differ by one tooth. The two gears mesh with the corresponding internal ring gears at both ends respectively. The internal ring gears are fastened to the nut housing. During pre-tensioning, the two internal ring gears are disengaged, allowing the two nuts to rotate the same number of teeth in the same direction; then the internal ring gears are re-engaged, and the relative axial position of the two nuts changes, thereby achieving the adjustment of the clearance and the application of the pre-tensioning force. Figure 8-30 Differential tooth clearance-adjusting ball screw and nut pair When both gears rotate by one tooth in the same direction, their axial displacement is: s=1/(Z1×Z2) This method allows the relative axial displacement of the two nuts to be as small as 1mm. Its adjustment accuracy is high, accurate, and reliable, but the structure is complex. top_chunks.text: 8.1 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Spindle Components. The spindle is the motion axis on a CNC machine tool that drives the tool or workpiece to rotate and generate cutting motion, and it is often the motion axis with the highest single-axis power consumption on a CNC machine tool. Generally, like conventional machine tools, CNC machine tools must also undergo speed variation to enable the spindle to obtain different rotational speeds to adapt to various processing requirements. While changing speeds, the spindle is also required to transmit a certain amount of power and sufficient torque to meet cutting needs. In addition to meeting the requirements of conventional machine tool spindles, CNC machine tool spindles also have the following requirements: 1. A larger speed regulation range and the realization of stepless speed regulation. Only when the machine tool spindle has a high rotational speed and a wide speed regulation range can it ensure that during processing, a more reasonable cutting parameter can be selected to give full play to the cutting performance of the tool. 2. High precision and rigidity, with smooth transmission and low noise. The improvement of machining accuracy of CNC machine tools is closely related to the rigidity of the machine tool's spindle structure, so the manufacturing accuracy and rigidity of its transmission components should be improved. For example, the tooth surface of gears should undergo high-frequency induction heating and quenching to increase wear resistance; the final stage should use helical gear transmission to improve transmission stability; using high-precision bearings and selecting reasonable support spans can improve the rigidity of spindle components. 3. Good vibration resistance and thermal stability. CNC machine tools generally perform rough and finish machining continuously, and during machining, interference from impact forces or alternating forces caused by uneven machining allowances, unbalanced moving parts, and self-excited vibration during the cutting process may cause the spindle to vibrate, affecting machining accuracy and surface roughness, and in severe cases, even destroying the tool or part, making machining impossible. Therefore, in the machine tool spindle structure, each main component must not only have a certain static rigidity but also sufficient vibration resistance to suppress vibrations caused by various interferences. Vibration resistance is usually measured by dynamic rigidity or dynamic compliance; for example, the dynamic rigidity of spindle components depends on parameters such as the equivalent static rigidity, damping ratio, and natural frequency of the spindle. During the cutting process of the machine tool, the heat generated by the spindle structure causes thermal deformation of its internal components, destroying the relative positional accuracy and motion accuracy between components, thereby causing machining errors; moreover, thermal deformation limits the improvement of cutting parameters, reduces transmission efficiency, and even affects productivity. The thermal stability of spindle components is often achieved through measures such as maintaining appropriate fit clearances between components, circulating lubrication, and maintaining thermal balance. 8.1.1 Typical Structure and Assembly Adjustment of Spindle Components. 1. Common Structures of Spindles. Currently, the transmission structures of CNC machine tool spindles can be roughly divided into the following categories: (1) Main transmission with a direct connection between the motor and the spindle. As shown in Figure 8-1a, this direct-drive structure is generally rotated directly by a variable-speed motor driving the spindle, which greatly simplifies the structure of the spindle box and spindle, and effectively improves the rigidity of the spindle components. However, the output torque of the spindle is small, and motor heating has a significant impact on spindle accuracy, so its application is subject to certain limitations. (2) Main transmission with one-stage speed variation. As shown in Figure 8-1b, one-stage speed variation is mostly accomplished by a synchronous belt. Its advantages are a simple structure, convenient installation and debugging, and to a certain extent, it can meet the speed and torque output requirements. However, the spindle speed regulation range ratio is still the same as the motor's, constrained by the motor's speed regulation range ratio. Its advantage is a wide speed variation range, with a maximum speed reaching 8000r/min, which basically meets the transmission requirements of most current CNC machine tools and is easy to realize rich control functions; its simple structure and convenient installation and debugging can meet the control requirements of current mid-to-high-end CNC machine tools. However, for increasingly high speed demands, this configuration method is difficult to satisfy. (3) Main transmission with variable speed gears. As shown in Figure 8-1c, this configuration method is mostly adopted in large and medium-sized CNC machine tools. In actual production, the spindle does not need to maintain constant power throughout the entire speed range; generally, constant power transmission is required in the medium and high-speed sections, and constant torque transmission is required in the low-speed section. To ensure that the CNC machine tool spindle has a large torque at low speeds and that the spindle's speed range is as large as possible, some CNC systems are equipped with gear speed variation on the basis of the stepless speed variation of the machine tool spindle motor, becoming segmented stepless speed variation. In the segmented stepless speed variation system with gear speed variation, the forward and reverse starting, stopping, and braking of the spindle are realized by directly controlling the motor, while the speed variation of the spindle is realized by the combination of the stepless speed variation of the motor speed and the stepped speed variation of the gears. Gear stepped speed variation mechanisms usually adopt two speed variation forms: hydraulic shift fork speed variation and electromagnetic clutch speed variation. 1) Hydraulic shift fork speed variation. The principle and form of the hydraulic shift fork speed variation mechanism are shown in Figure 8-2. The shift fork of the sliding gear is connected to the piston rod of the variable speed hydraulic cylinder. By changing different oil flow paths, the triple gear can obtain three different speed variation positions. As shown in Figure 8-2a, when hydraulic cylinder 1 is fed with pressure oil and hydraulic cylinder 5 is depressurized, piston rod 2 drives shift fork

motion. In order to ensure the transmission accuracy and working stability of the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, the following requirements should be noted when designing the mechanical transmission device: ① Improve transmission accuracy and rigidity. The accuracy of the CNC machine tool itself, especially the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the feed drive device, plays a key role in the machining accuracy of parts and is a characteristic indicator of CNC machine tools. Therefore, it is first necessary to ensure the machining accuracy of each transmission part, especially to improve the transmission accuracy of the ball screw and nut pair (linear feed system) and worm gear pair (circular feed system). In addition, adding reduction gears to the feed transmission chain to reduce the pulse equivalent (i.e., the distance the worktable moves when the servo system receives one command pulse) can also improve transmission accuracy from a system design perspective; transmission accuracy and rigidity can also be improved by pre-tensioning the transmission ball screw to eliminate the clearance of transmission parts such as gears and worm gears. ② Reduce the inertia of moving parts. The inertia of transmission parts affects both the starting and braking characteristics of the feed drive system, especially for parts running at high speeds, where the influence of inertia is even greater. Under the premise of satisfying transmission strength and rigidity, the mass of the actuating components should be minimized as much as possible, and the diameter and mass of rotating parts should be reduced to decrease the inertia of moving parts. ③ Reduce the frictional resistance of moving parts. The frictional resistance of the mechanical transmission structure mainly comes from the lead screw nut pair and the guide rails. In the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, to reduce frictional resistance, eliminate low-speed feed crawling, and improve the stability of the entire servo feed system, ball screws, rolling guides, plastic guides, and hydrostatic guides are widely used. ④ Fast response speed. The so-called fast response characteristic refers to the response speed of the feed drive system to input command signals and how quickly the transient process ends. Fast response is a dynamic performance of the servo feed system and reflects the tracking accuracy of the system. During the workpiece machining process, the worktable should be able to sensitively and accurately track instructions within the specified speed range, without missing steps or taking extra steps during operation. The response speed of the feed drive system not only affects the machining efficiency of the machine tool but also affects the machining accuracy. In the design, the rigidity, clearance, friction, and moment of inertia of the machine tool worktable and transmission mechanism should be optimized to the best possible values to improve the fast response characteristics of the servo feed system. ⑤ Strong overload capacity. Because the motor frequently changes direction and the acceleration and deceleration are very fast, the motor may work under overload conditions. This requires the motor to have a strong overload capacity, generally requiring it to withstand an overload of 4 to 6 times for several minutes without damage. ⑥ Good stability and long service life. Stability is the most basic condition for the normal operation of the servo feed drive system, particularly that it must not crawl under low feed speeds and must be able to adapt to changes in external loads without resonance. Stability is related to the system's inertia, rigidity, damping, and gain. Properly selecting these parameters to achieve optimal working performance is the goal of servo feed system design. The service life of a servo feed drive system mainly refers to the length of time it can maintain the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the CNC machine tool, that is, the ability of each transmission component to maintain its original manufacturing accuracy. Therefore, the materials, heat treatment methods, and processing technologies of each transmission component should be reasonably selected, and appropriate lubrication methods and protective measures should be adopted to extend its service life. ⑦ Convenient operation and maintenance. CNC machine tools are high-precision automatic control machine tools, mainly used for single-piece, small-to-medium batch, high-precision, and complex production and machining. CNC machine tools have a high utilization rate, so the structural design of the feed drive system should facilitate maintenance and care, minimizing the maintenance workload to improve the utilization rate of the machine tool. 8.2.1 Typical Structures of Feed Drive Components Common mechanical transmission devices include ball screw pairs, hydrostatic worm-rack drives, preloaded double gear-racks, and linear motors. 1. Its nut structure is compact, positioning is reliable, rigidity is good, it is not easy to wear, the return raceway is short, balls are not easily jammed, and friction loss is small. The disadvantage is that the structure is complex and manufacturing is difficult. When the external circulation ball screw pair is working, the balls leave contact with the screw. Structurally, issues such as tool clamping, bearing configuration, bearing clearance adjustment, lubrication, and sealing must be well resolved. (1) Spindle. The spindle is an important part of the spindle transmission structure. Its structural dimensions, shape, manufacturing accuracy, material, and heat treatment have a great impact on the working performance of the spindle component. Spindle structures come in various forms depending on the design requirements of the spindle transmission system. During design, a series of issues must be properly handled, such as the clamping of chucks or tools, spindle unloading, positioning and clearance adjustment of spindle bearings, and sealing and lubrication of spindle components. The main dimensional parameters of the spindle include: spindle diameter, inner hole diameter, overhang length, and support span. The basis for evaluating and considering the main dimensional parameters of the spindle is the rigidity of the spindle, structural manufacturability, and the process application range of the spindle assembly. (2) Spindle Bearings. Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

The tool magazine for storing tools has a large capacity; it can be installed on the side or top of the spindle box, or as an independent component outside the machine tool, with tools transported by a handling device. Compared with the turret spindle head, the automatic tool changing system with a tool magazine ensures that the CNC machine tool's spindle box has only one spindle, allowing the spindle component design to fully enhance its rigidity, thus meeting the requirements of precision machining. In addition, the tool magazine can store a large number of tools, enabling multi-process machining of complex parts, which significantly improves the machine's adaptability and processing efficiency. Therefore, automatic tool changing devices with tool magazines are particularly suitable for CNC drilling, milling, and boring machines. 2. Tool magazine. The tool magazine is the main component of the automatic tool changing device; its capacity, layout, and specific structure have a great impact on the design of CNC machine tools. Depending on the required capacity and tool retrieval method, tool magazines can be designed in various forms. Figure 8-59 lists the most commonly used types. Figures 8-59a to d show single-disk tool magazines. To adapt to the machine tool spindle layout, the tool axes in the magazine can be configured in different directions (as shown in Figures 8-59a to c). Figure 8-59d shows a disk tool magazine where tools can be flipped 90 degrees; this structure simplifies the tool retrieval action. The single-disk tool magazine has a simple structure, typically holding 15 to 30 tools, and tool retrieval is relatively convenient, making it the most widely used. Figure 8-59e is a drum-type (also known as hedgehog-type) tool magazine, which is very compact and offers a larger capacity within the same space, but the tool selection and retrieval actions are more complex. Figure 8-59f is a chain-type tool magazine, which provides great structural flexibility, can store a large number of tools, and makes tool selection and retrieval very simple. For long chains, the number of supporting sprockets can be increased to fold and loop the chain, improving space utilization. Figures 8-59g and 8-59h show multi-disk and grid-type tool magazines respectively. Although they are compact, their tool selection and retrieval actions are complex, so they are rarely used. The typical capacity of these tool magazines is 10 to 60 tools, but with the development of machining technology, there seems to be a trend toward even larger capacities. The chain-type tool magazine is one of the more frequently used forms. In this magazine, tool pockets are fixed on the chain links. A commonly used type is the single-row chain-type tool magazine, as shown in Figure 8-60a, generally storing fewer than 30 tools, occasionally up to 60. If a further increase in storage capacity is needed, a multi-row chain-type tool magazine can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60b; or a chain-type tool magazine with an extended chain can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60c. 3. Tool changing methods. In the automatic tool changing device of a CNC machine, the mechanism that transfers and loads/unloads tools between the tool magazine and the machine spindle is called the tool exchange device. Tool exchange methods in CNC machines are generally divided into two categories: tool changing without a manipulator and tool changing with a manipulator. (1) Tool changing without a manipulator. A tool changing system without a manipulator generally involves placing the tool magazine at a position the machine spindle can reach, or moving the entire magazine (or a specific tool position) to a location accessible by the spindle box. Additionally, the tool storage direction in the magazine is generally consistent with the tool loading direction on the spindle. During a tool change, the spindle moves to the changing position on the magazine and directly retrieves or returns the tool. For example, in the machining center shown in Figure 2-59, the tool change sequence is as follows: ① According to the tool change command, the machine worktable quickly moves to the right, moving the workpiece away from under the spindle, and the tool magazine moves under the spindle, aligning an empty tool pocket with the spindle. ② The spindle box descends, placing the used tool from the spindle into the empty pocket of the tool magazine. ③ The spindle box ascends, and the tool magazine rotates to align the tool required for the next step with the spindle. ④ The spindle box descends, inserting the tool into the machine spindle. ⑤ The spindle box and spindle ascend with the tool. ⑥ The machine worktable quickly returns to the left, the tool magazine moves away from under the spindle, and the workpiece moves under the spindle, aligning the tool with the machining surface of the workpiece. ⑦ The spindle box descends, and the tool on the spindle machines the workpiece. ⑧ After machining, the spindle box ascends, and the tool retracts from the workpiece. Tool changing without a manipulator has a relatively simple structure but involves cumbersome actions, long changing times, and relatively small magazine capacities. (2) Tool changing with a manipulator. In machining centers, using a manipulator (tool changing arm) for tool exchange is the most widely applied method because it requires short tool changing times and offers flexible actions. They feature low friction (0.003-0.005), flexible movement, consistent dynamic/static friction (no stick-slip), high preloaded rigidity, long life, high precision, and easy grease lubrication. Widely used in precision/CNC machines, their main drawback is poor impact resistance and sensitivity to dust, requiring good protection. They can be installed horizontally, vertically, or inclined, and parallel installations are common. Their error-averaging effect reduces base installation errors to about 1/3 in slider movement. Guideway and slider fixing methods include setscrews, wedges, or pressure plates. Installation requires thorough cleaning, checking for burrs/rust, and ensuring screw holes align perfectly to prevent accuracy loss. Installation involves gently bolting the guideway against the reference side, tightening side devices, placing the slider, and tightening screws diagonally. Post-installation checks ensure smooth, consistent resistance and proper straightness/parallelism. 3. Liquid Hydrostatic Guideways. (1) Basic principles. These guideways use pressurized oil pumped through restrictors into oil pockets, forming a load-bearing oil film that separates contacting surfaces (liquid friction). They offer low friction (0.001-0.005), high efficiency, long precision retention, excellent vibration absorption, and no low-speed stick-slip, but require complex, costly dedicated oil supply systems. Open types only bear vertical loads, while closed types have oil pockets on all surfaces to resist large overturning moments and increase rigidity. Oil supplies are constant pressure or constant flow. Oil must be filtered to 10μm and kept absolutely clean. (2) Guideway clearance and restrictor forms. 1) Guideway clearance represents oil film thickness. Larger clearances increase flow but reduce rigidity and cause drift; smaller clearances increase rigidity but are limited by geometric accuracy. Small/medium machines use 0.01-0.025mm unloaded clearances; large machines use 0.03-0.08mm. 2) Restrictor forms include constant pressure and quantitative systems. Large machines often use single-cavity single-pump quantitative systems for maximum rigidity without restrictors. Constant pressure systems use capillary restrictors (often adjustable spiral grooves, combined for compactness, used in small/medium machines) or membrane feedback restrictors (single/double-sided, used for heavy, unevenly loaded large machines). Each oil pocket requires its own restrictor control. 8.3.2 Common Faults of Guideways and Their Diagnosis and Maintenance Methods. Guideway clearance, rolling guideway preload, straightness, parallelism, lubrication, and protection are critical for machine operation and machining quality. 1. Common repair methods include scraping, fine planing, and grinding. (1) Fine planing is used for heavy machines or deep scratches, heavily dependent on the planer's accuracy. (2) Scraping requires multiple measurements to map wear curves, using equal-height blocks, parallel straightedges, and frame levels to establish scraping reference points every fixed distance, followed by sectioned rough and fine scraping until the entire surface is flat and straight. (3) Grinding can use a "one-time grinding method" where all surfaces are measured for unevenness, rough ground to remove peaks, and fine ground in one setup. The sequence should prioritize associated/high-precision, complex, large, and difficult-to-machine surfaces first. 2. Common problems in guideway repair and their elimination. (1) Guideway scoring/scratches: Caused by foundation settling (requires regular leveling), prolonged short workpiece machining (requires varying installation positions or repairing accuracy), poor lubrication (adjust oil volume/pressure), poor material (treat with electroplating, induction hardening, or add zinc-aluminum-copper alloy plates), poor scraping quality (improve quality), or poor maintenance (enhance care and protection). (2) Moving parts sticking or not moving: Caused by surface scratches (polish with 180-grit sandpaper), pressure plate scratches (remove and adjust clearance), or gibs adjusted too tight (loosen anti-loose screws, adjust gib bolts for flexible movement ensuring a 0.03mm feeler gauge cannot enter, then lock). (3) Uneven machining surfaces at tool joints: Caused by poor guideway straightness (adjust/scrape to within 0.015mm/500mm), loose or excessively bent table gibs (adjust clearance, ensure natural bending <0.05mm/full length), poor machine levelness bending the guideway (adjust installation level/verticality to within 0.02mm/1000mm), rough guideway surfaces or uneven/insufficient scraping contact points (remove table, polish burrs with oilstone/sandpaper, reassemble, and polish manually with chromium oxide and kerosene), tapered bed guideways causing uneven tightness (repair geometric accuracy), temperature changes deforming guideways (adjust seasonally, keep precision machine rooms at constant temperatures), wear losing accuracy (re-scrape/repair), improper oil viscosity or dirty oil causing poor lubrication (use proper viscosity and keep clean), or poor surface lubrication structure increasing resistance (break the full guideway surface into fragmented dot contacts; for large surfaces, divide the saddle guideway into three sections, making the contact points heavier at the outer thirds and lighter in the middle third).

Instance 2: For the CNC machine in Instance 1, during the tool change process when the spindle moves up to the tool claw, there is a misalignment of the magazine tool claw, and a noticeable noise occurs when pulling/inserting the tool, as if it is jamming. Fault analysis and processing: Misalignment of the magazine tool claw indicates that the magazine zero point may have shifted, or there is clearance in the magazine transmission, or the weight of the tools in the magazine is unbalanced, causing it to lean to one side. Because the tool insertion and pulling are unsmooth, it is estimated that the magazine zero point has shifted. Unload all tools from the magazine, manually crank the spindle to near the second reference point of the Y-axis, and use a feeler gauge to measure the gap between the magazine tool claw and the spindle drive key, confirming the shift. Pushing and pulling the magazine by hand cannot utilize the gap to correct it. Adjust parameter 7508 until the gaps between the magazine tool claw and the spindle drive key are basically equal; after restarting, tool changes execute normally. Instance 3: A VMC-65A machining center, after six months of use, experienced loose spindle tool pulling without any alarm information. Fault analysis and processing: The reasons a spindle fails to pull a tool tightly include: deformed or damaged spindle pulling disc springs; the pulling cylinder action not fully completing; or a loose threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet. Upon inspection, it was found that the threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet was loose, causing the tool holder collet to rotate with tool insertion/extraction and retract by about 1.5mm. This machine's pull stud and tool holder collet had no anti-loosening locking measures. When inserting/pulling tools, if the tool center deviates slightly from the spindle taper hole center, eccentric friction occurs between the tool holder collet and the tool holder. Under the combined action of this friction and impact, the thread loosens over time, resulting in the spindle's failure to hold the tool. After locking the threaded connection between the spindle pull stud and the tool holder collet with thread-locking sealant and tightening the lock nut, the fault was eliminated. Instance 4: The tool change system of a CNC machine did not actuate when executing a tool change command; the manipulator arm stopped mid-stroke, and the CRT displayed an alarm number. Checking the manual revealed this alarm number indicated that the tool change system manipulator position detection switch signal was '0' and 'magazine tool change position error'. Fault analysis and processing: Based on the alarm content, it can be diagnosed that the fault occurred in both the tool exchange device and the tool magazine. Because the corresponding position detection switches sent no signals to the PLC input interface, the machine interrupted the tool change. Causes for the switch having no output signal could include inductive switch failure or hydraulic/mechanical issues preventing complete actions. First, use a thin iron sheet to induce the proximity switch in the magazine to rule out the possibility of the magazine's proximity switch failing. Next, check the 'arm extended' switch SQ21 and 'arm retracted' switch SQ22 in the tool change device's manipulator. Since the arm stopped mid-stroke, the output signals of both switches were '0'; testing showed both switches were normal. Manually actuating the 'arm retract' solenoid valve Y21 to return the manipulator to the 'arm retracted' position restored the machine to normal, indicating that the manually controlled solenoid valve could position the tool exchange device, thus ruling out hydraulic or mechanical resistance causing the incomplete action. From the above analysis, the PLC input signals were normal, and the output action execution was correct, so the problem lay within the PLC or improper operation. Observation during operation revealed that the interval between two tool changes was less than the PLC's required time, causing an error in the PLC program execution and leading to the fault. For alarms with only numbers and no text, one must check the data bits, compare them with normal data, clarify the meaning of the data bit, and take corresponding measures. Spindle heating. (1) Front and rear spindle bearings are damaged or bearings are not clean. Elimination method: Replace bad bearings, clean out dirt. (2) Spindle bearing preload is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the preload. (3) Lubricating oil is dirty or contains impurities. Elimination method: Clean the spindle box, replace the lubricating oil. (4) The spindle front end cover and the spindle box body gland are galled. Elimination method: Grind the spindle box front end cover so that it presses tightly against the spindle front bearing, leaving a clearance of 0.02-0.05mm between the bearing and the cover. (5) Bearing lubricating grease is depleted or there is too much lubricating grease. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. 2. The spindle stops during heavy cutting. (1) The belt connecting the motor and the spindle is too loose. Elimination method: Move the motor base, tension the belt, and then retighten the motor base. (2) There is oil on the surface of the belt. Elimination method: Wash with gasoline and wipe clean before reinstalling. (3) The friction clutch is adjusted too loosely or is worn. Elimination method: Adjust the clutch, grind or replace the friction plates. (4) The belt has been used for too long and failed. Elimination method: Replace with a new belt. 3. Spindle noise. (1) Lack of lubrication. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. (2) Poor transmission balance between the small pulley and the large pulley. Elimination method: The balance weight on the pulley has fallen off; perform dynamic balancing again. (3) Bearings are scored or damaged. Elimination method: Replace the bearings. (4) Poor balance of parts at the end of the shaft. Elimination method: Redo dynamic balancing. (5) Gear meshing clearance is uneven or gears are damaged. Elimination method: Adjust the meshing clearance or replace with new gears. (6) The transmission bearing is damaged or the transmission shaft is bent. Elimination method: Repair or replace the bearing, straighten the transmission shaft. 4. Spindle has no lubricating oil circulation or insufficient lubrication. (1) The hydraulic pump rotation direction is incorrect, or the clearance is too large. Elimination method: Change the hydraulic pump rotation direction, repair the hydraulic pump. (2) The suction pipe is not inserted below the oil level of the oil tank. Elimination method: Insert the suction pipe 2/3 below the oil level. (3) Oil pipes or filters are blocked. Elimination method: Eliminate the blockage. (4) Lubricating oil pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply pressure. 5. Lubricating oil leakage. (1) The amount of lubricating oil is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply amount. (2) Check whether seals in various places are damaged. Elimination method: Replace seals. (3) Pipe fittings are damaged. Elimination method: Replace pipe fittings. 6. Tool cannot be clamped. (1) Belleville spring displacement is small. Elimination method: Adjust the stroke length of the Belleville spring. (2) Spring collet is damaged. Elimination method: Replace the spring collet. (3) Belleville spring failure. Elimination method: Replace the Belleville spring. (4) The pull stud on the tool holder is too large. Elimination method: Replace the pull stud and install it correctly. (5) Check whether the nut on the tool unclamp/clamp spring is loose. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the clamp spring clockwise so that its maximum working load is 13kN. 7. Tool cannot be unclamped after being clamped. (1) Unclamp spring is compressed too tightly. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the unclamp spring counterclockwise so that its maximum working load does not exceed 13kN. (2) Hydraulic cylinder pressure and stroke are insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust hydraulic pressure and piston stroke switch. 8. Spindle fails to change speeds. (1) Shifting hydraulic cylinder pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Detect working pressure; if lower than rated pressure, adjust it. (2) Shifting hydraulic cylinder is worn or stuck. Elimination method: Remove burrs or galling, clean and reassemble. (3) Shifting hydraulic cylinder fork has fallen off. Elimination method: Repair or replace. (4) Shifting hydraulic cylinder bypasses oil or leaks internally. Elimination method: Replace seal ring. (5) Shifting solenoid valve is stuck. Elimination method: Repair the solenoid valve and clean it. (6) Shifting composite switch has failed. Elimination method: Replace the switch. 8.1.3 Spindle Component Fault Maintenance Examples. Example 7: The spindle of an XK5040-1 could not rotate after starting up. Fault cause analysis and elimination: Checking the motor, the condition was good; the transmission key was not damaged. After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

8.3 Common Fault Analysis of Guideways. The quality of guideways has a great impact on the rigidity, machining accuracy, and service life of machine tools. As an important part of the machine tool feed system, CNC machine tools have higher requirements for guideways than ordinary machine tools. The basic requirements for guideways are as follows: ① High guiding accuracy. Guiding accuracy mainly refers to the straightness or roundness of moving parts when moving along the guideway. The main factors affecting guiding accuracy include the geometric accuracy of the guideway, contact accuracy of the guideway, structural form of the guideway, rigidity and thermal deformation of the moving and supporting guideways, assembly quality, and the stiffness of the oil film between hydrodynamic and hydrostatic guideways. ② Sufficient rigidity. Guideway rigidity refers to the ability of the guideway to resist deformation under dynamic and static loads. The guideway must have sufficient rigidity to ensure that it does not undergo excessive deformation under static loads, thereby ensuring the relative position and guiding accuracy between various components. ③ Good friction characteristics. The long-term operation of the moving guideway along the supporting guideway surface will cause uneven wear, destroy the guiding accuracy of the guideway, and thus affect the machining accuracy of the machine tool. The wear forms of guideways include abrasive wear, galling and thermal welding, fatigue, and crushing. ④ Smoothness of low-speed movement. When moving at low speeds, the moving guideway, acting as a moving component, is prone to stick-slip (crawling) phenomena.
