ening nut of the Z-axis screw, the effect was not obvious. Later, the Z-axis guide rail taper jib was adjusted, the machine load was significantly reduced, and the fault was eliminated.

8.3 Common Fault Analysis of Guideways. The quality of guideways has a great impact on the rigidity, machining accuracy, and service life of machine tools. As an important part of the machine tool feed system, CNC machine tools have higher requirements for guideways than ordinary machine tools. The basic requirements for guideways are as follows: ① High guiding accuracy. Guiding accuracy mainly refers to the straightness or roundness of moving parts when moving along the guideway. The main factors affecting guiding accuracy include the geometric accuracy of the guideway, contact accuracy of the guideway, structural form of the guideway, rigidity and thermal deformation of the moving and supporting guideways, assembly quality, and the stiffness of the oil film between hydrodynamic and hydrostatic guideways. ② Sufficient rigidity. Guideway rigidity refers to the ability of the guideway to resist deformation under dynamic and static loads. The guideway must have sufficient rigidity to ensure that it does not undergo excessive deformation under static loads, thereby ensuring the relative position and guiding accuracy between various components. ③ Good friction characteristics. The long-term operation of the moving guideway along the supporting guideway surface will cause uneven wear, destroy the guiding accuracy of the guideway, and thus affect the machining accuracy of the machine tool. The wear forms of guideways include abrasive wear, galling and thermal welding, fatigue, and crushing. ④ Smoothness of low-speed movement. When moving at low speeds, the moving guideway, acting as a moving component, is prone to stick-slip (crawling) phenomena. The stick-slip of feed motion will reduce workpiece accuracy, so it is required that the guideway moves smoothly at low speeds without stick-slip, which is especially important for high-precision machine tools. ⑤ Good damping characteristics (no vibration at high speeds). ⑥ Good structural manufacturability. 8.3.1 Structural Characteristics and Adjustment of Guideways. Currently, the guideways used in CNC machine tools are mainly of three types: sliding guideways, rolling guideways, and hydrostatic guideways. 1. Sliding Guideways. (1) Types of sliding guideways. The magnitude of rigidity, ease of manufacturing, adjustability, minimization of friction loss, and the ability to maintain initial precision of sliding guideways largely depend on their cross-sectional shapes (as shown in Figure 8-37). 1) Inverted-V (mountain-shaped) and V-shaped cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37a, this type of cross-section has high guiding accuracy, and after wear, it automatically compensates by sinking under its own weight. A convex lower guideway is conducive to discharging dirt but does not easily retain oil, often used in lathes; a concave lower guideway is the opposite, often used in grinders with a top angle generally at 90°. 2) Rectangular cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37b, this type is convenient to manufacture and repair, has a large load-bearing capacity, and new guideways have high guiding accuracy. However, it cannot automatically compensate after wear and requires gib adjustment, which affects guiding accuracy. 3) Cylindrical cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37c, this type is easy to manufacture and can achieve precision fits, but it is highly sensitive to temperature changes, easily jamming when clearances are small, and having poor guiding accuracy when clearances are large. Compared to the other cross-sections, it is less commonly used. 4) Flat annular cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37d, this type is suitable for rotary motion, easy to manufacture, and can withstand large axial forces, but guiding accuracy is relatively poor. Switching to a conical annular cross-section (Figure 8-37e) provides better guiding performance. 5) Dovetail cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37f, this type has a compact structure and can withstand overturning moments, but its rigidity is relatively poor, and manufacturing and maintenance are inconvenient. It is suitable for situations where guiding accuracy requirements are not excessively high. (2) Surface treatment of sliding guideways. The materials used for sliding guideways in CNC machine tools are cast iron attached with plastic or steel-inlaid attached with plastic. Commonly used guideway plastics include PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) soft tapes and epoxy-based wear-resistant coatings. 1) Characteristics of PTFE guideway soft tapes: ① Good friction characteristics: The dynamic and static friction coefficients of the metal-PTFE soft tape are basically consistent. ② Good wear resistance: The PTFE soft tape material contains bronze, copper disulfide, and graphite, so it has self-lubricating properties and does not require high-quality lubricating oil. In addition, the plastic is soft, so even if metal chips and dust are embedded, it will not damage the metal guideway surface and the soft tape itself, prolonging the service life of the guideway pair. ③ Good vibration damping: The damping performance of plastic is good, resulting in effective vibration reduction and noise elimination, which helps improve movement speed. ④ Good manufacturability: It lowers the hardness and surface quality requirements for the metal substrate to which the plastic is bonded, and the plastic is easy to process (milling, planing, grinding, scraping), allowing the guideway pair contact surface to achieve excellent surface quality. PTFE soft tapes are widely used in the motion guideways of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools. The application process is simple: first, machine the bonding surface to a roughness of

sliders, steel balls, retainers, and end caps. Sliders move along the fixed guideway, with balls rolling in circular arc grooves and circulating through end caps. They feature low friction (0.003-0.005), flexible movement, consistent dynamic/static friction (no stick-slip), high preloaded rigidity, long life, high precision, and easy grease lubrication. Widely used in precision/CNC machines, their main drawback is poor impact resistance and sensitivity to dust, requiring good protection. They can be installed horizontally, vertically, or inclined, and parallel installations are common. Their error-averaging effect reduces base installation errors to about 1/3 in slider movement. Guideway and slider fixing methods include setscrews, wedges, or pressure plates. Installation requires thorough cleaning, checking for burrs/rust, and ensuring screw holes align perfectly to prevent accuracy loss. Installation involves gently bolting the guideway against the reference side, tightening side devices, placing the slider, and tightening screws diagonally. Post-installation checks ensure smooth, consistent resistance and proper straightness/parallelism. 3. Liquid Hydrostatic Guideways. (1) Basic principles. These guideways use pressurized oil pumped through restrictors into oil pockets, forming a load-bearing oil film that separates contacting surfaces (liquid friction). They offer low friction (0.001-0.005), high efficiency, long precision retention, excellent vibration absorption, and no low-speed stick-slip, but require complex, costly dedicated oil supply systems. Open types only bear vertical loads, while closed types have oil pockets on all surfaces to resist large overturning moments and increase rigidity. Oil supplies are constant pressure or constant flow. Oil must be filtered to 10μm and kept absolutely clean. (2) Guideway clearance and restrictor forms. 1) Guideway clearance represents oil film thickness. Larger clearances increase flow but reduce rigidity and cause drift; smaller clearances increase rigidity but are limited by geometric accuracy. Small/medium machines use 0.01-0.025mm unloaded clearances; large machines use 0.03-0.08mm. 2) Restrictor forms include constant pressure and quantitative systems. Large machines often use single-cavity single-pump quantitative systems for maximum rigidity without restrictors. Constant pressure systems use capillary restrictors (often adjustable spiral grooves, combined for compactness, used in small/medium machines) or membrane feedback restrictors (single/double-sided, used for heavy, unevenly loaded large machines). Each oil pocket requires its own restrictor control. 8.3.2 Common Faults of Guideways and Their Diagnosis and Maintenance Methods. Guideway clearance, rolling guideway preload, straightness, parallelism, lubrication, and protection are critical for machine operation and machining quality. 1. Common repair methods include scraping, fine planing, and grinding. (1) Fine planing is used for heavy machines or deep scratches, heavily dependent on the planer's accuracy. (2) Scraping requires multiple measurements to map wear curves, using equal-height blocks, parallel straightedges, and frame levels to establish scraping reference points every fixed distance, followed by sectioned rough and fine scraping until the entire surface is flat and straight. (3) Grinding can use a "one-time grinding method" where all surfaces are measured for unevenness, rough ground to remove peaks, and fine ground in one setup. The sequence should prioritize associated/high-precision, complex, large, and difficult-to-machine surfaces first. 2. Common problems in guideway repair and their elimination. (1) Guideway scoring/scratches: Caused by foundation settling (requires regular leveling), prolonged short workpiece machining (requires varying installation positions or repairing accuracy), poor lubrication (adjust oil volume/pressure), poor material (treat with electroplating, induction hardening, or add zinc-aluminum-copper alloy plates), poor scraping quality (improve quality), or poor maintenance (enhance care and protection). (2) Moving parts sticking or not moving: Caused by surface scratches (polish with 180-grit sandpaper), pressure plate scratches (remove and adjust clearance), or gibs adjusted too tight (loosen anti-loose screws, adjust gib bolts for flexible movement ensuring a 0.03mm feeler gauge cannot enter, then lock). (3) Uneven machining surfaces at tool joints: Caused by poor guideway straightness (adjust/scrape to within 0.015mm/500mm), loose or excessively bent table gibs (adjust clearance, ensure natural bending <0.05mm/full length), poor machine levelness bending the guideway (adjust installation level/verticality to within 0.02mm/1000mm), rough guideway surfaces or uneven/insufficient scraping contact points (remove table, polish burrs with oilstone/sandpaper, reassemble, and polish manually with chromium oxide and kerosene), tapered bed guideways causing uneven tightness (repair geometric accuracy), temperature changes deforming guideways (adjust seasonally, keep precision machine rooms at constant temperatures), wear losing accuracy (re-scrape/repair), improper oil viscosity or dirty oil causing poor lubrication (use proper viscosity and keep clean), or poor surface lubrication structure increasing resistance (break the full guideway surface into fragmented dot contacts; for large surfaces, divide the saddle guideway into three sections, making the contact points heavier at the outer thirds and lighter in the middle third).

The tool magazine for storing tools has a large capacity; it can be installed on the side or top of the spindle box, or as an independent component outside the machine tool, with tools transported by a handling device. Compared with the turret spindle head, the automatic tool changing system with a tool magazine ensures that the CNC machine tool's spindle box has only one spindle, allowing the spindle component design to fully enhance its rigidity, thus meeting the requirements of precision machining. In addition, the tool magazine can store a large number of tools, enabling multi-process machining of complex parts, which significantly improves the machine's adaptability and processing efficiency. Therefore, automatic tool changing devices with tool magazines are particularly suitable for CNC drilling, milling, and boring machines. 2. Tool magazine. The tool magazine is the main component of the automatic tool changing device; its capacity, layout, and specific structure have a great impact on the design of CNC machine tools. Depending on the required capacity and tool retrieval method, tool magazines can be designed in various forms. Figure 8-59 lists the most commonly used types. Figures 8-59a to d show single-disk tool magazines. To adapt to the machine tool spindle layout, the tool axes in the magazine can be configured in different directions (as shown in Figures 8-59a to c). Figure 8-59d shows a disk tool magazine where tools can be flipped 90 degrees; this structure simplifies the tool retrieval action. The single-disk tool magazine has a simple structure, typically holding 15 to 30 tools, and tool retrieval is relatively convenient, making it the most widely used. Figure 8-59e is a drum-type (also known as hedgehog-type) tool magazine, which is very compact and offers a larger capacity within the same space, but the tool selection and retrieval actions are more complex. Figure 8-59f is a chain-type tool magazine, which provides great structural flexibility, can store a large number of tools, and makes tool selection and retrieval very simple. For long chains, the number of supporting sprockets can be increased to fold and loop the chain, improving space utilization. Figures 8-59g and 8-59h show multi-disk and grid-type tool magazines respectively. Although they are compact, their tool selection and retrieval actions are complex, so they are rarely used. The typical capacity of these tool magazines is 10 to 60 tools, but with the development of machining technology, there seems to be a trend toward even larger capacities. Figure 8-59 Common tool magazine forms: a) Single-disk magazine 1; b) Single-disk magazine 2; c) Single-disk magazine 3; d) Single-disk magazine 4; e) Drum-type magazine; f) Chain-type magazine; g) Multi-disk magazine; h) Grid-type magazine. The chain-type tool magazine is one of the more frequently used forms. In this magazine, tool pockets are fixed on the chain links. A commonly used type is the single-row chain-type tool magazine, as shown in Figure 8-60a, generally storing fewer than 30 tools, occasionally up to 60. If a further increase in storage capacity is needed, a multi-row chain-type tool magazine can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60b; or a chain-type tool magazine with an extended chain can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60c. 3. Tool changing methods. In the automatic tool changing device of a CNC machine, the mechanism that transfers and loads/unloads tools between the tool magazine and the machine spindle is called the tool exchange device. Tool exchange methods in CNC machines are generally divided into two categories: tool changing without a manipulator and tool changing with a manipulator. (1) Tool changing without a manipulator. A tool changing system without a manipulator generally involves placing the tool magazine at a position the machine spindle can reach, or moving the entire magazine (or a specific tool position) to a location accessible by the spindle box. Additionally, the tool storage direction in the magazine is generally consistent with the tool loading direction on the spindle. During a tool change, the spindle moves to the changing position on the magazine and directly retrieves or returns the tool. For example, in the machining center shown in Figure 2-59, the tool change sequence is as follows: ① According to the tool change command, the machine worktable quickly moves to the right, moving the workpiece away from under the spindle, and the tool magazine moves under the spindle, aligning an empty tool pocket with the spindle. ② The spindle box descends, placing the used tool from the spindle into the empty pocket of the tool magazine. ③ The spindle box ascends, and the tool magazine rotates to align the tool required for the next step with the spindle. ④ The spindle box descends, inserting the tool into the machine spindle. ⑤ The spindle box and spindle ascend with the tool. ⑥ The machine worktable quickly returns to the left, the tool magazine moves away from under the spindle, and the workpiece moves under the spindle, aligning the tool with the machining surface of the workpiece. ⑦ The spindle box descends, and the tool on the spindle machines the workpiece. ⑧ After machining, the spindle box ascends, and the tool retracts from the workpiece. Tool changing without a manipulator has a relatively simple structure but involves cumbersome actions, long changing times, and relatively small magazine capacities. (2) Tool changing with a manipulator. In machining centers, using a manipulator (tool changing arm) for tool exchange is the most widely applied method because it requires short tool changing times and offers flexible actions. Then check the magazine zero return switch and the magazine motor cable, which are found to be normal. Restart the machine, and the zero return is normal; tool changes in MDI mode are also normal. Suspecting interference, the grounding wire was addressed, and the fault never occurred again. Instance 2: For the CNC machine in Instance 1, during the tool change process when the spindle moves up to the tool claw, there is a misalignment of the magazine tool claw, and a noticeable noise occurs when pulling/inserting the tool, as if it is jamming. Fault analysis and processing: Misalignment of the magazine tool claw indicates that the magazine zero point may have shifted, or there is clearance in the magazine transmission, or the weight of the tools in the magazine is unbalanced, causing it to lean to one side. Because the tool insertion and pulling are unsmooth, it is estimated that the magazine zero point has shifted. Unload all tools from the magazine, manually crank the spindle to near the second reference point of the Y-axis, and use a feeler gauge to measure the gap between the magazine tool claw and the spindle drive key, confirming the shift. Pushing and pulling the magazine by hand cannot utilize the gap to correct it. Adjust parameter 7508 until the gaps between the magazine tool claw and the spindle drive key are basically equal; after restarting, tool changes execute normally. Instance 3: A VMC-65A machining center, after six months of use, experienced loose spindle tool pulling without any alarm information. Fault analysis and processing: The reasons a spindle fails to pull a tool tightly include: deformed or damaged spindle pulling disc springs; the pulling cylinder action not fully completing; or a loose threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet. Upon inspection, it was found that the threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet was loose, causing the tool holder collet to rotate with tool insertion/extraction and retract by about 1.5mm. This machine's pull stud and tool holder collet had no anti-loosening locking measures. When inserting/pulling tools, if the tool center deviates slightly from the spindle taper hole center, eccentric friction occurs between the tool holder collet and the tool holder. Under the combined action of this friction and impact, the thread loosens over time, resulting in the spindle's failure to hold the tool. After locking the threaded connection between the spindle pull stud and the tool holder collet with thread-locking sealant and tightening the lock nut, the fault was eliminated. Instance 4: The tool change system of a CNC machine did not actuate when executing a tool change command; the manipulator arm stopped mid-stroke, and the CRT displayed an alarm number. Checking the manual revealed this alarm number indicated that the tool change system manipulator position detection switch signal was '0' and 'magazine tool change position error'. Fault analysis and processing: Based on the alarm content, it can be diagnosed that the fault occurred in both the tool exchange device and the tool magazine. Because the corresponding position detection switches sent no signals to the PLC input interface, the machine interrupted the tool change. Causes for the switch having no output signal could include inductive switch failure or hydraulic/mechanical issues preventing complete actions. First, use a thin iron sheet to induce the proximity switch in the magazine to rule out the possibility of the magazine's proximity switch failing. Next, check the 'arm extended' switch SQ21 and 'arm retracted' switch SQ22 in the tool change device's manipulator. Since the arm stopped mid-stroke, the output signals of both switches were '0'; testing showed both switches were normal. Manually actuating the 'arm retract' solenoid valve Y21 to return the manipulator to the 'arm retracted' position restored the machine to normal, indicating that the manually controlled solenoid valve could position the tool exchange device, thus ruling out hydraulic or mechanical resistance causing the incomplete action. From the above analysis, the PLC input signals were normal, and the output action execution was correct, so the problem lay within the PLC or improper operation. Observation during operation revealed that the interval between two tool changes was less than the PLC's required time, causing an error in the PLC program execution and leading to the fault. For alarms with only numbers and no text, one must check the data bits, compare them with normal data, clarify the meaning of the data bit, and take corresponding measures. Instance 5: In a vertical machining center, when the tool change arm translates to C, there is no tool pulling action; its schematic is shown in Figure 8-66. Fault analysis and processing: Observing the mechanical motion process, the initial state of the ATC action is: the spindle holds the old tool to be exchanged; the tool change arm is at position B; the tool change arm is in the upper position; the tool magazine has positioned the new tool to be exchanged. The automatic tool change sequence is: Tool change arm moves left (B to A) -> Tool change arm descends (pulls tool from magazine) -> Tool change arm moves right (A to B) -> Tool change arm ascends -> Tool change arm moves right (B to C, grasps tool in spindle) -> Spindle hydraulic cylinder descends (releases tool) -> Tool change arm descends (pulls tool from spindle) -> Tool change arm rotates 180 degrees (swaps tool positions) -> Tool change arm ascends (inserts tools) -> Spindle hydraulic cylinder ascends (grasps tool) -> Tool change arm moves left (C to B) -> Tool magazine rotates (finds old tool position) -> Tool change arm moves left (B to A, returns old tool to magazine) -> Tool change arm

switch has failed. Elimination method: Replace the switch. 8.1.3 Spindle Component Fault Maintenance Examples. Example 1: In a machining center, the spindle motor vibrates enormously when the spindle speed is 600r/min, and the entire spindle head vibrates; at 1500r/min, the swing amplitude decreases, but the vibration frequency increases; when the spindle is rotating at high speed and the power is cut off, the motor continues to vibrate during the coasting process, proving it to be a non-electrical fault; disconnecting the transmission belt between the motor and the spindle and starting the motor, the vibration still exists. Analysis and processing: Based on the directly proportional relationship between vibration frequency and speed, it was preliminarily judged as rotor eccentricity or looseness. Disassembling the motor, it was found that the motor rotor bearing seat had worn more than 0.02mm due to the inner ring spinning. Considering that this machine tool had been used for more than ten years, expectations for its performance were not high, plus there was no ready-made rotor for replacement, it was decided to use a spray coating repair method for the bearing seat while replacing the bearing, achieving good results. Example 2: Spindle cannot orient. Fault phenomenon: In a vertical machining center using SINUMERIK 810M equipped with a 6SC6502 spindle drive, during debugging, when the spindle speed was greater than 200r/min, a fault occurred where the spindle could not be positioned. Analysis and processing: To confirm the cause of the fault, the following tests were conducted during maintenance: ① Input and sequentially execute the "S100M03; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ② Input and sequentially execute the "S100M04; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ③ Input and sequentially execute the "S200M03; M05; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ④ Directly input and sequentially execute the "S200M03; M19" command; the machine tool could not position. Based on the above tests, it can be confirmed that the system and drive are working normally. During maintenance, considering the possible cause of the fault could be poor high-speed characteristics of the encoder or excessively high actual positioning speed of the spindle. Checking the actual speed of the spindle motor, it was found that the actual spindle speed of this machine tool differed greatly from the commanded value. When executing the S200 command, the actual machine tool spindle speed was 300r/min. Adjusting the spindle drive parameters to match the actual spindle speed with the commanded value eliminated the fault, and the machine tool returned to normal. Example 3: Automatic process cannot proceed after spindle orientation. Fault phenomenon: In a vertical machining center using SINUMERIK 810M, when executing an automatic tool change command, after the spindle completes orientation (M19), the program stops executing. Analysis and processing: After the machine tool encountered the fault, it could be restored to normal by restarting. When executing a program block without an M19 command, the machine tool ran normally. Therefore, it can be determined that the fault was caused by the M19 spindle directional orientation, meaning the M19 command did not have an execution completion reply (FIN) signal. When checking the M19 status, it was found that the positioning position was correct, and the spindle also had a corresponding holding torque, so abnormal action of the spindle positioning itself could be ruled out. Checking against the machine tool's electrical schematic diagram, to improve the reliability of tool changing, the machine tool was equipped with a spindle in-position contactless switch. The cause of the fault was the damage to this switch, which prevented the generation of the M19 reply (FIN) signal. After replacing the switch, the machine tool returned to normal. Example 4: A vertical CNC milling machine using the SINUMERIK 802D CNC system failed to unload tools after a long period of downtime. This machine tool spindle uses pneumatic cylinders to control the unclamping and clamping of spindle tools and uses proximity switches as cylinder limit switches. Checking the CNC system PLC and output interfaces, they were all normal, and the two proximity switches at the rear also worked normally, but the rear cylinder had no action when unclamping the tool. Pressing the manual switch of the solenoid valve controlling the cylinder action, the sound of spraying air could be heard. Checking the machine tool air pump, the working pressure was normal, but there was no oil in the machine tool's lubricator. It was preliminarily judged that the fault was caused by the cylinder jamming, making the spindle unable to unclamp the tool. Disassembling the rear cylinder and opening it, it was found that the cylinder piston and cylinder wall were severely rusted and could not be separated. Later, after soaking in a rust remover for a week to remove the rust spots and reassembling the machine tool, tool loading and unloading returned to normal. Analysis of the cause of the fault: Although it was directly caused by the rusting of the cylinder, the fundamental cause of the fault was the lack of oil in the lubricator, preventing the piston from being lubricated. Long-term parking caused moisture in the compressed air to condense and rust on the cylinder wall and piston. Example 5: The roundness error of the bearing hole machined on the box by an NC800 horizontal machining center was 0.045mm. After ruling out the influence of other factors, the tool unclamping mechanism was inspected. First, the hydraulic system pressure was adjusted, gradually reducing it from the system setting of 6.3MPa, inspecting the tool unclamping situation for every 0.5MPa drop to see if unclamping was in place. When the pressure dropped to 4MP

, 2, and the inner spacer after pressing, excessive preload force will cause the bearings to heat up. If there is no torque measuring device, slightly dampening feeling when turning the spindle by hand is sufficient. Thereafter, testing and on-site cutting proved this method to be feasible. When boring the same ϕ80mm hole, the roundness error was reduced from 0.03mm to 0.005mm, fully meeting the machining requirements of the part. Example 7: The spindle of an XK5040-1 could not rotate after starting up. Fault cause analysis and elimination: Checking the motor, the condition was good; the transmission key was not damaged. After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

8.2 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Feed Drive Components The feed drive component is the main part of the servo feed system, mainly composed of a transmission mechanism, motion conversion mechanism, guiding mechanism, and executing component. It is the actuator that provides the motion and power required to realize the forming machining motion. Since the feed motion of CNC machine tools is the direct object of digital control, the final positional accuracy and contour accuracy of the machined workpiece are related to the transmission accuracy, sensitivity, and stability of the feed motion. In order to ensure the transmission accuracy and working stability of the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, the following requirements should be noted when designing the mechanical transmission device: ① Improve transmission accuracy and rigidity. The accuracy of the CNC machine tool itself, especially the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the feed drive device, plays a key role in the machining accuracy of parts and is a characteristic indicator of CNC machine tools. Therefore, it is first necessary to ensure the machining accuracy of each transmission part

Example 7: The spindle of an XK5040-1 could not rotate after starting up. Fault cause analysis and elimination: Checking the motor, the condition was good; the transmission key was not damaged. After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

8.2 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Feed Drive Components The feed drive component is the main part of the servo feed system, mainly composed of a transmission mechanism, motion conversion mechanism, guiding mechanism, and executing component. It is the actuator that provides the motion and power required to realize the forming machining motion. Since the feed motion of CNC machine tools is the direct object of digital control, the final positional accuracy and contour accuracy of the machined workpiece are related to the transmission accuracy, sensitivity, and stability of the feed motion. In order to ensure the transmission accuracy and working stability of the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, the following requirements should be noted when designing the mechanical transmission device: ① Improve transmission accuracy and rigidity. The accuracy of the CNC machine tool itself, especially the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the feed drive device, plays a key role in the machining accuracy of parts and is a characteristic indicator of CNC machine tools. Therefore, it is first necessary to ensure the machining accuracy of each transmission part

also be mechanisms such as automatic tool clamping devices, spindle orientation devices, and chip removal devices. Structurally, issues such as tool clamping, bearing configuration, bearing clearance adjustment, lubrication, and sealing must be well resolved. (1) Spindle. The spindle is an important part of the spindle transmission structure. Its structural dimensions, shape, manufacturing accuracy, material, and heat treatment have a great impact on the working performance of the spindle component. Spindle structures come in various forms depending on the design requirements of the spindle transmission system. During design, a series of issues must be properly handled, such as the clamping of chucks or tools, spindle unloading, positioning and clearance adjustment of spindle bearings, and sealing and lubrication of spindle components. The main dimensional parameters of the spindle include: spindle diameter, inner hole diameter, overhang length, and support span. The basis for evaluating and considering the main dimensional parameters of the spindle is the rigidity of the spindle, structural manufacturability, and the process application range of the spindle assembly. (2) Spindle Bearings. Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life. ① Preloading of double-row cylindrical roller bearings. This type of bearing relies on the tapered surface of the inner hole to expand the inner ring radially to achieve preloading, so it is called radial preloading. As shown in Figure 8-6a, what measures the amount of preload is the difference Δ = (D1 - D2) between the roller envelope circle diameter D2 and the outer ring raceway diameter D1, which is called the radial preload amount or simply "preload amount", with the unit of μm. During assembly, the outer ring is installed into the housing hole, and D1 is measured. Without installing spacer 1 first, the inner ring is installed on the spindle, as shown in Figure 8-6b. Tighten nut 2, and use a special envelope circle measuring instrument to measure the envelope circle diameter of the rolling elements until it is greater than D1 by Δ, measure distance ε, and grind the thickness of the spacer according to the ε value. Install the spacer and tighten the nut to obtain the predetermined preload amount. ② Preloading of angular contact bearings. This type of bearing achieves preloading by causing axial displacement between the inner and outer rings under the action of axial force Fa0, as shown in Figure 9-6c. What measures the preload is the axial preload force Fa0, referred to as preload force, with the unit of N. Multi-unit angular contact ball bearings are assembled based on preload force; bearing factories specify three levels of preload: light, medium, and heavy, and the preload level can be specified when ordering. Based on the preload force, the bearing factory grinds away an amount σ from the end face of the inner ring (for back-to-back assembly, as shown in Figure 9-6d) or the outer ring (for face-to-face assembly, as shown in Figure 9-6e). When pressed tightly during assembly, the predetermined preload force can be obtained. If a certain distance is required between two bearings, inner and outer spacers of the same thickness can be added between the two bearings. Under the action of axial load, the rolling elements and the raceway of the unloaded side bearing must not separate from contact. The minimum preload force meeting this condition is 35% of the maximum axial load for a duplex configuration (approximately taken as 1/3), and 24% for a triplex configuration (approximately taken as 1/4). 3) Lubrication and sealing of spindle bearings. Good lubrication can reduce the operating temperature of bearings and prolong service life. Sealing not only prevents dust, chips, and cutting fluid from entering, but also prevents the leakage of lubricating oil. ① Lubrication of spindle bearings. On CNC machine tools, spindle bearing lubrication methods include grease lubrication, oil lubrication, oil mist lubrication, and oil-air lubrication. Grease lubrication is currently the most commonly used lubrication method for spindle bearings on CNC machine tools, especially for front support bearings. Of course, if there is no cooling lubricating oil system in the spindle box, the rear support bearings and other bearings generally use grease lubrication. The grease filling amount for spindle bearings is usually 10% of the bearing's spatial volume, and must not be filled arbitrarily, otherwise it will exacerbate spindle heating. When using grease lubrication, effective sealing measures must be taken to prevent cutting fluid or lubricating oil from entering the bearing. Oil lubrication is also one of the common lubrication methods in CNC. Figure 8-7 shows a constant temperature oil lubrication and cooling method. Constant temperature oil controlled by an automatic oil temperature control box enters the spindle box via a hydraulic pump, flows along the spiral groove on the outer ring of the spindle front support sleeve to take away the heat generated by the spindle bearing; another path injects constant temperature oil onto the transmission gears and transmission shaft support bearings via an oil distributor in the spindle box to take away the heat they generate. When using oil lubrication for angular contact ball bearings, attention should be paid to the pumping effect of angular contact, and oil needs to be injected from the small opening of the bearing. Oil mist lubrication is a method where oil is atomized by high-pressure gas and sprayed from a nozzle onto the parts requiring lubrication. Because it is mist-like, the oil has good heat absorption and no oil stirring effect, so it is often used for the lubrication of high-speed spindle bearings. However, oil mist is easily blown out and pollutes the environment. Oil-air lubrication is a new lubrication method developed for high-speed spindles. As shown in Figure 8-8, it feeds a very small amount of oil (8~16 min, about 0.03 cm³) into compressed air, and then blows it into the bearing clearance, thereby lubricating the bearing and suppressing bearing heat. The oil level switch in the oil tank and the pressure switch in the pipeline can automatically cut off the power supply of the main motor when there is no oil in the tank or insufficient pressure. ② Sealing of the spindle. Spindle sealing includes contact sealing and non-contact sealing. Figure 8-9 shows several forms of non-contact sealing. Figure 8-9a utilizes the clearance between the bearing cover and the shaft for sealing; grooving inside the bearing cover hole is to improve the sealing effect. This seal is used in grease-lubricated areas

(4) Braking of Ball Screws The ball screw and nut pair has high transmission efficiency but cannot self-lock. A braking device needs to be provided (especially in vertical transmission or high-speed, large-inertia applications). The most common braking method is the electrical electromagnetic method, that is, the use of an electromagnetic brake, and this brake is located inside the motor. Figure 8-27 is a schematic diagram of the electromagnetic brake of a FANUC servo motor. When the machine tool is working, under the action of the electromagnetic force of the electromagnetic coil 7, the outer gear 8 disengages from the inner gear 9, and the spring is compressed; when stopping or during a power outage, the permanent magnet 5 loses power, and under the restoring force of the spring, gears 8 and 9 mesh, and the inner gear 9 becomes one with the motor end cover, thus braking the screw connected to the motor shaft. This electromagnetic brake is installed inside the motor housing, forming an integrated structure with the motor. (5) Elimination of Axial Clearance and Pre-tensioning of Ball Screw and Nut Pair Figure 8-27 Schematic diagram of servo motor electromagnetic brake 1—Resolver 2—Tachometer generator rotor 3—Tachometer generator stator 4—Brush 5—Permanent magnet 6—Servo motor rotor 7—Electromagnetic coil 8—Outer gear 9—Inner gear The ball screw and nut pair has strict requirements on axial clearance to ensure movement accuracy during reverse motion. The so-called axial clearance refers to the maximum axial movement between the screw and the nut when there is no relative rotation between them. In addition to the structural clearance itself, it also includes the movement caused by elastic deformation after an axial load is applied. Therefore, it is difficult to completely eliminate the axial clearance. The double-nut pre-tensioning method is usually used to control the elastic deformation to a minimum. Currently, there are three common structural forms for double-nut pre-tensioning: 1) Pre-tensioning with a lock nut Figure 8-28 shows a thread-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair. The left and right nuts of the ball screw are connected to the outer sleeve with flat keys. The extended end of the right nut has no flange and is threaded. Using two round nuts 1 and 2, the right nut can be moved axially relative to the screw, and then locked after eliminating the clearance. This adjustment method has the advantages of a compact structure and convenient adjustment, so it is widely used, but the displacement amount is not easily controlled precisely. Figure 8-28 Thread-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair 1—Round nut 2—Lock nut 2) Adjusting clearance by grinding a spacer As shown in Figure 8-29, by grinding and adjusting the thickness of the spacer, the left and right nuts of the ball screw generate axial displacement to achieve pre-tensioning. This method has a simple structure and good rigidity. When adjusting the clearance, the adjusting spacer needs to be removed for grinding. For the convenience of assembly and disassembly, it is best to make the adjusting spacer into a half-ring structure. Figure 8-29 Spacer-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair 3) Differential tooth adjustment Figure 8-30 shows a differential tooth clearance-adjusting ball screw and nut pair. External gears are machined on the ends of the left and right nuts, with the number of teeth being Z1 and Z2 respectively, and Z1 and Z2 differ by one tooth. The two gears mesh with the corresponding internal ring gears at both ends respectively. The internal ring gears are fastened to the nut housing. During pre-tensioning, the two internal ring gears are disengaged, allowing the two nuts to rotate the same number of teeth in the same direction; then the internal ring gears are re-engaged, and the relative axial position of the two nuts changes, thereby achieving the adjustment of the clearance and the application of the pre-tensioning force. Figure 8-30 Differential tooth clearance-adjusting ball screw and nut pair When both gears rotate by one tooth in the same direction, their axial displacement is: s=1/(Z1×Z2) This method allows the relative axial displacement of the two nuts to be as small as 1mm. Its adjustment accuracy is high, accurate, and reliable, but the structure is complex. If the ball screw pair is exposed on the machine tool, a closed protective cover should be used, such

Example 3: Poor protection caused synchronous belt aging and deformation, resulting in feed deviation. Fault Cause Analysis and Elimination: During automatic operation of a CNC lathe, the actual machining size occasionally differed from the program-specified size when the X-axis was feeding, with a difference of about 0.5~2mm. Because this phenomenon occurred occasionally rather than continuously, and the CNC system did not display an alarm number when it occurred, the fault was very unclear. During work, operators could not guarantee whether the machining size of the next workpiece would be qualified, and scrap products continued to appear. First, the control system output signals were checked and found to be normal; then, after resetting the system, the X-axis feed speed was tested, and the data displayed by the system was consistent with the settings; after adjusting the system parameters and re-testing, the fault remained. Therefore, it was suspected that the speed of the X-axis drive stepper motor was unstable, and there might be a "missing step" phenomenon. Opening the protective cover of the X-axis drive stepper motor of the machine tool, the input phase voltage and speed of the motor were measured, and both were within normal ranges. Using an adjustable wrench to test-rotate the X-axis drive screw, it felt alternately tight and loose. Opening the screw cover, it was found that the synchronous timing belt connecting the stepper motor and the screw was severely aged, deformed, and even missing teeth. The reason was that the fastening screws of the protective cover at the connection part were loose, and cutting fluid seeped into the synchronous belt during machine operation. After soaking, it became severely aged and deformed, making it impossible for the stepper motor to synchronize with the screw speed, causing the above fault. After replacing the synchronous belt and re-running the test program, the command size was consistent with the actual measured size, and the fault was eliminated. Example 4: Coupling connection screws were loose, causing excessive position deviation in the feed direction. Fault Cause Analysis and Elimination: During the operation of a horizontal machining center, an alarm message indicating that the Y-axis position deviation exceeded the set value appeared. This machining center uses a FANUC 0iM system and adopts a closed-loop control format. Grating scales installed on the guide rail side and the column serve as position measurement components, and the system control takes the position loop as the outer loop; a rotary encoder installed at the end of the servo motor serves as the angle measurement component, and the speed loop is the inner loop of the system control. The servo motor and the ball screw are directly connected by a coupling. Based on the machine tool control principles and the machine tool transmission connection method, it was preliminarily judged that the cause of the alarm was a poor connection of the Y-axis coupling. A check of the Y-axis transmission system revealed that the coupling connection screws were loose. After tightening all the fastening screws in the Y-axis transmission system, the fault was eliminated. Example 5: System overload alarm. Fault Cause Analysis and Elimination: For the XH716 CNC vertical machining center, the system is a FANUC OM system. This machine tool frequently experienced overload alarms during machining, with alarm number 434, manifesting as excessive Z-axis motor current and motor heating. The alarm disappeared after stopping for about 40 minutes, but after resuming work for a while, the same type of alarm appeared again. After inspection and analysis, it was believed that the electrical servo system had no faults, and it was estimated that it was caused by the load being too heavy to pull. In order to distinguish whether it was an electrical fault or a mechanical fault, the Z-axis motor was removed and disconnected from the mechanism. When running again, the fault no longer occurred, thus confirming that it was caused by the mechanical screw or moving parts being too tight. After adjusting the anti-loosening nut of the Z-axis screw, the effect was not obvious. Later, the Z-axis guide rail taper jib was adjusted, the machine load was significantly reduced, and the fault was eliminated.

8.3 Common Fault Analysis of Guideways. The quality of guideways has a great impact on the rigidity, machining accuracy, and service life of machine tools. As an important part of the machine tool feed system, CNC machine tools have higher requirements for guideways than ordinary machine tools. The basic requirements

sliders, steel balls, retainers, and end caps. Sliders move along the fixed guideway, with balls rolling in circular arc grooves and circulating through end caps. They feature low friction (0.003-0.005), flexible movement, consistent dynamic/static friction (no stick-slip), high preloaded rigidity, long life, high precision, and easy grease lubrication. Widely used in precision/CNC machines, their main drawback is poor impact resistance and sensitivity to dust, requiring good protection. They can be installed horizontally, vertically, or inclined, and parallel installations are common. Their error-averaging effect reduces base installation errors to about 1/3 in slider movement. Guideway and slider fixing methods include setscrews, wedges, or pressure plates. Installation requires thorough cleaning, checking for burrs/rust, and ensuring screw holes align perfectly to prevent accuracy loss. Installation involves gently bolting the guideway against the reference side, tightening side devices, placing the slider, and tightening screws diagonally. Post-installation checks ensure smooth, consistent resistance and proper straightness/parallelism. 3. Liquid Hydrostatic Guideways. (1) Basic principles. These guideways use pressurized oil pumped through restrictors into oil pockets, forming a load-bearing oil film that separates contacting surfaces (liquid friction). They offer low friction (0.001-0.005), high efficiency, long precision retention, excellent vibration absorption, and no low-speed stick-slip, but require complex, costly dedicated oil supply systems. Open types only bear vertical loads, while closed types have oil pockets on all surfaces to resist large overturning moments and increase rigidity. Oil supplies are constant pressure or constant flow. Oil must be filtered to 10μm and kept absolutely clean. (2) Guideway clearance and restrictor forms. 1) Guideway clearance represents oil film thickness. Larger clearances increase flow but reduce rigidity and cause drift; smaller clearances increase rigidity but are limited by geometric accuracy. Small/medium machines use 0.01-0.025mm unloaded clearances; large machines use 0.03-0.08mm. 2) Restrictor forms include constant pressure and quantitative systems. Large machines often use single-cavity single-pump quantitative systems for maximum rigidity without restrictors. Constant pressure systems use capillary restrictors (often adjustable spiral grooves, combined for compactness, used in small/medium machines) or membrane feedback restrictors (single/double-sided, used for heavy, unevenly loaded large machines). Each oil pocket requires its own restrictor control. 8.3.2 Common Faults of Guideways and Their Diagnosis and Maintenance Methods. Guideway clearance, rolling guideway preload, straightness, parallelism, lubrication, and protection are critical for machine operation and machining quality. 1. Common repair methods include scraping, fine planing, and grinding. (1) Fine planing is used for heavy machines or deep scratches, heavily dependent on the planer's accuracy. (2) Scraping requires multiple measurements to map wear curves, using equal-height blocks, parallel straightedges, and frame levels to establish scraping reference points every fixed distance, followed by sectioned rough and fine scraping until the entire surface is flat and straight. (3) Grinding can use a "one-time grinding method" where all surfaces are measured for unevenness, rough ground to remove peaks, and fine ground in one setup. The sequence should prioritize associated/high-precision, complex, large, and difficult-to-machine surfaces first. 2. Common problems in guideway repair and their elimination. (1) Guideway scoring/scratches: Caused by foundation settling (requires regular leveling), prolonged short workpiece machining (requires varying installation positions or repairing accuracy), poor lubrication (adjust oil volume/pressure), poor material (treat with electroplating, induction hardening, or add zinc-aluminum-copper alloy plates), poor scraping quality (improve quality), or poor maintenance (enhance care and protection). (2) Moving parts sticking or not moving: Caused by surface scratches (polish with 180-grit sandpaper), pressure plate scratches (remove and adjust clearance), or gibs adjusted too tight (loosen anti-loose screws, adjust gib bolts for flexible movement ensuring a 0.03mm feeler gauge cannot enter, then lock). (3) Uneven machining surfaces at tool joints: Caused by poor guideway straightness (adjust/scrape to within 0.015mm/500mm), loose or excessively bent table gibs (adjust clearance, ensure natural bending <0.05mm/full length), poor machine levelness bending the guideway (adjust installation level/verticality to within 0.02mm/1000mm), rough guideway surfaces or uneven/insufficient scraping contact points (remove table, polish burrs with oilstone/sandpaper, reassemble, and polish manually with chromium oxide and kerosene), tapered bed guideways causing uneven tightness (repair geometric accuracy), temperature changes deforming guideways (adjust seasonally, keep precision machine rooms at constant temperatures), wear losing accuracy (re-scrape/repair), improper oil viscosity or dirty oil causing poor lubrication (use proper viscosity and keep clean), or poor surface lubrication structure increasing resistance (break the full guideway surface into fragmented dot contacts; for large surfaces, divide the saddle guideway into three sections, making the contact points heavier at the outer thirds and lighter in the middle third).

Therefore, the lock thread profile on the screw used to install the bearing must be processed simultaneously with the bearing positioning shoulder surface to ensure perpendicularity; grinding is even better, and precision specialized lock nuts should be selected. ③ If the perpendicularity of the internal cavity positioning surface of the bearing housing and the gland installation surface to the axis of the bearing hole is out of tolerance, it will also cause the bearing to tilt, and the internal cavity positioning surface is difficult to process and measure. 5) Parallelism or flatness of the support housing surface is out of tolerance Whether the mating component surface is ground or scraped, as long as its parallelism or flatness exceeds the tolerance range, it will affect the positioning accuracy when the worktable moves. Usually, adjusting can be achieved by adding shims between the support housing and the base body. When the eccentricity is too large, the screw will bend or even become eccentric; even if it does not cause obvious bending, abnormal wear will continue to occur and rapidly reduce the accuracy of the screw. The higher the pre-tension set for the nut, the higher the requirement for eccentric accuracy. (3) Temperature Rise Problems 1) The influence of lubrication The choice of lubricating oil directly affects the temperature rise of the ball screw. Poor lubrication of the ball screw will produce a larger temperature rise, which may cause steel balls to crack or be damaged, thereby damaging the nut or screw ball grooves. Therefore, the timely replenishment of lubricating oil must be considered during the design process. If an automatic lubrication system cannot be used, the replenishment cycle of lubricating oil (grease) must be included in the maintenance manual. Generally, it is recommended to use bearing lubricating oil for ball screw oil lubrication, and lithium-soap-based grease for grease lubrication. The viscosity of the oil should be selected based on operating speed, working temperature, and load conditions. For high speed and low load conditions, it is best to use low viscosity oil; for low speed and high load, high viscosity oil is recommended. When applied in high-speed, heavy-load situations, forced cooling must be used to lower the temperature, and hollow screws should be used to introduce cooling oil to achieve the cooling effect. 2) The influence of pre-tension Generally, ball screws require certain pre-tension to achieve the purposes of improving accuracy and rigidity, but applying pre-tensioning force to the nut will increase the friction torque and resistance of the raceway, raising the temperature during work. It is recommended that the pre-tension should not exceed 8% of the screw's dynamic load. 3) The influence of pre-stretching When the temperature of the ball screw rises, the thermal stress effect will cause a slight elongation of the screw, so the length of the screw becomes unstable. Pre-compensation measures are often used to make up for this. The target value for pre-stretching compensation is to give a negative compensation value in advance. It is generally recommended that the compensation value per 1000mm is 0.02~0.03mm. Excessive pre-stretching will burn out the support bearings. Therefore, it is recommended to use a pre-stretching value corresponding to less than 5°C. However, if the screw diameter exceeds 50mm, it is not suitable for pre-stretching. A large screw diameter requires a large pre-stretching force, which leads to overheating and burning of support bearings. It is recommended to use a temperature rise of about 3°C as the compensation value. 4) The influence of the dn value The dn value is the product of the screw pitch circle diameter and the maximum rotational speed. For example, if the pitch circle diameter is Φ40mm and the maximum speed is 2000r/min, its dn value is 80000. The dn value has a significant impact on the noise, working temperature, circulation system, and service life of the screw. It is generally recommended that the dn value not exceed 70000. Spindle sealing includes contact sealing and non-contact sealing. Figure 8-9 shows several forms of non-contact sealing. This seal is used in grease-lubricated areas with relatively clean working environments. Figure 8-9b cuts a sawtooth annular groove on the outer diameter of the nut. When oil flows outward, the centrifugal force of the spindle rotation throws the oil along the slope into the cavity of end cover 1, and the oil flows back into the box. Figure 8-9c is a labyrinth seal structure, which provides reliable sealing effects in working environments with many chips and heavy dust; this structure is suitable for sealing grease or oil lubrication. When using a non-contact seal, to prevent leakage, the smoothness of the oil return hole must be ensured so that the return oil can be drained as soon as possible. Figure 8-11 shows the spindle of a certain model of CNC lathe. Its rotation accuracy includes two items: radial runout and axial movement. Radial runout is guaranteed by a double-row radial short cylindrical roller bearing at the front end of the spindle and a radial thrust ball bearing at the rear end; axial movement is guaranteed by the radial thrust bearing at the rear end of the spindle. Normally, this accuracy is adjusted before leaving the factory and generally requires no adjustment. If tool holder collision with the workpiece or other reasons affect the spindle's accuracy, spindle accuracy adjustment must be performed. During adjustment, loosen the lock screw on nut 1 or nut 2 for adjustment. After adjustment, retighten the lock screw. If requirements are still not met, repeat the above steps. After adjustment, perform an idling test for a certain period of time (usually about 1 hour). 3. Other Auxiliary Components of the Spindle. (1) Hydraulic power chuck. In CNC lathes, the hydraulic power chuck is the most commonly used workpiece fixture. It is the connecting interface between the machine tool spindle and the workpiece; the speed, torque, and rotation accuracy of the machine tool spindle are transmitted to the workpiece through the power chuck. Hydraulic power chucks are very widely used in CNC machine tools and have become indispensable fundamental functional components for mid-to-high-speed CNC lathes, CNC grinders, and CNC turn-mill centers. Hydraulic power chucks mainly include self-centering chucks, floating chucks, crankshaft chucks, and indexing chucks. Among them, the linearly driven self-centering hydraulic power chuck shown in Figure 8-12a is highly versatile and widely used. The hydraulic power chuck is fixedly mounted on the front end of the spindle. The rotary hydraulic cylinder 1 is connected to the connector 5 with screws 7, and the connector 5 is connected to the rear end face of the spindle with screws, causing the rotary hydraulic cylinder to rotate together with the spindle. The clamping and unclamping of the chuck are driven by the rotary hydraulic cylinder through a hollow draw tube 2. The rear end of the draw tube is threaded to the piston 6 inside the hydraulic cylinder, and the threads on both ends of the connection sleeve 3 are connected to the draw tube 2 and the slide sleeve 4 respectively. When the pressure oil in the hydraulic cylinder pushes piston 6 and draw tube 2 towards the chuck, slide sleeve 4 moves to the right. Due to the action of the wedge groove on the slide sleeve and the chuck body, jaw base 11 moves radially outwards with jaw 12, thereby loosening the chuck; conversely, when the pressure oil in the hydraulic cylinder pushes the piston and draw tube towards the rear end of the spindle, the chuck clamps the workpiece through the wedge mechanism. The piston rod of the hollow rotary hydraulic cylinder has a center hole, while other aspects are the same as the solid hydraulic cylinder. When the pressure dropped to 4MPa, there was a problem with the displacement of the clamping claws of the unclamping mechanism, and the tool could not be unclamped. Under normal circumstances, if the system pressure is below 5.8MPa, tools cannot be properly loaded and unloaded. If the displacement of the unclamping mechanism, i.e., the unclamping stroke, remains unchanged, and the restoring force of the spring is directly proportional to the pressure of the hydraulic cylinder compressing the spring, the reduction in hydraulic pressure required for unclamping proves that the stiffness of the spring has decreased, which actually indicates a problem with the Belleville spring. Disassembling the spindle tool clamping mechanism, it was found that part of the Belleville spring was damaged. It was completely replaced, and the lock nut was tightened to its pre-loosening position. After installation, the pressure required to unclamp the tool returned to a normal level of about 5.8MPa. Performing a boring test again, the roundness error decreased to within 0.01mm, restoring to normal levels. The spindle tool locking mechanisms of various machining centers are basically similar, mostly using hydraulic or pneumatic unclamping, and relying on the restoring force of Belleville springs to pull the tool tight. Long-term use of Belleville springs will cause fatigue and damage, leading to a decrease in the pull force on the tool.
