Spindle heating. (1) Front and rear spindle bearings are damaged or bearings are not clean. Elimination method: Replace bad bearings, clean out dirt. (2) Spindle bearing preload is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the preload. (3) Lubricating oil is dirty or contains impurities. Elimination method: Clean the spindle box, replace the lubricating oil. (4) The spindle front end cover and the spindle box body gland are galled. Elimination method: Grind the spindle box front end cover so that it presses tightly against the spindle front bearing, leaving a clearance of 0.02-0.05mm between the bearing and the cover. (5) Bearing lubricating grease is depleted or there is too much lubricating grease. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. 2. The spindle stops during heavy cutting. (1) The belt connecting the motor and the spindle is too loose. Elimination method: Move the motor base, tension the belt, and then retighten the motor base. (2) There is oil on the surface of the belt. Elimination method: Wash with gasoline and wipe clean before reinstalling. (3) The friction clutch is adjusted too loosely or is worn. Elimination method: Adjust the clutch, grind or replace the friction plates. (4) The belt has been used for too long and failed. Elimination method: Replace with a new belt. 3. Spindle noise. (1) Lack of lubrication. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. (2) Poor transmission balance between the small pulley and the large pulley. Elimination method: The balance weight on the pulley has fallen off; perform dynamic balancing again. (3) Bearings are scored or damaged. Elimination method: Replace the bearings. (4) Poor balance of parts at the end of the shaft. Elimination method: Redo dynamic balancing. (5) Gear meshing clearance is uneven or gears are damaged. Elimination method: Adjust the meshing clearance or replace with new gears. (6) The transmission bearing is damaged or the transmission shaft is bent. Elimination method: Repair or replace the bearing, straighten the transmission shaft. 4. Spindle has no lubricating oil circulation or insufficient lubrication. (1) The hydraulic pump rotation direction is incorrect, or the clearance is too large. Elimination method: Change the hydraulic pump rotation direction, repair the hydraulic pump. (2) The suction pipe is not inserted below the oil level of the oil tank. Elimination method: Insert the suction pipe 2/3 below the oil level. (3) Oil pipes or filters are blocked. Elimination method: Eliminate the blockage. (4) Lubricating oil pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply pressure. 5. Lubricating oil leakage. (1) The amount of lubricating oil is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply amount. (2) Check whether seals in various places are damaged. Elimination method: Replace seals. (3) Pipe fittings are damaged. Elimination method: Replace pipe fittings. 6. Tool cannot be clamped. (1) Belleville spring displacement is small. Elimination method: Adjust the stroke length of the Belleville spring. (2) Spring collet is damaged. Elimination method: Replace the spring collet. (3) Belleville spring failure. Elimination method: Replace the Belleville spring. (4) The pull stud on the tool holder is too large. Elimination method: Replace the pull stud and install it correctly. (5) Check whether the nut on the tool unclamp/clamp spring is loose. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the clamp spring clockwise so that its maximum working load is 13kN. 7. Tool cannot be unclamped after being clamped. (1) Unclamp spring is compressed too tightly. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the unclamp spring counterclockwise so that its maximum working load does not exceed 13kN. (2) Hydraulic cylinder pressure and stroke are insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust hydraulic pressure and piston stroke switch. 8. Spindle fails to change speeds. (1) Shifting hydraulic cylinder pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Detect working pressure; if lower than rated pressure, adjust it. (2) Shifting hydraulic cylinder is worn or stuck. Elimination method: Remove burrs or galling, clean and reassemble. (3) Shifting hydraulic cylinder fork has fallen off. Elimination method: Repair or replace. (4) Shifting hydraulic cylinder bypasses oil or leaks internally. Elimination method: Replace seal ring. (5) Shifting solenoid valve is stuck. Elimination method: Repair the solenoid valve and clean it. (6) Shifting composite switch has failed. Elimination method: Replace the switch. 8.1.3 Spindle Component Fault Maintenance Examples. 8.4 Structure and common fault analysis of rotary moving parts 8.4.1 Structure of rotary moving parts The circular feed of the CNC machine tool is completed by the rotary worktable, which is called the fourth axis of the CNC machine tool. Figure 8-54 shows the rotary worktable of a five-axis simultaneous machining center. The rotary worktable can linkage with the three coordinate axes X, Y, and Z, thereby machining various spheres, arc curves, etc. The rotary worktable can also achieve precise automatic indexing, expanding the machining range of CNC machine tools. Commonly used rotary worktables include CNC rotary worktables and indexing worktables. In addition to being used for various circular arc machining or surface machining in linkage with linear feed, the CNC rotary worktable can also achieve precise automatic indexing work. The function of the indexing worktable is to index and change the surface of the workpiece, complete the indexing movement, and use it in conjunction with the automatic tool changer to achieve multiple processes on several surfaces with a single workpiece installation. In order to ensure machining accuracy, the positioning accuracy of the indexing worktable is required to be high (ordinary grade ±10″, precision grade ±5″, high precision grade ±3″). 1. CNC rotary worktable The CNC rotary worktable is mainly used for CNC boring and milling machines. Its appearance is almost the same as that of a general-purpose worktable, but its drive is a servo system drive method. It can linkage with other servo feed axes. Figure 8-55 shows the rotary worktable of an automatic tool changing CNC boring machine. Its feed, indexing rotation, and positioning locking are all controlled by given commands. The movement of the worktable is realized by the servo motor transmitting power to the worm wheel 2 via the worm 1 after gear deceleration. Figure 8-55 Rotary worktable of automatic tool changing CNC boring machine 1—Worm 2—Worm wheel 3, 4—Clamping pad 5—Small hydraulic cylinder 6—Piston 7—Spring 8—Steel ball 9—Base 10—Circular grating 11, 12—Bearing In order to eliminate the transmission clearance of the worm pair, a dual-pitch gradually thicker worm is adopted, and the clearance is adjusted by moving the axial position of the worm. The left and right sides of this worm have different pitches, so the tooth thickness of the worm gradually increases from beginning to end. However, because the pitch on the same side is the same, normal meshing can still be maintained. When the worktable is stationary, it must be in a locked state. Therefore, eight pairs of clamping pads 4 and 3 are installed in the radial direction at the bottom of the worm wheel, and the same number of small hydraulic cylinders 5 are evenly distributed on the base 9. When the upper cavity of the small hydraulic cylinder is connected to pressure oil, the piston presses against the steel ball 8, pushes open the clamping pad, and clamps the worm wheel 2. When the worktable needs to rotate, first connect the upper cavity of the small hydraulic cylinder to the oil return circuit. Under the action of the spring 7, the steel ball 8 is lifted, and the clamping pad releases the worm wheel. The guide rail surface of the rotary worktable is supported by large rolling bearings, and the accurate rotation center is maintained by tapered roller bearings 12 and cylindrical roller bearings 11. The positioning accuracy of the CNC rotary worktable mainly depends on the transmission accuracy of the worm pair, so a high-precision worm pair must be used. In a semi-closed loop control system, after actually measuring the static positioning error of the worktable, the position of the angle to be compensated and the compensation value can be determined and memorized in the compensation circuit, and the error compensation is performed by the CNC device. In a fully closed-loop control system, a high-precision circular grating 10 issues an accurate in-position signal of the worktable, which is fed back to the CNC device for control. The rotary worktable is equipped with a zero point. When it performs a zero-return movement, it first presses the limit switch with a stop iron to decelerate the worktable, and then the circular grating or encoder issues a zero signal to accurately stop the worktable at the zero position. The CNC rotary worktable can perform arbitrary angle rotation and indexing, and can also perform continuous rotary feed movement. 2. Indexing worktable The indexing, rotation, and positioning work of the indexing worktable are automatically performed according to the commands of the control system. Guideway and slider fixing methods include setscrews, wedges, or pressure plates. Installation requires thorough cleaning, checking for burrs/rust, and ensuring screw holes align perfectly to prevent accuracy loss. Installation involves gently bolting the guideway against the reference side, tightening side devices, placing the slider, and tightening screws diagonally. Post-installation checks ensure smooth, consistent resistance and proper straightness/parallelism. 3. Liquid Hydrostatic Guideways. (1) Basic principles. These guideways use pressurized oil pumped through restrictors into oil pockets, forming a load-bearing oil film that separates contacting surfaces (liquid friction). They offer low friction (0.001-0.005), high efficiency, long precision retention, excellent vibration absorption, and no low-speed stick-slip, but require complex, costly dedicated oil supply systems. Open types only bear vertical loads, while closed types have oil pockets on all surfaces to resist large overturning moments and increase rigidity. Oil supplies are constant pressure or constant flow. Oil must be filtered to 10μm and kept absolutely clean. (2) Guideway clearance and restrictor forms. 1) Guideway clearance represents oil film thickness. Larger clearances increase flow but reduce rigidity and cause drift; smaller clearances increase rigidity but are limited by geometric accuracy. Small/medium machines use 0.01-0.025mm unloaded clearances; large machines use 0.03-0.08mm. 2) Restrictor forms include constant pressure and quantitative systems. Large machines often use single-cavity single-pump quantitative systems for maximum rigidity without restrictors. Constant pressure systems use capillary restrictors (often adjustable spiral grooves, combined for compactness, used in small/medium machines) or membrane feedback restrictors (single/double-sided, used for heavy, unevenly loaded large machines). Each oil pocket requires its own restrictor control. 8.3.2 Common Faults of Guideways and Their Diagnosis and Maintenance Methods. Guideway clearance, rolling guideway preload, straightness, parallelism, lubrication, and protection are critical for machine operation and machining quality. 1. Common repair methods include scraping, fine planing, and grinding. (1) Fine planing is used for heavy machines or deep scratches, heavily dependent on the planer's accuracy. (2) Scraping requires multiple measurements to map wear curves, using equal-height blocks, parallel straightedges, and frame levels to establish scraping reference points every fixed distance, followed by sectioned rough and fine scraping until the entire surface is flat and straight. (3) Grinding can use a "one-time grinding method" where all surfaces are measured for unevenness, rough ground to remove peaks, and fine ground in one setup. The sequence should prioritize associated/high-precision, complex, large, and difficult-to-machine surfaces first. 2. Common problems in guideway repair and their elimination. (1) Guideway scoring/scratches: Caused by foundation settling (requires regular leveling), prolonged short workpiece machining (requires varying installation positions or repairing accuracy), poor lubrication (adjust oil volume/pressure), poor material (treat with electroplating, induction hardening, or add zinc-aluminum-copper alloy plates), poor scraping quality (improve quality), or poor maintenance (enhance care and protection). (2) Moving parts sticking or not moving: Caused by surface scratches (polish with 180-grit sandpaper), pressure plate scratches (remove and adjust clearance), or gibs adjusted too tight (loosen anti-loose screws, adjust gib bolts for flexible movement ensuring a 0.03mm feeler gauge cannot enter, then lock). (3) Uneven machining surfaces at tool joints: Caused by poor guideway straightness (adjust/scrape to within 0.015mm/500mm), loose or excessively bent table gibs (adjust clearance, ensure natural bending <0.05mm/full length), poor machine levelness bending the guideway (adjust installation level/verticality to within 0.02mm/1000mm), rough guideway surfaces or uneven/insufficient scraping contact points (remove table, polish burrs with oilstone/sandpaper, reassemble, and polish manually with chromium oxide and kerosene), tapered bed guideways causing uneven tightness (repair geometric accuracy), temperature changes deforming guideways (adjust seasonally, keep precision machine rooms at constant temperatures), wear losing accuracy (re-scrape/repair), improper oil viscosity or dirty oil causing poor lubrication (use proper viscosity and keep clean), or poor surface lubrication structure increasing resistance (break the full guideway surface into fragmented dot contacts; for large surfaces, divide the saddle guideway into three sections, making the contact points heavier at the outer thirds and lighter in the middle third).

After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

Structurally, issues such as tool clamping, bearing configuration, bearing clearance adjustment, lubrication, and sealing must be well resolved. (1) Spindle. The spindle is an important part of the spindle transmission structure. Its structural dimensions, shape, manufacturing accuracy, material, and heat treatment have a great impact on the working performance of the spindle component. Spindle structures come in various forms depending on the design requirements of the spindle transmission system. During design, a series of issues must be properly handled, such as the clamping of chucks or tools, spindle unloading, positioning and clearance adjustment of spindle bearings, and sealing and lubrication of spindle components. The main dimensional parameters of the spindle include: spindle diameter, inner hole diameter, overhang length, and support span. The basis for evaluating and considering the main dimensional parameters of the spindle is the rigidity of the spindle, structural manufacturability, and the process application range of the spindle assembly. (2) Spindle Bearings. Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

8.1 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Spindle Components. The spindle is the motion axis on a CNC machine tool that drives the tool or workpiece to rotate and generate cutting motion, and it is often the motion axis with the highest single-axis power consumption on a CNC machine tool. Generally, like conventional machine tools, CNC machine tools must also undergo speed variation to enable the spindle to obtain different rotational speeds to adapt to various processing requirements. While changing speeds, the spindle is also required to transmit a certain amount of power and sufficient torque to meet cutting needs. In addition to meeting the requirements of conventional machine tool spindles, CNC machine tool spindles also have the following requirements: 1. A larger speed regulation range and the realization of stepless speed regulation. Only when the machine tool spindle has a high rotational speed and a wide speed regulation range can it ensure that during processing, a more reasonable cutting parameter can be selected to give full play to the cutting performance of the tool. 2. High precision and rigidity, with smooth transmission and low noise. The improvement of machining accuracy of CNC machine tools is closely related to the rigidity of the machine tool's spindle structure, so the manufacturing accuracy and rigidity of its transmission components should be improved. For example, the tooth surface of gears should undergo high-frequency induction heating and quenching to increase wear resistance; the final stage should use helical gear transmission to improve transmission stability; using high-precision bearings and selecting reasonable support spans can improve the rigidity of spindle components. 3. Good vibration resistance and thermal stability. CNC machine tools generally perform rough and finish machining continuously, and during machining, interference from impact forces or alternating forces caused by uneven machining allowances, unbalanced moving parts, and self-excited vibration during the cutting process may cause the spindle to vibrate, affecting machining accuracy and surface roughness, and in severe cases, even destroying the tool or part, making machining impossible. Therefore, in the machine tool spindle structure, each main component must not only have a certain static rigidity but also sufficient vibration resistance to suppress vibrations caused by various interferences. Vibration resistance is usually measured by dynamic rigidity or dynamic compliance; for example, the dynamic rigidity of spindle components depends on parameters such as the equivalent static rigidity, damping ratio, and natural frequency of the spindle. During the cutting process of the machine tool, the heat generated by the spindle structure causes thermal deformation of its internal components, destroying the relative positional accuracy and motion accuracy between components, thereby causing machining errors; moreover, thermal deformation limits the improvement of cutting parameters, reduces transmission efficiency, and even affects productivity. The thermal stability of spindle components is often achieved through measures such as maintaining appropriate fit clearances between components, circulating lubrication, and maintaining thermal balance. 8.1.1 Typical Structure and Assembly Adjustment of Spindle Components. 1. Common Structures of Spindles. Currently, the transmission structures of CNC machine tool spindles can be roughly divided into the following categories: (1) Main transmission with a direct connection between the motor and the spindle. As shown in Figure 8-1a, this direct-drive structure is generally rotated directly by a variable-speed motor driving the spindle, which greatly simplifies the structure of the spindle box and spindle, and effectively improves the rigidity of the spindle components. However, the output torque of the spindle is small, and motor heating has a significant impact on spindle accuracy, so its application is subject to certain limitations. (2) Main transmission with one-stage speed variation. As shown in Figure 8-1b, one-stage speed variation is mostly accomplished by a synchronous belt. Its advantages are a simple structure, convenient installation and debugging, and to a certain extent, it can meet the speed and torque output requirements. However, the spindle speed regulation range ratio is still the same as the motor's, constrained by the motor's speed regulation range ratio. Its advantage is a wide speed variation range, with a maximum speed reaching 8000r/min, which basically meets the transmission requirements of most current CNC machine tools and is easy to realize rich control functions; its simple structure and convenient installation and debugging can meet the control requirements of current mid-to-high-end CNC machine tools. However, for increasingly high speed demands, this configuration method is difficult to satisfy. (3) Main transmission with variable speed gears. As shown in Figure 8-1c, this configuration method is mostly adopted in large and medium-sized CNC machine tools. In actual production, the spindle does not need to maintain constant power throughout the entire speed range; generally, constant power transmission is required in the medium and high-speed sections, and constant torque transmission is required in the low-speed section. To ensure that the CNC machine tool spindle has a large torque at low speeds and that the spindle's speed range is as large as possible, some CNC systems are equipped with gear speed variation on the basis of the stepless speed variation of the machine tool spindle motor, becoming segmented stepless speed variation. In the segmented stepless speed variation system with gear speed variation, the forward and reverse starting, stopping, and braking of the spindle are realized by directly controlling the motor, while the speed variation of the spindle is realized by the combination of the stepless speed variation of the motor speed and the stepped speed variation of the gears. Gear stepped speed variation mechanisms usually adopt two speed variation forms: hydraulic shift fork speed variation and electromagnetic clutch speed variation. 1) Hydraulic shift fork speed variation. The principle and form of the hydraulic shift fork speed variation mechanism are shown in Figure 8-2. The shift fork of the sliding gear is connected to the piston rod of the variable speed hydraulic cylinder. By changing different oil flow paths, the triple gear can obtain three different speed variation positions. As shown in Figure 8-2a, when hydraulic cylinder 1 is fed with pressure oil and hydraulic cylinder 5 is depressurized, piston rod 2 drives shift fork

motion. In order to ensure the transmission accuracy and working stability of the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, the following requirements should be noted when designing the mechanical transmission device: ① Improve transmission accuracy and rigidity. The accuracy of the CNC machine tool itself, especially the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the feed drive device, plays a key role in the machining accuracy of parts and is a characteristic indicator of CNC machine tools. Therefore, it is first necessary to ensure the machining accuracy of each transmission part, especially to improve the transmission accuracy of the ball screw and nut pair (linear feed system) and worm gear pair (circular feed system). In addition, adding reduction gears to the feed transmission chain to reduce the pulse equivalent (i.e., the distance the worktable moves when the servo system receives one command pulse) can also improve transmission accuracy from a system design perspective; transmission accuracy and rigidity can also be improved by pre-tensioning the transmission ball screw to eliminate the clearance of transmission parts such as gears and worm gears. ② Reduce the inertia of moving parts. The inertia of transmission parts affects both the starting and braking characteristics of the feed drive system, especially for parts running at high speeds, where the influence of inertia is even greater. Under the premise of satisfying transmission strength and rigidity, the mass of the actuating components should be minimized as much as possible, and the diameter and mass of rotating parts should be reduced to decrease the inertia of moving parts. ③ Reduce the frictional resistance of moving parts. The frictional resistance of the mechanical transmission structure mainly comes from the lead screw nut pair and the guide rails. In the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, to reduce frictional resistance, eliminate low-speed feed crawling, and improve the stability of the entire servo feed system, ball screws, rolling guides, plastic guides, and hydrostatic guides are widely used. ④ Fast response speed. The so-called fast response characteristic refers to the response speed of the feed drive system to input command signals and how quickly the transient process ends. Fast response is a dynamic performance of the servo feed system and reflects the tracking accuracy of the system. During the workpiece machining process, the worktable should be able to sensitively and accurately track instructions within the specified speed range, without missing steps or taking extra steps during operation. The response speed of the feed drive system not only affects the machining efficiency of the machine tool but also affects the machining accuracy. In the design, the rigidity, clearance, friction, and moment of inertia of the machine tool worktable and transmission mechanism should be optimized to the best possible values to improve the fast response characteristics of the servo feed system. ⑤ Strong overload capacity. Because the motor frequently changes direction and the acceleration and deceleration are very fast, the motor may work under overload conditions. This requires the motor to have a strong overload capacity, generally requiring it to withstand an overload of 4 to 6 times for several minutes without damage. ⑥ Good stability and long service life. Stability is the most basic condition for the normal operation of the servo feed drive system, particularly that it must not crawl under low feed speeds and must be able to adapt to changes in external loads without resonance. Stability is related to the system's inertia, rigidity, damping, and gain. Properly selecting these parameters to achieve optimal working performance is the goal of servo feed system design. The service life of a servo feed drive system mainly refers to the length of time it can maintain the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the CNC machine tool, that is, the ability of each transmission component to maintain its original manufacturing accuracy. Therefore, the materials, heat treatment methods, and processing technologies of each transmission component should be reasonably selected, and appropriate lubrication methods and protective measures should be adopted to extend its service life. ⑦ Convenient operation and maintenance. CNC machine tools are high-precision automatic control machine tools, mainly used for single-piece, small-to-medium batch, high-precision, and complex production and machining. CNC machine tools have a high utilization rate, so the structural design of the feed drive system should facilitate maintenance and care, minimizing the maintenance workload to improve the utilization rate of the machine tool. 8.2.1 Typical Structures of Feed Drive Components Common mechanical transmission devices include ball screw pairs, hydrostatic worm-rack drives, preloaded double gear-racks, and linear motors. 1. Ball Screw Pair (1) Composition and Structure A ball screw consists of four parts: a lead screw, a nut, balls, and a ball return device. Arc-shaped helical grooves are machined on the screw and the nut. When they are assembled together, a helical raceway is formed, and the raceway is filled with balls. When the screw rotates, to maintain the continuous operation of the screw and nut, the balls complete their circulation through the return device on the nut. Based on the ball circulation method, ball screw and nut pairs are divided into internal circulation and external circulation types, as shown in Figures 8-23 and 8-24. Figures 8-23b and 8-24b respectively show the number of rotating turns of the balls in the internal and external circulation ball screw and nut pairs, usually 2 to 6 turns. When the internal circulation ball screw pair is working, the balls are always in contact with the screw. Its nut structure is compact, positioning is reliable, rigidity is good, it is not easy to wear, the return raceway is short, balls are not easily jammed, and friction loss is small. The disadvantage is that the structure is complex and manufacturing is difficult. When the external circulation ball screw pair is working, the balls leave contact with the screw. The tool magazine for storing tools has a large capacity; it can be installed on the side or top of the spindle box, or as an independent component outside the machine tool, with tools transported by a handling device. Compared with the turret spindle head, the automatic tool changing system with a tool magazine ensures that the CNC machine tool's spindle box has only one spindle, allowing the spindle component design to fully enhance its rigidity, thus meeting the requirements of precision machining. In addition, the tool magazine can store a large number of tools, enabling multi-process machining of complex parts, which significantly improves the machine's adaptability and processing efficiency. Therefore, automatic tool changing devices with tool magazines are particularly suitable for CNC drilling, milling, and boring machines. 2. Tool magazine. The tool magazine is the main component of the automatic tool changing device; its capacity, layout, and specific structure have a great impact on the design of CNC machine tools. Depending on the required capacity and tool retrieval method, tool magazines can be designed in various forms. Figure 8-59 lists the most commonly used types. Figures 8-59a to d show single-disk tool magazines. To adapt to the machine tool spindle layout, the tool axes in the magazine can be configured in different directions (as shown in Figures 8-59a to c). Figure 8-59d shows a disk tool magazine where tools can be flipped 90 degrees; this structure simplifies the tool retrieval action. The single-disk tool magazine has a simple structure, typically holding 15 to 30 tools, and tool retrieval is relatively convenient, making it the most widely used. Figure 8-59e is a drum-type (also known as hedgehog-type) tool magazine, which is very compact and offers a larger capacity within the same space, but the tool selection and retrieval actions are more complex. Figure 8-59f is a chain-type tool magazine, which provides great structural flexibility, can store a large number of tools, and makes tool selection and retrieval very simple. For long chains, the number of supporting sprockets can be increased to fold and loop the chain, improving space utilization. Figures 8-59g and 8-59h show multi-disk and grid-type tool magazines respectively. Although they are compact, their tool selection and retrieval actions are complex, so they are rarely used. The typical capacity of these tool magazines is 10 to 60 tools, but with the development of machining technology, there seems to be a trend toward even larger capacities. The chain-type tool magazine is one of the more frequently used forms. In this magazine, tool pockets are fixed on the chain links. A commonly used type is the single-row chain-type tool magazine, as shown in Figure 8-60a, generally storing fewer than 30 tools, occasionally up to 60. Tool changing methods. In the automatic tool changing device of a CNC machine, the mechanism that transfers and loads/unloads tools between the tool magazine and the machine spindle is called the tool exchange device. Tool exchange methods in CNC machines are generally divided into two categories: tool changing without a manipulator and tool changing with a manipulator. (1) Tool changing without a manipulator. A tool changing system without a manipulator generally involves placing the tool magazine at a position the machine spindle can reach, or moving the entire magazine (or a specific tool position) to a location accessible by the spindle box. Additionally, the tool storage direction in the magazine is generally consistent with the tool loading direction on the spindle. During a tool change, the spindle moves to the changing position on the magazine and directly retrieves or returns the tool. For example, in the machining center shown in Figure 2-59, the tool change sequence is as follows: ① According to the tool change command, the machine worktable quickly moves to the right, moving the workpiece away from under the spindle, and the tool magazine moves under the spindle, aligning an empty tool pocket with the spindle. ② The spindle box descends, placing the used tool from the spindle into the empty pocket of the tool magazine. ③ The spindle box ascends, and the tool magazine rotates to align the tool required for the next step with the spindle. ④ The spindle box descends, inserting the tool into the machine spindle. ⑤ The spindle box and spindle ascend with the tool. ⑥ The machine worktable quickly returns to the left, the tool magazine moves away from under the spindle, and the workpiece moves under the spindle, aligning the tool with the machining surface of the workpiece. ⑦ The spindle box descends, and the tool on the spindle machines the workpiece. ⑧ After machining, the spindle box ascends, and the tool retracts from the workpiece. Tool changing without a manipulator has a relatively simple structure but involves cumbersome actions, long changing times, and relatively small magazine capacities. (2) Tool changing with a manipulator. In machining centers, using a manipulator (tool changing arm) for tool exchange is the most widely applied method because it requires short tool changing times and offers flexible actions. Spindle heating. (1) Front and rear spindle bearings are damaged or bearings are not clean. Elimination method: Replace bad bearings, clean out dirt. (2) Spindle bearing preload is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the preload. (3) Lubricating oil is dirty or contains impurities. Elimination method: Clean the spindle box, replace the lubricating oil. (4) The spindle front end cover and the spindle box body gland are galled. Elimination method: Grind the spindle box front end cover so that it presses tightly against the spindle front bearing, leaving a clearance of 0.02-0.05mm between the bearing and the cover. (5) Bearing lubricating grease is depleted or there is too much lubricating grease. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. 2. The spindle stops during heavy cutting. (1) The belt connecting the motor and the spindle is too loose. Elimination method: Move the motor base, tension the belt, and then retighten the motor base. (2) There is oil on the surface of the belt. Elimination method: Wash with gasoline and wipe clean before reinstalling. (3) The friction clutch is adjusted too loosely or is worn. Elimination method: Adjust the clutch, grind or replace the friction plates. (4) The belt has been used for too long and failed. Elimination method: Replace with a new belt. 3. Spindle noise. (1) Lack of lubrication. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. (2) Poor transmission balance between the small pulley and the large pulley. Elimination method: The balance weight on the pulley has fallen off; perform dynamic balancing again. (3) Bearings are scored or damaged. Elimination method: Replace the bearings. (4) Poor balance of parts at the end of the shaft. Elimination method: Redo dynamic balancing. (5) Gear meshing clearance is uneven or gears are damaged. Elimination method: Adjust the meshing clearance or replace with new gears. (6) The transmission bearing is damaged or the transmission shaft is bent. Elimination method: Repair or replace the bearing, straighten the transmission shaft. 4. Spindle has no lubricating oil circulation or insufficient lubrication. (1) The hydraulic pump rotation direction is incorrect, or the clearance is too large. Elimination method: Change the hydraulic pump rotation direction, repair the hydraulic pump. (2) The suction pipe is not inserted below the oil level of the oil tank. Elimination method: Insert the suction pipe 2/3 below the oil level. (3) Oil pipes or filters are blocked. Elimination method: Eliminate the blockage. (4) Lubricating oil pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply pressure. 5. Lubricating oil leakage. (1) The amount of lubricating oil is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply amount. (2) Check whether seals in various places are damaged. Elimination method: Replace seals. (3) Pipe fittings are damaged. Elimination method: Replace pipe fittings. 6. Tool cannot be clamped. (1) Belleville spring displacement is small. Elimination method: Adjust the stroke length of the Belleville spring. (2) Spring collet is damaged. Elimination method: Replace the spring collet. (3) Belleville spring failure. Elimination method: Replace the Belleville spring. (4) The pull stud on the tool holder is too large. Elimination method: Replace the pull stud and install it correctly. (5) Check whether the nut on the tool unclamp/clamp spring is loose. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the clamp spring clockwise so that its maximum working load is 13kN. 7. Tool cannot be unclamped after being clamped. (1) Unclamp spring is compressed too tightly. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the unclamp spring counterclockwise so that its maximum working load does not exceed 13kN. (2) Hydraulic cylinder pressure and stroke are insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust hydraulic pressure and piston stroke switch. 8. Spindle fails to change speeds. (1) Shifting hydraulic cylinder pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Detect working pressure; if lower than rated pressure, adjust it. (2) Shifting hydraulic cylinder is worn or stuck. Elimination method: Remove burrs or galling, clean and reassemble. (3) Shifting hydraulic cylinder fork has fallen off. Elimination method: Repair or replace. (4) Shifting hydraulic cylinder bypasses oil or leaks internally. Elimination method: Replace seal ring. (5) Shifting solenoid valve is stuck. Elimination method: Repair the solenoid valve and clean it. (6) Shifting composite switch has failed. Elimination method: Replace the switch. 8.1.3 Spindle Component Fault Maintenance Examples. (3) Tool selection methods. Based on the tool change command, the operation of the tool exchange device picking the required tool from the tool magazine for each process is called automatic tool selection. Common tool selection methods mainly include sequential tool selection and random tool selection. Random tool selection is further divided into tool coding selection, tool pocket coding selection, and memory-based selection. 1) Sequential tool selection method. Before machining, tools are sequentially inserted into the tool pockets of the magazine according to the predetermined machining process order, and tools are selected in order during machining. Used tools are returned to their original pockets, or they can be placed in the next pocket according to the machining sequence. However, when machining different workpieces, the tool sequence must be readjusted, making operations very cumbersome; moreover, when machining the same workpiece across different processes, tools cannot be reused, which increases the number of tools and the required magazine capacity, reducing the utilization rate of tools and the magazine. Furthermore, great caution must be exercised when loading tools, as failing to load them in order can lead to severe consequences. Because this method requires no tool identification device and features simple drive control and reliable operation, it is suitable for small and medium-sized automatic tool changing CNC machines that process large batches with a small variety of workpieces. 2) Tool coding selection method. This method uses a special tool holder structure to encode each tool based on binary principles. During a tool change, an encoding identification device recognizes the required tool in the magazine. This allows tools to be stored in any pocket of the magazine and reused across different processes, reducing the required magazine capacity; used tools do not necessarily need to return to their original pockets, which avoids accidents caused by errors in tool storage sequences, shortens the magazine operation time, and simplifies the automatic tool change control circuit. However, because each tool must be equipped with a dedicated coding system, the tool length increases, making manufacturing difficult and reducing rigidity, while the structures of the manipulator and tool magazine also become more complex. 8.4 Structure and common fault analysis of rotary moving parts 8.4.1 Structure of rotary moving parts The circular feed of the CNC machine tool is completed by the rotary worktable, which is called the fourth axis of the CNC machine tool. Figure 8-54 shows the rotary worktable of a five-axis simultaneous machining center. The rotary worktable can linkage with the three coordinate axes X, Y, and Z, thereby machining various spheres, arc curves, etc. The rotary worktable can also achieve precise automatic indexing, expanding the machining range of CNC machine tools. Commonly used rotary worktables include CNC rotary worktables and indexing worktables. In addition to being used for various circular arc machining or surface machining in linkage with linear feed, the CNC rotary worktable can also achieve precise automatic indexing work. The function of the indexing worktable is to index and change the surface of the workpiece, complete the indexing movement, and use it in conjunction with the automatic tool changer to achieve multiple processes on several surfaces with a single workpiece installation. In order to ensure machining accuracy, the positioning accuracy of the indexing worktable is required to be high (ordinary grade ±10″, precision grade ±5″, high precision grade ±3″). 1. CNC rotary worktable The CNC rotary worktable is mainly used for CNC boring and milling machines. Its appearance is almost the same as that of a general-purpose worktable, but its drive is a servo system drive method. It can linkage with other servo feed axes. Figure 8-55 shows the rotary worktable of an automatic tool changing CNC boring machine. Its feed, indexing rotation, and positioning locking are all controlled by given commands. The movement of the worktable is realized by the servo motor transmitting power to the worm wheel 2 via the worm 1 after gear deceleration. Figure 8-55 Rotary worktable of automatic tool changing CNC boring machine 1—Worm 2—Worm wheel 3, 4—Clamping pad 5—Small hydraulic cylinder 6—Piston 7—Spring 8—Steel ball 9—Base 10—Circular grating 11, 12—Bearing In order to eliminate the transmission clearance of the worm pair, a dual-pitch gradually thicker worm is adopted, and the clearance is adjusted by moving the axial position of the worm. The left and right sides of this worm have different pitches, so the tooth thickness of the worm gradually increases from beginning to end. However, because the pitch on the same side is the same, normal meshing can still be maintained. When the worktable is stationary, it must be in a locked state. Therefore, eight pairs of clamping pads 4 and 3 are installed in the radial direction at the bottom of the worm wheel, and the same number of small hydraulic cylinders 5 are evenly distributed on the base 9. When the upper cavity of the small hydraulic cylinder is connected to pressure oil, the piston presses against the steel ball 8, pushes open the clamping pad, and clamps the worm wheel 2. When the worktable needs to rotate, first connect the upper cavity of the small hydraulic cylinder to the oil return circuit. Under the action of the spring 7, the steel ball 8 is lifted, and the clamping pad releases the worm wheel. The guide rail surface of the rotary worktable is supported by large rolling bearings, and the accurate rotation center is maintained by tapered roller bearings 12 and cylindrical roller bearings 11. The positioning accuracy of the CNC rotary worktable mainly depends on the transmission accuracy of the worm pair, so a high-precision worm pair must be used. In a semi-closed loop control system, after actually measuring the static positioning error of the worktable, the position of the angle to be compensated and the compensation value can be determined and memorized in the compensation circuit, and the error compensation is performed by the CNC device. In a fully closed-loop control system, a high-precision circular grating 10 issues an accurate in-position signal of the worktable, which is fed back to the CNC device for control. The rotary worktable is equipped with a zero point. When it performs a zero-return movement, it first presses the limit switch with a stop iron to decelerate the worktable, and then the circular grating or encoder issues a zero signal to accurately stop the worktable at the zero position. The CNC rotary worktable can perform arbitrary angle rotation and indexing, and can also perform continuous rotary feed movement. 2. Indexing worktable The indexing, rotation, and positioning work of the indexing worktable are automatically performed according to the commands of the control system. Usually, the indexing movement is limited to certain specified angles (45°, 60°, 90°, 180°, etc.), but the mechanisms that realize the rotation of the worktable are difficult to meet the requirements of indexing accuracy, so special positioning components are needed to ensure it. Commonly used positioning components include pin positioning, reverse positioning, toothed disk positioning, and steel ball positioning. They feature low friction (0.003-0.005), flexible movement, consistent dynamic/static friction (no stick-slip), high preloaded rigidity, long life, high precision, and easy grease lubrication. Widely used in precision/CNC machines, their main drawback is poor impact resistance and sensitivity to dust, requiring good protection. These guideways use pressurized oil pumped through restrictors into oil pockets, forming a load-bearing oil film that separates contacting surfaces (liquid friction). They offer low friction (0.001-0.005), high efficiency, long precision retention, excellent vibration absorption, and no low-speed stick-slip, but require complex, costly dedicated oil supply systems. Open types only bear vertical loads, while closed types have oil pockets on all surfaces to resist large overturning moments and increase rigidity. Oil supplies are constant pressure or constant flow. Oil must be filtered to 10μm and kept absolutely clean. (2) Guideway clearance and restrictor forms. 1) Guideway clearance represents oil film thickness. Larger clearances increase flow but reduce rigidity and cause drift; smaller clearances increase rigidity but are limited by geometric accuracy. Small/medium machines use 0.01-0.025mm unloaded clearances; large machines use 0.03-0.08mm. 2) Restrictor forms include constant pressure and quantitative systems. Large machines often use single-cavity single-pump quantitative systems for maximum rigidity without restrictors. Constant pressure systems use capillary restrictors (often adjustable spiral grooves, combined for compactness, used in small/medium machines) or membrane feedback restrictors (single/double-sided, used for heavy, unevenly loaded large machines). Each oil pocket requires its own restrictor control. 8.3.2 Common Faults of Guideways and Their Diagnosis and Maintenance Methods. Guideway clearance, rolling guideway preload, straightness, parallelism, lubrication, and protection are critical for machine operation and machining quality. 1. Common repair methods include scraping, fine planing, and grinding. (1) Fine planing is used for heavy machines or deep scratches, heavily dependent on the planer's accuracy. (2) Scraping requires multiple measurements to map wear curves, using equal-height blocks, parallel straightedges, and frame levels to establish scraping reference points every fixed distance, followed by sectioned rough and fine scraping until the entire surface is flat and straight. (3) Grinding can use a "one-time grinding method" where all surfaces are measured for unevenness, rough ground to remove peaks, and fine ground in one setup. The sequence should prioritize associated/high-precision, complex, large, and difficult-to-machine surfaces first. 2. Common problems in guideway repair and their elimination. (1) Guideway scoring/scratches: Caused by foundation settling (requires regular leveling), prolonged short workpiece machining (requires varying installation positions or repairing accuracy), poor lubrication (adjust oil volume/pressure), poor material (treat with electroplating, induction hardening, or add zinc-aluminum-copper alloy plates), poor scraping quality (improve quality), or poor maintenance (enhance care and protection). (2) Moving parts sticking or not moving: Caused by surface scratches (polish with 180-grit sandpaper), pressure plate scratches (remove and adjust clearance), or gibs adjusted too tight (loosen anti-loose screws, adjust gib bolts for flexible movement ensuring a 0.03mm feeler gauge cannot enter, then lock). (3) Uneven machining surfaces at tool joints: Caused by poor guideway straightness (adjust/scrape to within 0.015mm/500mm), loose or excessively bent table gibs (adjust clearance, ensure natural bending <0.05mm/full length), poor machine levelness bending the guideway (adjust installation level/verticality to within 0.02mm/1000mm), rough guideway surfaces or uneven/insufficient scraping contact points (remove table, polish burrs with oilstone/sandpaper, reassemble, and polish manually with chromium oxide and kerosene), tapered bed guideways causing uneven tightness (repair geometric accuracy), temperature changes deforming guideways (adjust seasonally, keep precision machine rooms at constant temperatures), wear losing accuracy (re-scrape/repair), improper oil viscosity or dirty oil causing poor lubrication (use proper viscosity and keep clean), or poor surface lubrication structure increasing resistance (break the full guideway surface into fragmented dot contacts; for large surfaces, divide the saddle guideway into three sections, making the contact points heavier at the outer thirds and lighter in the middle third).

Instance 2: For the CNC machine in Instance 1, during the tool change process when the spindle moves up to the tool claw, there is a misalignment of the magazine tool claw, and a noticeable noise occurs when pulling/inserting the tool, as if it is jamming. Fault analysis and processing: Misalignment of the magazine tool claw indicates that the magazine zero point may have shifted, or there is clearance in the magazine transmission, or the weight of the tools in the magazine is unbalanced, causing it to lean to one side. Because the tool insertion and pulling are unsmooth, it is estimated that the magazine zero point has shifted. Unload all tools from the magazine, manually crank the spindle to near the second reference point of the Y-axis, and use a feeler gauge to measure the gap between the magazine tool claw and the spindle drive key, confirming the shift. Pushing and pulling the magazine by hand cannot utilize the gap to correct it. Adjust parameter 7508 until the gaps between the magazine tool claw and the spindle drive key are basically equal; after restarting, tool changes execute normally. Instance 3: A VMC-65A machining center, after six months of use, experienced loose spindle tool pulling without any alarm information. Fault analysis and processing: The reasons a spindle fails to pull a tool tightly include: deformed or damaged spindle pulling disc springs; the pulling cylinder action not fully completing; or a loose threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet. Upon inspection, it was found that the threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet was loose, causing the tool holder collet to rotate with tool insertion/extraction and retract by about 1.5mm. This machine's pull stud and tool holder collet had no anti-loosening locking measures. When inserting/pulling tools, if the tool center deviates slightly from the spindle taper hole center, eccentric friction occurs between the tool holder collet and the tool holder. Under the combined action of this friction and impact, the thread loosens over time, resulting in the spindle's failure to hold the tool. After locking the threaded connection between the spindle pull stud and the tool holder collet with thread-locking sealant and tightening the lock nut, the fault was eliminated. Instance 4: The tool change system of a CNC machine did not actuate when executing a tool change command; the manipulator arm stopped mid-stroke, and the CRT displayed an alarm number. Checking the manual revealed this alarm number indicated that the tool change system manipulator position detection switch signal was '0' and 'magazine tool change position error'. Fault analysis and processing: Based on the alarm content, it can be diagnosed that the fault occurred in both the tool exchange device and the tool magazine. Because the corresponding position detection switches sent no signals to the PLC input interface, the machine interrupted the tool change. Causes for the switch having no output signal could include inductive switch failure or hydraulic/mechanical issues preventing complete actions. First, use a thin iron sheet to induce the proximity switch in the magazine to rule out the possibility of the magazine's proximity switch failing. Next, check the 'arm extended' switch SQ21 and 'arm retracted' switch SQ22 in the tool change device's manipulator. Since the arm stopped mid-stroke, the output signals of both switches were '0'; testing showed both switches were normal. Manually actuating the 'arm retract' solenoid valve Y21 to return the manipulator to the 'arm retracted' position restored the machine to normal, indicating that the manually controlled solenoid valve could position the tool exchange device, thus ruling out hydraulic or mechanical resistance causing the incomplete action. From the above analysis, the PLC input signals were normal, and the output action execution was correct, so the problem lay within the PLC or improper operation. Observation during operation revealed that the interval between two tool changes was less than the PLC's required time, causing an error in the PLC program execution and leading to the fault. For alarms with only numbers and no text, one must check the data bits, compare them with normal data, clarify the meaning of the data bit, and take corresponding measures. The automatic tool change sequence is: Tool change arm moves left (B to A) -> Tool change arm descends (pulls tool from magazine) -> Tool change arm moves right (A to B) -> Tool change arm ascends -> Tool change arm moves right (B to C, grasps tool in spindle) -> Spindle hydraulic cylinder descends (releases tool) -> Tool change arm descends (pulls tool from spindle) -> Tool change arm rotates 180 degrees (swaps tool positions) -> Tool change arm ascends (inserts tools) -> Spindle hydraulic cylinder ascends (grasps tool) -> Tool change arm moves left (C to B) -> Tool magazine rotates (finds old tool position) -> Tool change arm moves left (B to A, returns old tool to magazine) -> Tool change arm

(2) Automatic tool clamping and chip removal device inside the spindle of the machining center. On machining centers, to achieve automatic loading and unloading of tools on the spindle, their spindles are often designed with automatic tool clamping mechanisms. Figure 8-14 shows the structural diagram of the spindle component of the JCS-018 machining center, with an automatic tool clamping mechanism installed inside and at the rear of the spindle. Tool holder 1 uses a steep taper shank of 7:24, which is conducive to centering and brings convenience for clamping and releasing. While the tail journal of the taper shank is tensioned, the tool bar is clamped at the end of the spindle through the centering and frictional action of the taper shank. Under the action of Belleville spring 5, drawbar 4 constantly maintains a tension of about 10000N, and tightens the tail journal of tool holder 1 through steel ball 12 at the right end of the drawbar. When changing tools, first feed pressure oil into the left cavity of hydraulic cylinder 7 at the tail of the spindle, and hydraulic cylinder piston 6 pushes drawbar 4 to the right. This loosens the tool shank while compressing Belleville spring 5. The rightward movement of drawbar 4 places steel ball 12 at the right end into the flared opening of the sleeve, eliminating the tension on the tool holder. When drawbar 4 continues to move right, the end of the air nozzle pushes the tool loose, allowing the manipulator to easily extract tool holder 1. After the manipulator inserts the replacement tool, the solenoid directional valve acts to feed pressure oil into the right cavity of hydraulic cylinder 7, piston 6 returns leftward to its original position, Belleville spring 5 recovers, and pulls tool holder 1 tight again. When there is no pressure in the right cavity of hydraulic cylinder 7, helical spring 11 makes piston 6 retreat to the leftmost end. When piston 6 is at the left and right limit positions, the corresponding limit travel switches 8 and 10 send unclamping and clamping signals. To keep the spindle taper hole clean, the commonly used method is to blow chips away with compressed air. In Figure 8-14, when the spindle component is in the unclamped tool state, the hydraulic cylinder at the top of the spindle is in tight contact with the drawbar.
