Structurally, issues such as tool clamping, bearing configuration, bearing clearance adjustment, lubrication, and sealing must be well resolved. (1) Spindle. The spindle is an important part of the spindle transmission structure. Its structural dimensions, shape, manufacturing accuracy, material, and heat treatment have a great impact on the working performance of the spindle component. Spindle structures come in various forms depending on the design requirements of the spindle transmission system. During design, a series of issues must be properly handled, such as the clamping of chucks or tools, spindle unloading, positioning and clearance adjustment of spindle bearings, and sealing and lubrication of spindle components. The main dimensional parameters of the spindle include: spindle diameter, inner hole diameter, overhang length, and support span. The basis for evaluating and considering the main dimensional parameters of the spindle is the rigidity of the spindle, structural manufacturability, and the process application range of the spindle assembly. (2) Spindle Bearings. Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

8.1 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Spindle Components. The spindle is the motion axis on a CNC machine tool that drives the tool or workpiece to rotate and generate cutting motion, and it is often the motion axis with the highest single-axis power consumption on a CNC machine tool. Generally, like conventional machine tools, CNC machine tools must also undergo speed variation to enable the spindle to obtain different rotational speeds to adapt to various processing requirements. While changing speeds, the spindle is also required to transmit a certain amount of power and sufficient torque to meet cutting needs. In addition to meeting the requirements of conventional machine tool spindles, CNC machine tool spindles also have the following requirements: 1. A larger speed regulation range and the realization of stepless speed regulation. Only when the machine tool spindle has a high rotational speed and a wide speed regulation range can it ensure that during processing, a more reasonable cutting parameter can be selected to give full play to the cutting performance of the tool. 2. High precision and rigidity, with smooth transmission and low noise. The improvement of machining accuracy of CNC machine tools is closely related to the rigidity of the machine tool's spindle structure, so the manufacturing accuracy and rigidity of its transmission components should be improved. For example, the tooth surface of gears should undergo high-frequency induction heating and quenching to increase wear resistance; the final stage should use helical gear transmission to improve transmission stability; using high-precision bearings and selecting reasonable support spans can improve the rigidity of spindle components. 3. Good vibration resistance and thermal stability. CNC machine tools generally perform rough and finish machining continuously, and during machining, interference from impact forces or alternating forces caused by uneven machining allowances, unbalanced moving parts, and self-excited vibration during the cutting process may cause the spindle to vibrate, affecting machining accuracy and surface roughness, and in severe cases, even destroying the tool or part, making machining impossible. Therefore, in the machine tool spindle structure, each main component must not only have a certain static rigidity but also sufficient vibration resistance to suppress vibrations caused by various interferences. Vibration resistance is usually measured by dynamic rigidity or dynamic compliance; for example, the dynamic rigidity of spindle components depends on parameters such as the equivalent static rigidity, damping ratio, and natural frequency of the spindle. During the cutting process of the machine tool, the heat generated by the spindle structure causes thermal deformation of its internal components, destroying the relative positional accuracy and motion accuracy between components, thereby causing machining errors; moreover, thermal deformation limits the improvement of cutting parameters, reduces transmission efficiency, and even affects productivity. The thermal stability of spindle components is often achieved through measures such as maintaining appropriate fit clearances between components, circulating lubrication, and maintaining thermal balance. 8.1.1 Typical Structure and Assembly Adjustment of Spindle Components. 1. Common Structures of Spindles. Currently, the transmission structures of CNC machine tool spindles can be roughly divided into the following categories: (1) Main transmission with a direct connection between the motor and the spindle. As shown in Figure 8-1a, this direct-drive structure is generally rotated directly by a variable-speed motor driving the spindle, which greatly simplifies the structure of the spindle box and spindle, and effectively improves the rigidity of the spindle components. However, the output torque of the spindle is small, and motor heating has a significant impact on spindle accuracy, so its application is subject to certain limitations. (2) Main transmission with one-stage speed variation. As shown in Figure 8-1b, one-stage speed variation is mostly accomplished by a synchronous belt. Its advantages are a simple structure, convenient installation and debugging, and to a certain extent, it can meet the speed and torque output requirements. However, the spindle speed regulation range ratio is still the same as the motor's, constrained by the motor's speed regulation range ratio. Its advantage is a wide speed variation range, with a maximum speed reaching 8000r/min, which basically meets the transmission requirements of most current CNC machine tools and is easy to realize rich control functions; its simple structure and convenient installation and debugging can meet the control requirements of current mid-to-high-end CNC machine tools. However, for increasingly high speed demands, this configuration method is difficult to satisfy. (3) Main transmission with variable speed gears. As shown in Figure 8-1c, this configuration method is mostly adopted in large and medium-sized CNC machine tools. In actual production, the spindle does not need to maintain constant power throughout the entire speed range; generally, constant power transmission is required in the medium and high-speed sections, and constant torque transmission is required in the low-speed section. To ensure that the CNC machine tool spindle has a large torque at low speeds and that the spindle's speed range is as large as possible, some CNC systems are equipped with gear speed variation on the basis of the stepless speed variation of the machine tool spindle motor, becoming segmented stepless speed variation. In the segmented stepless speed variation system with gear speed variation, the forward and reverse starting, stopping, and braking of the spindle are realized by directly controlling the motor, while the speed variation of the spindle is realized by the combination of the stepless speed variation of the motor speed and the stepped speed variation of the gears. Gear stepped speed variation mechanisms usually adopt two speed variation forms: hydraulic shift fork speed variation and electromagnetic clutch speed variation. 1) Hydraulic shift fork speed variation. The principle and form of the hydraulic shift fork speed variation mechanism are shown in Figure 8-2. The shift fork of the sliding gear is connected to the piston rod of the variable speed hydraulic cylinder. By changing different oil flow paths, the triple gear can obtain three different speed variation positions. As shown in Figure 8-2a, when hydraulic cylinder 1 is fed with pressure oil and hydraulic cylinder 5 is depressurized, piston rod 2 drives shift fork

motion. In order to ensure the transmission accuracy and working stability of the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, the following requirements should be noted when designing the mechanical transmission device: ① Improve transmission accuracy and rigidity. The accuracy of the CNC machine tool itself, especially the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the feed drive device, plays a key role in the machining accuracy of parts and is a characteristic indicator of CNC machine tools. Therefore, it is first necessary to ensure the machining accuracy of each transmission part, especially to improve the transmission accuracy of the ball screw and nut pair (linear feed system) and worm gear pair (circular feed system). In addition, adding reduction gears to the feed transmission chain to reduce the pulse equivalent (i.e., the distance the worktable moves when the servo system receives one command pulse) can also improve transmission accuracy from a system design perspective; transmission accuracy and rigidity can also be improved by pre-tensioning the transmission ball screw to eliminate the clearance of transmission parts such as gears and worm gears. ② Reduce the inertia of moving parts. The inertia of transmission parts affects both the starting and braking characteristics of the feed drive system, especially for parts running at high speeds, where the influence of inertia is even greater. Under the premise of satisfying transmission strength and rigidity, the mass of the actuating components should be minimized as much as possible, and the diameter and mass of rotating parts should be reduced to decrease the inertia of moving parts. ③ Reduce the frictional resistance of moving parts. The frictional resistance of the mechanical transmission structure mainly comes from the lead screw nut pair and the guide rails. In the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, to reduce frictional resistance, eliminate low-speed feed crawling, and improve the stability of the entire servo feed system, ball screws, rolling guides, plastic guides, and hydrostatic guides are widely used. ④ Fast response speed. The so-called fast response characteristic refers to the response speed of the feed drive system to input command signals and how quickly the transient process ends. Fast response is a dynamic performance of the servo feed system and reflects the tracking accuracy of the system. During the workpiece machining process, the worktable should be able to sensitively and accurately track instructions within the specified speed range, without missing steps or taking extra steps during operation. The response speed of the feed drive system not only affects the machining efficiency of the machine tool but also affects the machining accuracy. In the design, the rigidity, clearance, friction, and moment of inertia of the machine tool worktable and transmission mechanism should be optimized to the best possible values to improve the fast response characteristics of the servo feed system. ⑤ Strong overload capacity. Because the motor frequently changes direction and the acceleration and deceleration are very fast, the motor may work under overload conditions. This requires the motor to have a strong overload capacity, generally requiring it to withstand an overload of 4 to 6 times for several minutes without damage. ⑥ Good stability and long service life. Stability is the most basic condition for the normal operation of the servo feed drive system, particularly that it must not crawl under low feed speeds and must be able to adapt to changes in external loads without resonance. Stability is related to the system's inertia, rigidity, damping, and gain. Properly selecting these parameters to achieve optimal working performance is the goal of servo feed system design. The service life of a servo feed drive system mainly refers to the length of time it can maintain the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the CNC machine tool, that is, the ability of each transmission component to maintain its original manufacturing accuracy. Therefore, the materials, heat treatment methods, and processing technologies of each transmission component should be reasonably selected, and appropriate lubrication methods and protective measures should be adopted to extend its service life. ⑦ Convenient operation and maintenance. CNC machine tools are high-precision automatic control machine tools, mainly used for single-piece, small-to-medium batch, high-precision, and complex production and machining. CNC machine tools have a high utilization rate, so the structural design of the feed drive system should facilitate maintenance and care, minimizing the maintenance workload to improve the utilization rate of the machine tool. 8.2.1 Typical Structures of Feed Drive Components Common mechanical transmission devices include ball screw pairs, hydrostatic worm-rack drives, preloaded double gear-racks, and linear motors. 1. Ball Screw Pair (1) Composition and Structure A ball screw consists of four parts: a lead screw, a nut, balls, and a ball return device. Arc-shaped helical grooves are machined on the screw and the nut. When they are assembled together, a helical raceway is formed, and the raceway is filled with balls. When the screw rotates, to maintain the continuous operation of the screw and nut, the balls complete their circulation through the return device on the nut. Based on the ball circulation method, ball screw and nut pairs are divided into internal circulation and external circulation types, as shown in Figures 8-23 and 8-24. Figures 8-23b and 8-24b respectively show the number of rotating turns of the balls in the internal and external circulation ball screw and nut pairs, usually 2 to 6 turns. When the internal circulation ball screw pair is working, the balls are always in contact with the screw. Its nut structure is compact, positioning is reliable, rigidity is good, it is not easy to wear, the return raceway is short, balls are not easily jammed, and friction loss is small. The disadvantage is that the structure is complex and manufacturing is difficult. When the external circulation ball screw pair is working, the balls leave contact with the screw. Its manufacturing process is simple, it is widely used, and the radial dimension of the nut is large; however, because the end of the bent pipe is used as a ball blocker, it has poor rigidity, is

and has a large-range speed variation capability; its disadvantages are a complex structure, the need for an additional lubrication and temperature control system, and higher costs. In addition, manufacturing and maintenance are more difficult. Figure 8-21 is a schematic diagram of the spindle structure of the XH754 horizontal machining center, which achieves speed variation through single-stage belt transmission. 8.1.2 Common Faults and Diagnostics of Spindle Components. 1. Spindle heating. (1) Front and rear spindle bearings are damaged or bearings are not clean. Elimination method: Replace bad bearings, clean out dirt. (2) Spindle bearing preload is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the preload. (3) Lubricating oil is dirty or contains impurities. Elimination method: Clean the spindle box, replace the lubricating oil. (4) The spindle front end cover and the spindle box body gland are galled. Elimination method: Grind the spindle box front end cover so that it presses tightly against the spindle front bearing, leaving a clearance of 0.02-0.05mm between the bearing and the cover. (5) Bearing lubricating grease is depleted or there is too much lubricating grease. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. 2. The spindle stops during heavy cutting. (1) The belt connecting the motor and the spindle is too loose. Elimination method: Move the motor base, tension the belt, and then retighten the motor base. (2) There is oil on the surface of the belt. Elimination method: Wash with gasoline and wipe clean before reinstalling. (3) The friction clutch is adjusted too loosely or is worn. Elimination method: Adjust the clutch, grind or replace the friction plates. (4) The belt has been used for too long and failed. Elimination method: Replace with a new belt. 3. Spindle noise. (1) Lack of lubrication. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. (2) Poor transmission balance between the small pulley and the large pulley. Elimination method: The balance weight on the pulley has fallen off; perform dynamic balancing again. (3) Bearings are scored or damaged. Elimination method: Replace the bearings. (4) Poor balance of parts at the end of the shaft. Elimination method: Redo dynamic balancing. (5) Gear meshing clearance is uneven or gears are damaged. Elimination method: Adjust the meshing clearance or replace with new gears. (6) The transmission bearing is damaged or the transmission shaft is bent. Elimination method: Repair or replace the bearing, straighten the transmission shaft. 4. Spindle has no lubricating oil circulation or insufficient lubrication. (1) The hydraulic pump rotation direction is incorrect, or the clearance is too large. Elimination method: Change the hydraulic pump rotation direction, repair the hydraulic pump. (2) The suction pipe is not inserted below the oil level of the oil tank. Elimination method: Insert the suction pipe 2/3 below the oil level. (3) Oil pipes or filters are blocked. Elimination method: Eliminate the blockage. (4) Lubricating oil pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply pressure. 5. Lubricating oil leakage. (1) The amount of lubricating oil is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply amount. (2) Check whether seals in various places are damaged. Elimination method: Replace seals. (3) Pipe fittings are damaged. Elimination method: Replace pipe fittings. 6. Tool cannot be clamped. (1) Belleville spring displacement is small. Elimination method: Adjust the stroke length of the Belleville spring. (2) Spring collet is damaged. Elimination method: Replace the spring collet. (3) Belleville spring failure. Elimination method: Replace the Belleville spring. (4) The pull stud on the tool holder is too large. Elimination method: Replace the pull stud and install it correctly. (5) Check whether the nut on the tool unclamp/clamp spring is loose. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the clamp spring clockwise so that its maximum working load is 13kN. 7. Tool cannot be unclamped after being clamped. (1) Unclamp spring is compressed too tightly. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the unclamp spring counterclockwise so that its maximum working load does not exceed 13kN. (2) Hydraulic cylinder pressure and stroke are insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust hydraulic pressure and piston stroke switch. 8. Spindle fails to change speeds. (1) Shifting hydraulic cylinder pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Detect working pressure; if lower than rated pressure, adjust it. (2) Shifting hydraulic cylinder is worn or stuck. Elimination method: Remove burrs or galling, clean and reassemble. (3) Shifting hydraulic cylinder fork has fallen off. Elimination method: Repair or replace. (4) Shifting hydraulic cylinder bypasses oil or leaks internally. Elimination method: Replace seal ring. (5) Shifting solenoid valve is stuck. Elimination method: Repair the solenoid valve and clean it. (6) Shifting composite switch has failed. Elimination method: Replace the switch. 8.1.3 Spindle Component Fault Maintenance Examples. The tool magazine for storing tools has a large capacity; it can be installed on the side or top of the spindle box, or as an independent component outside the machine tool, with tools transported by a handling device. Compared with the turret spindle head, the automatic tool changing system with a tool magazine ensures that the CNC machine tool's spindle box has only one spindle, allowing the spindle component design to fully enhance its rigidity, thus meeting the requirements of precision machining. In addition, the tool magazine can store a large number of tools, enabling multi-process machining of complex parts, which significantly improves the machine's adaptability and processing efficiency. Therefore, automatic tool changing devices with tool magazines are particularly suitable for CNC drilling, milling, and boring machines. 2. Tool magazine. The tool magazine is the main component of the automatic tool changing device; its capacity, layout, and specific structure have a great impact on the design of CNC machine tools. Depending on the required capacity and tool retrieval method, tool magazines can be designed in various forms. Figure 8-59 lists the most commonly used types. Figures 8-59a to d show single-disk tool magazines. To adapt to the machine tool spindle layout, the tool axes in the magazine can be configured in different directions (as shown in Figures 8-59a to c). Figure 8-59d shows a disk tool magazine where tools can be flipped 90 degrees; this structure simplifies the tool retrieval action. The single-disk tool magazine has a simple structure, typically holding 15 to 30 tools, and tool retrieval is relatively convenient, making it the most widely used. Figure 8-59e is a drum-type (also known as hedgehog-type) tool magazine, which is very compact and offers a larger capacity within the same space, but the tool selection and retrieval actions are more complex. Figure 8-59f is a chain-type tool magazine, which provides great structural flexibility, can store a large number of tools, and makes tool selection and retrieval very simple. For long chains, the number of supporting sprockets can be increased to fold and loop the chain, improving space utilization. Figures 8-59g and 8-59h show multi-disk and grid-type tool magazines respectively. Although they are compact, their tool selection and retrieval actions are complex, so they are rarely used. The typical capacity of these tool magazines is 10 to 60 tools, but with the development of machining technology, there seems to be a trend toward even larger capacities. The chain-type tool magazine is one of the more frequently used forms. In this magazine, tool pockets are fixed on the chain links. A commonly used type is the single-row chain-type tool magazine, as shown in Figure 8-60a, generally storing fewer than 30 tools, occasionally up to 60. If a further increase in storage capacity is needed, a multi-row chain-type tool magazine can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60b; or a chain-type tool magazine with an extended chain can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60c. 3. Tool changing methods. In the automatic tool changing device of a CNC machine, the mechanism that transfers and loads/unloads tools between the tool magazine and the machine spindle is called the tool exchange device. Tool exchange methods in CNC machines are generally divided into two categories: tool changing without a manipulator and tool changing with a manipulator. (1) Tool changing without a manipulator. A tool changing system without a manipulator generally involves placing the tool magazine at a position the machine spindle can reach, or moving the entire magazine (or a specific tool position) to a location accessible by the spindle box. Additionally, the tool storage direction in the magazine is generally consistent with the tool loading direction on the spindle. During a tool change, the spindle moves to the changing position on the magazine and directly retrieves or returns the tool. For example, in the machining center shown in Figure 2-59, the tool change sequence is as follows: ① According to the tool change command, the machine worktable quickly moves to the right, moving the workpiece away from under the spindle, and the tool magazine moves under the spindle, aligning an empty tool pocket with the spindle. ② The spindle box descends, placing the used tool from the spindle into the empty pocket of the tool magazine. ③ The spindle box ascends, and the tool magazine rotates to align the tool required for the next step with the spindle. ④ The spindle box descends, inserting the tool into the machine spindle. ⑤ The spindle box and spindle ascend with the tool. ⑥ The machine worktable quickly returns to the left, the tool magazine moves away from under the spindle, and the workpiece moves under the spindle, aligning the tool with the machining surface of the workpiece. ⑦ The spindle box descends, and the tool on the spindle machines the workpiece. ⑧ After machining, the spindle box ascends, and the tool retracts from the workpiece. Tool changing without a manipulator has a relatively simple structure but involves cumbersome actions, long changing times, and relatively small magazine capacities. (2) Tool changing with a manipulator. In machining centers, using a manipulator (tool changing arm) for tool exchange is the most widely applied method because it requires short tool changing times and offers flexible actions. Fault analysis and processing: Misalignment of the magazine tool claw indicates that the magazine zero point may have shifted, or there is clearance in the magazine transmission, or the weight of the tools in the magazine is unbalanced, causing it to lean to one side. Because the tool insertion and pulling are unsmooth, it is estimated that the magazine zero point has shifted. Unload all tools from the magazine, manually crank the spindle to near the second reference point of the Y-axis, and use a feeler gauge to measure the gap between the magazine tool claw and the spindle drive key, confirming the shift. Pushing and pulling the magazine by hand cannot utilize the gap to correct it. Instance 3: A VMC-65A machining center, after six months of use, experienced loose spindle tool pulling without any alarm information. Fault analysis and processing: The reasons a spindle fails to pull a tool tightly include: deformed or damaged spindle pulling disc springs; the pulling cylinder action not fully completing; or a loose threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet. Upon inspection, it was found that the threaded connection between the pull stud and the tool holder collet was loose, causing the tool holder collet to rotate with tool insertion/extraction and retract by about 1.5mm. This machine's pull stud and tool holder collet had no anti-loosening locking measures. When inserting/pulling tools, if the tool center deviates slightly from the spindle taper hole center, eccentric friction occurs between the tool holder collet and the tool holder. Under the combined action of this friction and impact, the thread loosens over time, resulting in the spindle's failure to hold the tool. After locking the threaded connection between the spindle pull stud and the tool holder collet with thread-locking sealant and tightening the lock nut, the fault was eliminated. Instance 4: The tool change system of a CNC machine did not actuate when executing a tool change command; the manipulator arm stopped mid-stroke, and the CRT displayed an alarm number. Checking the manual revealed this alarm number indicated that the tool change system manipulator position detection switch signal was '0' and 'magazine tool change position error'. Fault analysis and processing: Based on the alarm content, it can be diagnosed that the fault occurred in both the tool exchange device and the tool magazine. Because the corresponding position detection switches sent no signals to the PLC input interface, the machine interrupted the tool change. Causes for the switch having no output signal could include inductive switch failure or hydraulic/mechanical issues preventing complete actions. First, use a thin iron sheet to induce the proximity switch in the magazine to rule out the possibility of the magazine's proximity switch failing. Next, check the 'arm extended' switch SQ21 and 'arm retracted' switch SQ22 in the tool change device's manipulator. Since the arm stopped mid-stroke, the output signals of both switches were '0'; testing showed both switches were normal. Manually actuating the 'arm retract' solenoid valve Y21 to return the manipulator to the 'arm retracted' position restored the machine to normal, indicating that the manually controlled solenoid valve could position the tool exchange device, thus ruling out hydraulic or mechanical resistance causing the incomplete action. From the above analysis, the PLC input signals were normal, and the output action execution was correct, so the problem lay within the PLC or improper operation. Observation during operation revealed that the interval between two tool changes was less than the PLC's required time, causing an error in the PLC program execution and leading to the fault. For alarms with only numbers and no text, one must check the data bits, compare them with normal data, clarify the meaning of the data bit, and take corresponding measures. Instance 5: In a vertical machining center, when the tool change arm translates to C, there is no tool pulling action; its schematic is shown in Figure 8-66. Fault analysis and processing: Observing the mechanical motion process, the initial state of the ATC action is: the spindle holds the old tool to be exchanged; the tool change arm is at position B; the tool change arm is in the upper position; the tool magazine has positioned the new tool to be exchanged. The automatic tool change sequence is: Tool change arm moves left (B to A) -> Tool change arm descends (pulls tool from magazine) -> Tool change arm moves right (A to B) -> Tool change arm ascends -> Tool change arm moves right (B to C, grasps tool in spindle) -> Spindle hydraulic cylinder descends (releases tool) -> Tool change arm descends (pulls tool from spindle) -> Tool change arm rotates 180 degrees (swaps tool positions) -> Tool change arm ascends (inserts tools) -> Spindle hydraulic cylinder ascends (grasps tool) -> Tool change arm moves left (C to B) -> Tool magazine rotates (finds old tool position) -> Tool change arm moves left (B to A, returns old tool to magazine) -> Tool change arm

If there is no torque measuring device, slightly dampening feeling when turning the spindle by hand is sufficient. Thereafter, testing and on-site cutting proved this method to be feasible. When boring the same ϕ80mm hole, the roundness error was reduced from 0.03mm to 0.005mm, fully meeting the machining requirements of the part. Example 7: The spindle of an XK5040-1 could not rotate after starting up. Fault cause analysis and elimination: Checking the motor, the condition was good; the transmission key was not damaged. After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

8.2 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Feed Drive Components The feed drive component is the main part of the servo feed system, mainly composed of a transmission mechanism, motion conversion mechanism, guiding mechanism, and executing component. It is the actuator that provides the motion and power required to realize the forming machining motion. Since the feed motion of CNC machine tools is the direct object of digital control, the final positional accuracy and contour accuracy of the machined workpiece are related to the transmission accuracy, sensitivity, and stability of the feed motion. In order to ensure the transmission accuracy and working stability of the feed drive system of CNC machine tools, the following requirements should be noted when designing the mechanical transmission device: ① Improve transmission accuracy and rigidity. The accuracy of the CNC machine tool itself, especially the transmission accuracy and positioning accuracy of the feed drive device, plays a key role in the machining accuracy of parts and is a characteristic indicator of CNC machine tools. Therefore, it is first necessary to ensure the machining accuracy of each transmission part

Example 1: In a machining center, the spindle motor vibrates enormously when the spindle speed is 600r/min, and the entire spindle head vibrates; at 1500r/min, the swing amplitude decreases, but the vibration frequency increases; when the spindle is rotating at high speed and the power is cut off, the motor continues to vibrate during the coasting process, proving it to be a non-electrical fault; disconnecting the transmission belt between the motor and the spindle and starting the motor, the vibration still exists. Analysis and processing: Based on the directly proportional relationship between vibration frequency and speed, it was preliminarily judged as rotor eccentricity or looseness. Disassembling the motor, it was found that the motor rotor bearing seat had worn more than 0.02mm due to the inner ring spinning. Considering that this machine tool had been used for more than ten years, expectations for its performance were not high, plus there was no ready-made rotor for replacement, it was decided to use a spray coating repair method for the bearing seat while replacing the bearing, achieving good results. Example 2: Spindle cannot orient. Fault phenomenon: In a vertical machining center using SINUMERIK 810M equipped with a 6SC6502 spindle drive, during debugging, when the spindle speed was greater than 200r/min, a fault occurred where the spindle could not be positioned. Analysis and processing: To confirm the cause of the fault, the following tests were conducted during maintenance: ① Input and sequentially execute the "S100M03; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ② Input and sequentially execute the "S100M04; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ③ Input and sequentially execute the "S200M03; M05; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ④ Directly input and sequentially execute the "S200M03; M19" command; the machine tool could not position. Based on the above tests, it can be confirmed that the system and drive are working normally. Checking the actual speed of the spindle motor, it was found that the actual spindle speed of this machine tool differed greatly from the commanded value. When executing the S200 command, the actual machine tool spindle speed was 300r/min. Adjusting the spindle drive parameters to match the actual spindle speed with the commanded value eliminated the fault, and the machine tool returned to normal. Example 3: Automatic process cannot proceed after spindle orientation. Fault phenomenon: In a vertical machining center using SINUMERIK 810M, when executing an automatic tool change command, after the spindle completes orientation (M19), the program stops executing. Analysis and processing: After the machine tool encountered the fault, it could be restored to normal by restarting. When executing a program block without an M19 command, the machine tool ran normally. Therefore, it can be determined that the fault was caused by the M19 spindle directional orientation, meaning the M19 command did not have an execution completion reply (FIN) signal. When checking the M19 status, it was found that the positioning position was correct, and the spindle also had a corresponding holding torque, so abnormal action of the spindle positioning itself could be ruled out. Checking against the machine tool's electrical schematic diagram, to improve the reliability of tool changing, the machine tool was equipped with a spindle in-position contactless switch. The cause of the fault was the damage to this switch, which prevented the generation of the M19 reply (FIN) signal. After replacing the switch, the machine tool returned to normal. Example 4: A vertical CNC milling machine using the SINUMERIK 802D CNC system failed to unload tools after a long period of downtime. Checking the CNC system PLC and output interfaces, they were all normal, and the two proximity switches at the rear also worked normally, but the rear cylinder had no action when unclamping the tool. Checking the machine tool air pump, the working pressure was normal, but there was no oil in the machine tool's lubricator. It was preliminarily judged that the fault was caused by the cylinder jamming, making the spindle unable to unclamp the tool. Later, after soaking in a rust remover for a week to remove the rust spots and reassembling the machine tool, tool loading and unloading returned to normal. Analysis of the cause of the fault: Although it was directly caused by the rusting of the cylinder, the fundamental cause of the fault was the lack of oil in the lubricator, preventing the piston from being lubricated. Long-term parking caused moisture in the compressed air to condense and rust on the cylinder wall and piston. After ruling out the influence of other factors, the tool unclamping mechanism was inspected. When the pressure dropped to 4MP

8.3 Common Fault Analysis of Guideways. The quality of guideways has a great impact on the rigidity, machining accuracy, and service life of machine tools. As an important part of the machine tool feed system, CNC machine tools have higher requirements for guideways than ordinary machine tools. The basic requirements for guideways are as follows: ① High guiding accuracy. Guiding accuracy mainly refers to the straightness or roundness of moving parts when moving along the guideway. The main factors affecting guiding accuracy include the geometric accuracy of the guideway, contact accuracy of the guideway, structural form of the guideway, rigidity and thermal deformation of the moving and supporting guideways, assembly quality, and the stiffness of the oil film between hydrodynamic and hydrostatic guideways. ② Sufficient rigidity. Guideway rigidity refers to the ability of the guideway to resist deformation under dynamic and static loads. The guideway must have sufficient rigidity to ensure that it does not undergo excessive deformation under static loads, thereby ensuring the relative position and guiding accuracy between various components. ③ Good friction characteristics. The long-term operation of the moving guideway along the supporting guideway surface will cause uneven wear, destroy the guiding accuracy of the guideway, and thus affect the machining accuracy of the machine tool. The wear forms of guideways include abrasive wear, galling and thermal welding, fatigue, and crushing. ④ Smoothness of low-speed movement. When moving at low speeds, the moving guideway, acting as a moving component, is prone to stick-slip (crawling) phenomena. The stick-slip of feed motion will reduce workpiece accuracy, so it is required that the guideway moves smoothly at low speeds without stick-slip, which is especially important for high-precision machine tools. ⑤ Good damping characteristics (no vibration at high speeds). ⑥ Good structural manufacturability. 8.3.1 Structural Characteristics and Adjustment of Guideways. Currently, the guideways used in CNC machine tools are mainly of three types: sliding guideways, rolling guideways, and hydrostatic guideways. 1. Sliding Guideways. (1) Types of sliding guideways. The magnitude of rigidity, ease of manufacturing, adjustability, minimization of friction loss, and the ability to maintain initial precision of sliding guideways largely depend on their cross-sectional shapes (as shown in Figure 8-37). 1) Inverted-V (mountain-shaped) and V-shaped cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37a, this type of cross-section has high guiding accuracy, and after wear, it automatically compensates by sinking under its own weight. A convex lower guideway is conducive to discharging dirt but does not easily retain oil, often used in lathes; a concave lower guideway is the opposite, often used in grinders with a top angle generally at 90°. 2) Rectangular cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37b, this type is convenient to manufacture and repair, has a large load-bearing capacity, and new guideways have high guiding accuracy. However, it cannot automatically compensate after wear and requires gib adjustment, which affects guiding accuracy. 3) Cylindrical cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37c, this type is easy to manufacture and can achieve precision fits, but it is highly sensitive to temperature changes, easily jamming when clearances are small, and having poor guiding accuracy when clearances are large. Compared to the other cross-sections, it is less commonly used. 4) Flat annular cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37d, this type is suitable for rotary motion, easy to manufacture, and can withstand large axial forces, but guiding accuracy is relatively poor. Switching to a conical annular cross-section (Figure 8-37e) provides better guiding performance. 5) Dovetail cross-sections. As shown in Figure 8-37f, this type has a compact structure and can withstand overturning moments, but its rigidity is relatively poor, and manufacturing and maintenance are inconvenient. It is suitable for situations where guiding accuracy requirements are not excessively high. (2) Surface treatment of sliding guideways. The materials used for sliding guideways in CNC machine tools are cast iron attached with plastic or steel-inlaid attached with plastic. Commonly used guideway plastics include PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) soft tapes and epoxy-based wear-resistant coatings. 1) Characteristics of PTFE guideway soft tapes: ① Good friction characteristics: The dynamic and static friction coefficients of the metal-PTFE soft tape are basically consistent. ② Good wear resistance: The PTFE soft tape material contains bronze, copper disulfide, and graphite, so it has self-lubricating properties and does not require high-quality lubricating oil. In addition, the plastic is soft, so even if metal chips and dust are embedded, it will not damage the metal guideway surface and the soft tape itself, prolonging the service life of the guideway pair. ③ Good vibration damping: The damping performance of plastic is good, resulting in effective vibration reduction and noise elimination, which helps improve movement speed. ④ Good manufacturability: It lowers the hardness and surface quality requirements for the metal substrate to which the plastic is bonded, and the plastic is easy to process (milling, planing, grinding, scraping), allowing the guideway pair contact surface to achieve excellent surface quality. PTFE soft tapes are widely used in the motion guideways of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools. The application process is simple: first, machine the bonding surface to a roughness of

sliders, steel balls, retainers, and end caps. Sliders move along the fixed guideway, with balls rolling in circular arc grooves and circulating through end caps. They feature low friction (0.003-0.005), flexible movement, consistent dynamic/static friction (no stick-slip), high preloaded rigidity, long life, high precision, and easy grease lubrication. Widely used in precision/CNC machines, their main drawback is poor impact resistance and sensitivity to dust, requiring good protection. They can be installed horizontally, vertically, or inclined, and parallel installations are common. Their error-averaging effect reduces base installation errors to about 1/3 in slider movement. Guideway and slider fixing methods include setscrews, wedges, or pressure plates. Installation requires thorough cleaning, checking for burrs/rust, and ensuring screw holes align perfectly to prevent accuracy loss. Installation involves gently bolting the guideway against the reference side, tightening side devices, placing the slider, and tightening screws diagonally. Post-installation checks ensure smooth, consistent resistance and proper straightness/parallelism. 3. Liquid Hydrostatic Guideways. (1) Basic principles. These guideways use pressurized oil pumped through restrictors into oil pockets, forming a load-bearing oil film that separates contacting surfaces (liquid friction). They offer low friction (0.001-0.005), high efficiency, long precision retention, excellent vibration absorption, and no low-speed stick-slip, but require complex, costly dedicated oil supply systems. Open types only bear vertical loads, while closed types have oil pockets on all surfaces to resist large overturning moments and increase rigidity. Oil supplies are constant pressure or constant flow. Oil must be filtered to 10μm and kept absolutely clean. (2) Guideway clearance and restrictor forms. 1) Guideway clearance represents oil film thickness. Larger clearances increase flow but reduce rigidity and cause drift; smaller clearances increase rigidity but are limited by geometric accuracy. Small/medium machines use 0.01-0.025mm unloaded clearances; large machines use 0.03-0.08mm. 2) Restrictor forms include constant pressure and quantitative systems. Large machines often use single-cavity single-pump quantitative systems for maximum rigidity without restrictors. Constant pressure systems use capillary restrictors (often adjustable spiral grooves, combined for compactness, used in small/medium machines) or membrane feedback restrictors (single/double-sided, used for heavy, unevenly loaded large machines). Each oil pocket requires its own restrictor control. 8.3.2 Common Faults of Guideways and Their Diagnosis and Maintenance Methods. Guideway clearance, rolling guideway preload, straightness, parallelism, lubrication, and protection are critical for machine operation and machining quality. 1. Common repair methods include scraping, fine planing, and grinding. (1) Fine planing is used for heavy machines or deep scratches, heavily dependent on the planer's accuracy. (2) Scraping requires multiple measurements to map wear curves, using equal-height blocks, parallel straightedges, and frame levels to establish scraping reference points every fixed distance, followed by sectioned rough and fine scraping until the entire surface is flat and straight. (3) Grinding can use a "one-time grinding method" where all surfaces are measured for unevenness, rough ground to remove peaks, and fine ground in one setup. The sequence should prioritize associated/high-precision, complex, large, and difficult-to-machine surfaces first. 2. Common problems in guideway repair and their elimination. (1) Guideway scoring/scratches: Caused by foundation settling (requires regular leveling), prolonged short workpiece machining (requires varying installation positions or repairing accuracy), poor lubrication (adjust oil volume/pressure), poor material (treat with electroplating, induction hardening, or add zinc-aluminum-copper alloy plates), poor scraping quality (improve quality), or poor maintenance (enhance care and protection). (2) Moving parts sticking or not moving: Caused by surface scratches (polish with 180-grit sandpaper), pressure plate scratches (remove and adjust clearance), or gibs adjusted too tight (loosen anti-loose screws, adjust gib bolts for flexible movement ensuring a 0.03mm feeler gauge cannot enter, then lock). (3) Uneven machining surfaces at tool joints: Caused by poor guideway straightness (adjust/scrape to within 0.015mm/500mm), loose or excessively bent table gibs (adjust clearance, ensure natural bending <0.05mm/full length), poor machine levelness bending the guideway (adjust installation level/verticality to within 0.02mm/1000mm), rough guideway surfaces or uneven/insufficient scraping contact points (remove table, polish burrs with oilstone/sandpaper, reassemble, and polish manually with chromium oxide and kerosene), tapered bed guideways causing uneven tightness (repair geometric accuracy), temperature changes deforming guideways (adjust seasonally, keep precision machine rooms at constant temperatures), wear losing accuracy (re-scrape/repair), improper oil viscosity or dirty oil causing poor lubrication (use proper viscosity and keep clean), or poor surface lubrication structure increasing resistance (break the full guideway surface into fragmented dot contacts; for large surfaces, divide the saddle guideway into three sections, making the contact points heavier at the outer thirds and lighter in the middle third).

top_chunks.text: 8.1 Structure and Common Fault Analysis of Spindle Components. The spindle is the motion axis on a CNC machine tool that drives the tool or workpiece to rotate and generate cutting motion, and it is often the motion axis with the highest single-axis power consumption on a CNC machine tool. Generally, like conventional machine tools, CNC machine tools must also undergo speed variation to enable the spindle to obtain different rotational speeds to adapt to various processing requirements. While changing speeds, the spindle is also required to transmit a certain amount of power and sufficient torque to meet cutting needs. In addition to meeting the requirements of conventional machine tool spindles, CNC machine tool spindles also have the following requirements: 1. A larger speed regulation range and the realization of stepless speed regulation. Only when the machine tool spindle has a high rotational speed and a wide speed regulation range can it ensure that during processing, a more reasonable cutting parameter can be selected to give full play to the cutting performance of the tool. 2. High precision and rigidity, with smooth transmission and low noise. The improvement of machining accuracy of CNC machine tools is closely related to the rigidity of the machine tool's spindle structure, so the manufacturing accuracy and rigidity of its transmission components should be improved. For example, the tooth surface of gears should undergo high-frequency induction heating and quenching to increase wear resistance; the final stage should use helical gear transmission to improve transmission stability; using high-precision bearings and selecting reasonable support spans can improve the rigidity of spindle components. 3. Good vibration resistance and thermal stability. CNC machine tools generally perform rough and finish machining continuously, and during machining, interference from impact forces or alternating forces caused by uneven machining allowances, unbalanced moving parts, and self-excited vibration during the cutting process may cause the spindle to vibrate, affecting machining accuracy and surface roughness, and in severe cases, even destroying the tool or part, making machining impossible. Therefore, in the machine tool spindle structure, each main component must not only have a certain static rigidity but also sufficient vibration resistance to suppress vibrations caused by various interferences. Vibration resistance is usually measured by dynamic rigidity or dynamic compliance; for example, the dynamic rigidity of spindle components depends on parameters such as the equivalent static rigidity, damping ratio, and natural frequency of the spindle. During the cutting process of the machine tool, the heat generated by the spindle structure causes thermal deformation of its internal components, destroying the relative positional accuracy and motion accuracy between components, thereby causing machining errors; moreover, thermal deformation limits the improvement of cutting parameters, reduces transmission efficiency, and even affects productivity. The thermal stability of spindle components is often achieved through measures such as maintaining appropriate fit clearances between components, circulating lubrication, and maintaining thermal balance. 8.1.1 Typical Structure and Assembly Adjustment of Spindle Components. 1. Common Structures of Spindles. Currently, the transmission structures of CNC machine tool spindles can be roughly divided into the following categories: (1) Main transmission with a direct connection between the motor and the spindle. As shown in Figure 8-1a, this direct-drive structure is generally rotated directly by a variable-speed motor driving the spindle, which greatly simplifies the structure of the spindle box and spindle, and effectively improves the rigidity of the spindle components. However, the output torque of the spindle is small, and motor heating has a significant impact on spindle accuracy, so its application is subject to certain limitations. (2) Main transmission with one-stage speed variation. As shown in Figure 8-1b, one-stage speed variation is mostly accomplished by a synchronous belt. Its advantages are a simple structure, convenient installation and debugging, and to a certain extent, it can meet the speed and torque output requirements. However, the spindle speed regulation range ratio is still the same as the motor's, constrained by the motor's speed regulation range ratio. Its advantage is a wide speed variation range, with a maximum speed reaching 8000r/min, which basically meets the transmission requirements of most current CNC machine tools and is easy to realize rich control functions; its simple structure and convenient installation and debugging can meet the control requirements of current mid-to-high-end CNC machine tools. However, for increasingly high speed demands, this configuration method is difficult to satisfy. (3) Main transmission with variable speed gears. As shown in Figure 8-1c, this configuration method is mostly adopted in large and medium-sized CNC machine tools. In actual production, the spindle does not need to maintain constant power throughout the entire speed range; generally, constant power transmission is required in the medium and high-speed sections, and constant torque transmission is required in the low-speed section. To ensure that the CNC machine tool spindle has a large torque at low speeds and that the spindle's speed range is as large as possible, some CNC systems are equipped with gear speed variation on the basis of the stepless speed variation of the machine tool spindle motor, becoming segmented stepless speed variation. In the segmented stepless speed variation system with gear speed variation, the forward and reverse starting, stopping, and braking of the spindle are realized by directly controlling the motor, while the speed variation of the spindle is realized by the combination of the stepless speed variation of the motor speed and the stepped speed variation of the gears. Gear stepped speed variation mechanisms usually adopt two speed variation forms: hydraulic shift fork speed variation and electromagnetic clutch speed variation. 1) Hydraulic shift fork speed variation. The principle and form of the hydraulic shift fork speed variation mechanism are shown in Figure 8-2. The shift fork of the sliding gear is connected to the piston rod of the variable speed hydraulic cylinder. By changing different oil flow paths, the triple gear can obtain three different speed variation positions. As shown in Figure 8-2a, when hydraulic cylinder 1 is fed with pressure oil and hydraulic cylinder 5 is depressurized, piston rod 2 drives shift fork

also be mechanisms such as automatic tool clamping devices, spindle orientation devices, and chip removal devices. Structurally, issues such as tool clamping, bearing configuration, bearing clearance adjustment, lubrication, and sealing must be well resolved. (1) Spindle. The spindle is an important part of the spindle transmission structure. Its structural dimensions, shape, manufacturing accuracy, material, and heat treatment have a great impact on the working performance of the spindle component. Spindle structures come in various forms depending on the design requirements of the spindle transmission system. During design, a series of issues must be properly handled, such as the clamping of chucks or tools, spindle unloading, positioning and clearance adjustment of spindle bearings, and sealing and lubrication of spindle components. The main dimensional parameters of the spindle include: spindle diameter, inner hole diameter, overhang length, and support span. The basis for evaluating and considering the main dimensional parameters of the spindle is the rigidity of the spindle, structural manufacturability, and the process application range of the spindle assembly. (2) Spindle Bearings. Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

The tool magazine for storing tools has a large capacity; it can be installed on the side or top of the spindle box, or as an independent component outside the machine tool, with tools transported by a handling device. Compared with the turret spindle head, the automatic tool changing system with a tool magazine ensures that the CNC machine tool's spindle box has only one spindle, allowing the spindle component design to fully enhance its rigidity, thus meeting the requirements of precision machining. In addition, the tool magazine can store a large number of tools, enabling multi-process machining of complex parts, which significantly improves the machine's adaptability and processing efficiency. Therefore, automatic tool changing devices with tool magazines are particularly suitable for CNC drilling, milling, and boring machines. 2. Tool magazine. The tool magazine is the main component of the automatic tool changing device; its capacity, layout, and specific structure have a great impact on the design of CNC machine tools. Depending on the required capacity and tool retrieval method, tool magazines can be designed in various forms. Figure 8-59 lists the most commonly used types. Figures 8-59a to d show single-disk tool magazines. To adapt to the machine tool spindle layout, the tool axes in the magazine can be configured in different directions (as shown in Figures 8-59a to c). Figure 8-59d shows a disk tool magazine where tools can be flipped 90 degrees; this structure simplifies the tool retrieval action. The single-disk tool magazine has a simple structure, typically holding 15 to 30 tools, and tool retrieval is relatively convenient, making it the most widely used. Figure 8-59e is a drum-type (also known as hedgehog-type) tool magazine, which is very compact and offers a larger capacity within the same space, but the tool selection and retrieval actions are more complex. Figure 8-59f is a chain-type tool magazine, which provides great structural flexibility, can store a large number of tools, and makes tool selection and retrieval very simple. For long chains, the number of supporting sprockets can be increased to fold and loop the chain, improving space utilization. Figures 8-59g and 8-59h show multi-disk and grid-type tool magazines respectively. Although they are compact, their tool selection and retrieval actions are complex, so they are rarely used. The typical capacity of these tool magazines is 10 to 60 tools, but with the development of machining technology, there seems to be a trend toward even larger capacities. The chain-type tool magazine is one of the more frequently used forms. In this magazine, tool pockets are fixed on the chain links. A commonly used type is the single-row chain-type tool magazine, as shown in Figure 8-60a, generally storing fewer than 30 tools, occasionally up to 60. If a further increase in storage capacity is needed, a multi-row chain-type tool magazine can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60b; or a chain-type tool magazine with an extended chain can be used, as shown in Figure 8-60c. 3. Tool changing methods. In the automatic tool changing device of a CNC machine, the mechanism that transfers and loads/unloads tools between the tool magazine and the machine spindle is called the tool exchange device. Tool exchange methods in CNC machines are generally divided into two categories: tool changing without a manipulator and tool changing with a manipulator. (1) Tool changing without a manipulator. A tool changing system without a manipulator generally involves placing the tool magazine at a position the machine spindle can reach, or moving the entire magazine (or a specific tool position) to a location accessible by the spindle box. Additionally, the tool storage direction in the magazine is generally consistent with the tool loading direction on the spindle. During a tool change, the spindle moves to the changing position on the magazine and directly retrieves or returns the tool. For example, in the machining center shown in Figure 2-59, the tool change sequence is as follows: ① According to the tool change command, the machine worktable quickly moves to the right, moving the workpiece away from under the spindle, and the tool magazine moves under the spindle, aligning an empty tool pocket with the spindle. ② The spindle box descends, placing the used tool from the spindle into the empty pocket of the tool magazine. ③ The spindle box ascends, and the tool magazine rotates to align the tool required for the next step with the spindle. ④ The spindle box descends, inserting the tool into the machine spindle. ⑤ The spindle box and spindle ascend with the tool. ⑥ The machine worktable quickly returns to the left, the tool magazine moves away from under the spindle, and the workpiece moves under the spindle, aligning the tool with the machining surface of the workpiece. ⑦ The spindle box descends, and the tool on the spindle machines the workpiece. ⑧ After machining, the spindle box ascends, and the tool retracts from the workpiece. Tool changing without a manipulator has a relatively simple structure but involves cumbersome actions, long changing times, and relatively small magazine capacities. (2) Tool changing with a manipulator. In machining centers, using a manipulator (tool changing arm) for tool exchange is the most widely applied method because it requires short tool changing times and offers flexible actions.
