Example 1: In a machining center, the spindle motor vibrates enormously when the spindle speed is 600r/min, and the entire spindle head vibrates; at 1500r/min, the swing amplitude decreases, but the vibration frequency increases; when the spindle is rotating at high speed and the power is cut off, the motor continues to vibrate during the coasting process, proving it to be a non-electrical fault; disconnecting the transmission belt between the motor and the spindle and starting the motor, the vibration still exists. Analysis and processing: Based on the directly proportional relationship between vibration frequency and speed, it was preliminarily judged as rotor eccentricity or looseness. Disassembling the motor, it was found that the motor rotor bearing seat had worn more than 0.02mm due to the inner ring spinning. Considering that this machine tool had been used for more than ten years, expectations for its performance were not high, plus there was no ready-made rotor for replacement, it was decided to use a spray coating repair method for the bearing seat while replacing the bearing, achieving good results. Example 2: Spindle cannot orient. Fault phenomenon: In a vertical machining center using SINUMERIK 810M equipped with a 6SC6502 spindle drive, during debugging, when the spindle speed was greater than 200r/min, a fault occurred where the spindle could not be positioned. Analysis and processing: To confirm the cause of the fault, the following tests were conducted during maintenance: ① Input and sequentially execute the "S100M03; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ② Input and sequentially execute the "S100M04; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ③ Input and sequentially execute the "S200M03; M05; M19" command; machine tool positioning was normal. ④ Directly input and sequentially execute the "S200M03; M19" command; the machine tool could not position. Based on the above tests, it can be confirmed that the system and drive are working normally. During maintenance, considering the possible cause of the fault could be poor high-speed characteristics of the encoder or excessively high actual positioning speed of the spindle. Checking the actual speed of the spindle motor, it was found that the actual spindle speed of this machine tool differed greatly from the commanded value. When executing the S200 command, the actual machine tool spindle speed was 300r/min. Adjusting the spindle drive parameters to match the actual spindle speed with the commanded value eliminated the fault, and the machine tool returned to normal. Example 3: Automatic process cannot proceed after spindle orientation. Fault phenomenon: In a vertical machining center using SINUMERIK 810M, when executing an automatic tool change command, after the spindle completes orientation (M19), the program stops executing. Analysis and processing: After the machine tool encountered the fault, it could be restored to normal by restarting. When executing a program block without an M19 command, the machine tool ran normally. Therefore, it can be determined that the fault was caused by the M19 spindle directional orientation, meaning the M19 command did not have an execution completion reply (FIN) signal. When checking the M19 status, it was found that the positioning position was correct, and the spindle also had a corresponding holding torque, so abnormal action of the spindle positioning itself could be ruled out. Checking against the machine tool's electrical schematic diagram, to improve the reliability of tool changing, the machine tool was equipped with a spindle in-position contactless switch. The cause of the fault was the damage to this switch, which prevented the generation of the M19 reply (FIN) signal. After replacing the switch, the machine tool returned to normal. Example 4: A vertical CNC milling machine using the SINUMERIK 802D CNC system failed to unload tools after a long period of downtime. This machine tool spindle uses pneumatic cylinders to control the unclamping and clamping of spindle tools and uses proximity switches as cylinder limit switches. Checking the CNC system PLC and output interfaces, they were all normal, and the two proximity switches at the rear also worked normally, but the rear cylinder had no action when unclamping the tool. Pressing the manual switch of the solenoid valve controlling the cylinder action, the sound of spraying air could be heard. Checking the machine tool air pump, the working pressure was normal, but there was no oil in the machine tool's lubricator. It was preliminarily judged that the fault was caused by the cylinder jamming, making the spindle unable to unclamp the tool. Disassembling the rear cylinder and opening it, it was found that the cylinder piston and cylinder wall were severely rusted and could not be separated. Later, after soaking in a rust remover for a week to remove the rust spots and reassembling the machine tool, tool loading and unloading returned to normal. Analysis of the cause of the fault: Although it was directly caused by the rusting of the cylinder, the fundamental cause of the fault was the lack of oil in the lubricator, preventing the piston from being lubricated. Long-term parking caused moisture in the compressed air to condense and rust on the cylinder wall and piston. In machining centers, using a manipulator (tool changing arm) for tool exchange is the most widely applied method because it requires short tool changing times and offers flexible actions. Figure 8-61 shows the automatic tool change process of the TH5632 CNC machine. ① First, the tool magazine rotates the tool prepared for replacement to a fixed tool change position, which is at the very bottom of the magazine. ② After the previous step ends, the tool magazine rotates the tool pocket at the tool change position counterclockwise by 90 degrees; after the spindle box rises to the tool change position, the manipulator rotates 75 degrees to simultaneously grasp the tool holders on the spindle and the magazine tool pocket. ③ After the spindle automatically releases the tool holder, the manipulator descends, simultaneously pulling the tool holders out of the spindle hole and the tool pocket. When using a manipulator for tool exchange, depending on the tool magazine and exchange method, the manipulator can take various forms, such as single-arm or double-arm. Figure 8-62 shows the most common structures of double-arm manipulators: Figure 8-62a is a hook arm, Figure 8-62b is a hugging arm, Figure 8-62c is a telescopic arm, and Figure 8-62d is a fork arm. These manipulators can perform all actions including grasping, pulling out, rotating, inserting, and returning. To prevent tools from dropping, the movable jaws of all manipulators must be equipped with self-locking mechanisms. Figure 8-63 shows the claw mechanism of a certain model of manipulator. The hydraulic cylinder 11 and positioning block 8 are fixed on the tool change arm 10, and the piston is fixed on the positioning block 8. The tool change arm moves from the preparation position to the tool change position, and key 2 slides into the tool positioning slot. At this time, hydraulic cylinder 11 pushes piston assembly 9 to slide forward under the guidance of positioning block 8, causing the two claws 1 and 3 to rotate around shafts 4 and 5 respectively, until the claws clamp the tool, and piston assembly 9 locks the claws. To release the claws, the spring in hydraulic cylinder 11 drives piston assembly 9 backward; claws 1 and 3 maintain contact with piston assembly 9 under the action of spring balls 6 and 7 respectively, and after the claws open, the tool change arm retreats to the preparation position. (3) Tool selection methods. Based on the tool change command, the operation of the tool exchange device picking the required tool from the tool magazine for each process is called automatic tool selection. Common tool selection methods mainly include sequential tool selection and random tool selection. Random tool selection is further divided into tool coding selection, tool pocket coding selection, and memory-based selection. 1) Sequential tool selection method. Before machining, tools are sequentially inserted into the tool pockets of the magazine according to the predetermined machining process order, and tools are selected in order during machining. Used tools are returned to their original pockets, or they can be placed in the next pocket according to the machining sequence. However, when machining different workpieces, the tool sequence must be readjusted, making operations very cumbersome; moreover, when machining the same workpiece across different processes, tools cannot be reused, which increases the number of tools and the required magazine capacity, reducing the utilization rate of tools and the magazine. Furthermore, great caution must be exercised when loading tools, as failing to load them in order can lead to severe consequences. Because this method requires no tool identification device and features simple drive control and reliable operation, it is suitable for small and medium-sized automatic tool changing CNC machines that process large batches with a small variety of workpieces. 2) Tool coding selection method. This method uses a special tool holder structure to encode each tool based on binary principles. During a tool change, an encoding identification device recognizes the required tool in the magazine. This allows tools to be stored in any pocket of the magazine and reused across different processes, reducing the required magazine capacity; used tools do not necessarily need to return to their original pockets, which avoids accidents caused by errors in tool storage sequences, shortens the magazine operation time, and simplifies the automatic tool change control circuit. However, because each tool must be equipped with a dedicated coding system, the tool length increases, making manufacturing difficult and reducing rigidity, while the structures of the manipulator and tool magazine also become more complex. Good lubrication can reduce the operating temperature of bearings and prolong service life. Sealing not only prevents dust, chips, and cutting fluid from entering, but also prevents the leakage of lubricating oil. ① Lubrication of spindle bearings. On CNC machine tools, spindle bearing lubrication methods include grease lubrication, oil lubrication, oil mist lubrication, and oil-air lubrication. Grease lubrication is currently the most commonly used lubrication method for spindle bearings on CNC machine tools, especially for front support bearings. Of course, if there is no cooling lubricating oil system in the spindle box, the rear support bearings and other bearings generally use grease lubrication. The grease filling amount for spindle bearings is usually 10% of the bearing's spatial volume, and must not be filled arbitrarily, otherwise it will exacerbate spindle heating. When using grease lubrication, effective sealing measures must be taken to prevent cutting fluid or lubricating oil from entering the bearing. Oil lubrication is also one of the common lubrication methods in CNC. Figure 8-7 shows a constant temperature oil lubrication and cooling method. Constant temperature oil controlled by an automatic oil temperature control box enters the spindle box via a hydraulic pump, flows along the spiral groove on the outer ring of the spindle front support sleeve to take away the heat generated by the spindle bearing; another path injects constant temperature oil onto the transmission gears and transmission shaft support bearings via an oil distributor in the spindle box to take away the heat they generate. When using oil lubrication for angular contact ball bearings, attention should be paid to the pumping effect of angular contact, and oil needs to be injected from the small opening of the bearing. Oil mist lubrication is a method where oil is atomized by high-pressure gas and sprayed from a nozzle onto the parts requiring lubrication. Because it is mist-like, the oil has good heat absorption and no oil stirring effect, so it is often used for the lubrication of high-speed spindle bearings. However, oil mist is easily blown out and pollutes the environment. Oil-air lubrication is a new lubrication method developed for high-speed spindles. As shown in Figure 8-8, it feeds a very small amount of oil (8~16 min, about 0.03 cm³) into compressed air, and then blows it into the bearing clearance, thereby lubricating the bearing and suppressing bearing heat. (3) Temperature Rise Problems 1) The influence of lubrication The choice of lubricating oil directly affects the temperature rise of the ball screw. Poor lubrication of the ball screw will produce a larger temperature rise, which may cause steel balls to crack or be damaged, thereby damaging the nut or screw ball grooves. Therefore, the timely replenishment of lubricating oil must be considered during the design process. If an automatic lubrication system cannot be used, the replenishment cycle of lubricating oil (grease) must be included in the maintenance manual. Generally, it is recommended to use bearing lubricating oil for ball screw oil lubrication, and lithium-soap-based grease for grease lubrication. The viscosity of the oil should be selected based on operating speed, working temperature, and load conditions. For high speed and low load conditions, it is best to use low viscosity oil; for low speed and high load, high viscosity oil is recommended. When applied in high-speed, heavy-load situations, forced cooling must be used to lower the temperature, and hollow screws should be used to introduce cooling oil to achieve the cooling effect. 2) The influence of pre-tension Generally, ball screws require certain pre-tension to achieve the purposes of improving accuracy and rigidity, but applying pre-tensioning force to the nut will increase the friction torque and resistance of the raceway, raising the temperature during work. It is recommended that the pre-tension should not exceed 8% of the screw's dynamic load. 3) The influence of pre-stretching When the temperature of the ball screw rises, the thermal stress effect will cause a slight elongation of the screw, so the length of the screw becomes unstable. Pre-compensation measures are often used to make up for this. The target value for pre-stretching compensation is to give a negative compensation value in advance. It is generally recommended that the compensation value per 1000mm is 0.02~0.03mm. Excessive pre-stretching will burn out the support bearings. Therefore, it is recommended to use a pre-stretching value corresponding to less than 5°C. However, if the screw diameter exceeds 50mm, it is not suitable for pre-stretching. A large screw diameter requires a large pre-stretching force, which leads to overheating and burning of support bearings. It is recommended to use a temperature rise of about 3°C as the compensation value. 4) The influence of the dn value The dn value is the product of the screw pitch circle diameter and the maximum rotational speed. For example, if the pitch circle diameter is Φ40mm and the maximum speed is 2000r/min, its dn value is 80000. The dn value has a significant impact on the noise, working temperature, circulation system, and service life of the screw. It is generally recommended that the dn value not exceed 70000. (6) Protection and Lubrication of Ball Screw Pairs 1) Protection of ball screw pairs Like other rolling friction transmission devices, the ball screw pair should avoid the entry of hard dust or chip dirt, so a protective device must be installed. If the ball screw pair is exposed on the machine tool, a closed protective cover should be used, such as a spiral spring steel strip sleeve, a telescopic sleeve, and a folding sleeve. During installation, one end of the protective cover is connected to the side of the ball nut, and the other end is fixed to the support housing of the ball screw. If the ball screw pair is in a hidden position, sealing rings can be used for protection. Sealing rings are installed at both ends of the nut. The contact elastic sealing ring is made of oil-resistant rubber or nylon, and its inner hole is shaped to match the screw thread raceway; the contact sealing ring has a good dust-proof effect, but due to contact pressure, the friction torque slightly increases. The non-contact sealing ring, also known as a labyrinth sealing ring, is made of hard plastic. The shape of its inner hole is opposite to the screw thread raceway, with a slight gap, which avoids friction torque but has a poor dust-proof effect. Avoid hitting the protective device during work. If the protective device is damaged, it should be replaced in time. 2) Lubrication of ball screw pairs Lubricants can improve wear resistance and transmission efficiency, and are divided into two main categories: lubricating oils and lubricating greases. Lubricating oil is generally oil for total loss systems, and lithium-based grease can be used as lubricating grease. Lubricating grease is generally added to the thread raceway and the housing space where the nut is installed, while lubricating oil is injected into the nut space through the oil hole on the housing. The lubricating grease on the ball screw should be replaced every six months. Clean the old grease on the screw and apply new grease. Example 7: The spindle of an XK5040-1 could not rotate after starting up. Fault cause analysis and elimination: Checking the motor, the condition was good; the transmission key was not damaged. After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

Example 3: Poor protection caused synchronous belt aging and deformation, resulting in feed deviation. Fault Cause Analysis and Elimination: During automatic operation of a CNC lathe, the actual machining size occasionally differed from the program-specified size when the X-axis was feeding, with a difference of about 0.5~2mm. Because this phenomenon occurred occasionally rather than continuously, and the CNC system did not display an alarm number when it occurred, the fault was very unclear. During work, operators could not guarantee whether the machining size of the next workpiece would be qualified, and scrap products continued to appear. First, the control system output signals were checked and found to be normal; then, after resetting the system, the X-axis feed speed was tested, and the data displayed by the system was consistent with the settings; after adjusting the system parameters and re-testing, the fault remained. Therefore, it was suspected that the speed of the X-axis drive stepper motor was unstable, and there might be a "missing step" phenomenon. Opening the protective cover of the X-axis drive stepper motor of the machine tool, the input phase voltage and speed of the motor were measured, and both were within normal ranges. Using an adjustable wrench to test-rotate the X-axis drive screw, it felt alternately tight and loose. Opening the screw cover, it was found that the synchronous timing belt connecting the stepper motor and the screw was severely aged, deformed, and even missing teeth. The reason was that the fastening screws of the protective cover at the connection part were loose, and cutting fluid seeped into the synchronous belt during machine operation. After soaking, it became severely aged and deformed, making it impossible for the stepper motor to synchronize with the screw speed, causing the above fault. After replacing the synchronous belt and re-running the test program, the command size was consistent with the actual measured size, and the fault was eliminated. The servo motor and the ball screw are directly connected by a coupling. Based on the machine tool control principles and the machine tool transmission connection method, it was preliminarily judged that the cause of the alarm was a poor connection of the Y-axis coupling. A check of the Y-axis transmission system revealed that the coupling connection screws were loose. These guideways use pressurized oil pumped through restrictors into oil pockets, forming a load-bearing oil film that separates contacting surfaces (liquid friction). They offer low friction (0.001-0.005), high efficiency, long precision retention, excellent vibration absorption, and no low-speed stick-slip, but require complex, costly dedicated oil supply systems. Open types only bear vertical loads, while closed types have oil pockets on all surfaces to resist large overturning moments and increase rigidity. Oil supplies are constant pressure or constant flow. Oil must be filtered to 10μm and kept absolutely clean. (2) Guideway clearance and restrictor forms. 1) Guideway clearance represents oil film thickness. Larger clearances increase flow but reduce rigidity and cause drift; smaller clearances increase rigidity but are limited by geometric accuracy. Small/medium machines use 0.01-0.025mm unloaded clearances; large machines use 0.03-0.08mm. 2) Restrictor forms include constant pressure and quantitative systems. Large machines often use single-cavity single-pump quantitative systems for maximum rigidity without restrictors. Constant pressure systems use capillary restrictors (often adjustable spiral grooves, combined for compactness, used in small/medium machines) or membrane feedback restrictors (single/double-sided, used for heavy, unevenly loaded large machines). Each oil pocket requires its own restrictor control. 8.3.2 Common Faults of Guideways and Their Diagnosis and Maintenance Methods. Guideway clearance, rolling guideway preload, straightness, parallelism, lubrication, and protection are critical for machine operation and machining quality. 1. Common repair methods include scraping, fine planing, and grinding. (1) Fine planing is used for heavy machines or deep scratches, heavily dependent on the planer's accuracy. (2) Scraping requires multiple measurements to map wear curves, using equal-height blocks, parallel straightedges, and frame levels to establish scraping reference points every fixed distance, followed by sectioned rough and fine scraping until the entire surface is flat and straight. (3) Grinding can use a "one-time grinding method" where all surfaces are measured for unevenness, rough ground to remove peaks, and fine ground in one setup. The sequence should prioritize associated/high-precision, complex, large, and difficult-to-machine surfaces first. 2. Common problems in guideway repair and their elimination. (1) Guideway scoring/scratches: Caused by foundation settling (requires regular leveling), prolonged short workpiece machining (requires varying installation positions or repairing accuracy), poor lubrication (adjust oil volume/pressure), poor material (treat with electroplating, induction hardening, or add zinc-aluminum-copper alloy plates), poor scraping quality (improve quality), or poor maintenance (enhance care and protection). (2) Moving parts sticking or not moving: Caused by surface scratches (polish with 180-grit sandpaper), pressure plate scratches (remove and adjust clearance), or gibs adjusted too tight (loosen anti-loose screws, adjust gib bolts for flexible movement ensuring a 0.03mm feeler gauge cannot enter, then lock). (3) Uneven machining surfaces at tool joints: Caused by poor guideway straightness (adjust/scrape to within 0.015mm/500mm), loose or excessively bent table gibs (adjust clearance, ensure natural bending <0.05mm/full length), poor machine levelness bending the guideway (adjust installation level/verticality to within 0.02mm/1000mm), rough guideway surfaces or uneven/insufficient scraping contact points (remove table, polish burrs with oilstone/sandpaper, reassemble, and polish manually with chromium oxide and kerosene), tapered bed guideways causing uneven tightness (repair geometric accuracy), temperature changes deforming guideways (adjust seasonally, keep precision machine rooms at constant temperatures), wear losing accuracy (re-scrape/repair), improper oil viscosity or dirty oil causing poor lubrication (use proper viscosity and keep clean), or poor surface lubrication structure increasing resistance (break the full guideway surface into fragmented dot contacts; for large surfaces, divide the saddle guideway into three sections, making the contact points heavier at the outer thirds and lighter in the middle third).

The spindle is an important part of the spindle transmission structure. Its structural dimensions, shape, manufacturing accuracy, material, and heat treatment have a great impact on the working performance of the spindle component. Spindle structures come in various forms depending on the design requirements of the spindle transmission system. During design, a series of issues must be properly handled, such as the clamping of chucks or tools, spindle unloading, positioning and clearance adjustment of spindle bearings, and sealing and lubrication of spindle components. The main dimensional parameters of the spindle include: spindle diameter, inner hole diameter, overhang length, and support span. The basis for evaluating and considering the main dimensional parameters of the spindle is the rigidity of the spindle, structural manufacturability, and the process application range of the spindle assembly. (2) Spindle Bearings. Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

Good lubrication can reduce the operating temperature of bearings and prolong service life. Sealing not only prevents dust, chips, and cutting fluid from entering, but also prevents the leakage of lubricating oil. ① Lubrication of spindle bearings. On CNC machine tools, spindle bearing lubrication methods include grease lubrication, oil lubrication, oil mist lubrication, and oil-air lubrication. Grease lubrication is currently the most commonly used lubrication method for spindle bearings on CNC machine tools, especially for front support bearings. Of course, if there is no cooling lubricating oil system in the spindle box, the rear support bearings and other bearings generally use grease lubrication. The grease filling amount for spindle bearings is usually 10% of the bearing's spatial volume, and must not be filled arbitrarily, otherwise it will exacerbate spindle heating. When using grease lubrication, effective sealing measures must be taken to prevent cutting fluid or lubricating oil from entering the bearing. Oil lubrication is also one of the common lubrication methods in CNC. Figure 8-7 shows a constant temperature oil lubrication and cooling method. Constant temperature oil controlled by an automatic oil temperature control box enters the spindle box via a hydraulic pump, flows along the spiral groove on the outer ring of the spindle front support sleeve to take away the heat generated by the spindle bearing; another path injects constant temperature oil onto the transmission gears and transmission shaft support bearings via an oil distributor in the spindle box to take away the heat they generate. When using oil lubrication for angular contact ball bearings, attention should be paid to the pumping effect of angular contact, and oil needs to be injected from the small opening of the bearing. Oil mist lubrication is a method where oil is atomized by high-pressure gas and sprayed from a nozzle onto the parts requiring lubrication. Because it is mist-like, the oil has good heat absorption and no oil stirring effect, so it is often used for the lubrication of high-speed spindle bearings. However, oil mist is easily blown out and pollutes the environment. Oil-air lubrication is a new lubrication method developed for high-speed spindles. As shown in Figure 8-8, it feeds a very small amount of oil (8~16 min, about 0.03 cm³) into compressed air, and then blows it into the bearing clearance, thereby lubricating the bearing and suppressing bearing heat. The oil level switch in the oil tank and the pressure switch in the pipeline can automatically cut off the power supply of the main motor when there is no oil in the tank or insufficient pressure. ② Sealing of the spindle. Example 7: The spindle of an XK5040-1 could not rotate after starting up. Fault cause analysis and elimination: Checking the motor, the condition was good; the transmission key was not damaged. After adjusting the tension of the V-belt, the spindle still could not rotate. Checking the spindle electromagnetic brake, no problems were found with the armature's return spring or the friction disc. It was analyzed that it might be a damaged gear or bearing on the transmission shaft, causing the transmission to jam. Disassembling the transmission shaft, it was found that the bearing (EZ12) had burned out due to lack of lubrication. After removing it and turning the spindle by hand, it rotated normally. After installing a new bearing and testing, the spindle moved normally, but the spindle braking time was long. At this point, the clearance between the friction disc and the armature needed to be adjusted. First, loosen the lock nut, and then evenly adjust the four screws to move the armature upwards. After adjusting the clearance between the armature and the friction disc to 1mm, lock it with the nut and perform a test run. The spindle braked rapidly, and the fault was completely eliminated. Example 8: A machining center had poor spindle positioning, causing an interruption during the tool change process. Fault cause analysis and elimination: When this fault first appeared, the machine tool worked normally again after restarting, but subsequently, this fault appeared repeatedly. Carefully observing the machine tool, it was found that the fault was caused by a positional shift after the spindle was oriented. After the spindle was positioned, if touched by hand, the spindle would drift in the opposite direction. Checking the electrical unit, there were no alarms. According to the machine tool's manual, this machine tool uses an encoder for positioning; based on the fault phenomena and the possible parts involved, the likelihood of an electrical problem was relatively small. It was analyzed as a mechanical connection problem, so the connections of various parts of the spindle were inspected. When checking the encoder connection, it was found that the set screw on the encoder's connecting sleeve was loose, causing the connecting sleeve to retreat and resulting in excessive clearance in the connection with the spindle, making the rotation out of sync. After fixing the set screw according to the requirements, the fault was eliminated. Example 9: During the working process of a CNC milling machine, the mechanical variable-speed sliding gear in the spindle box automatically disengaged from meshing, and the spindle stopped rotating. Fault cause analysis and elimination: The variable-speed structure of this machine tool is a hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism. The hydraulic cylinder pushes the sliding gear for speed variation and also locks the sliding gear. Therefore, the automatic disengagement of the shifting sliding gear is highly likely to be caused by pressure changes inside the hydraulic cylinder. Checking the hydraulic control oil circuit, it was found that the three-position four-way directional valve controlling the hydraulic cylinder was in the middle function position and could not seal completely. The oil circuits in the front and rear cavities of the hydraulic cylinder leaked into each other, causing the thrust in the upper cavity of the hydraulic cylinder to be greater than that in the lower cavity, causing the piston rod to move downwards gradually, gradually making the sliding gear disengage from meshing and causing the spindle to stop rotating. After replacing with a new three-position four-way directional valve, the fault was eliminated. Example 10: After a CNC milling machine issued a spindle box shifting command, the spindle entered a slow reciprocating swing state and could never engage the gear. Fault cause analysis and elimination: This machine tool adopts the hydraulic shift fork variable-speed mechanism shown in Figure 8-2 to achieve machine tool spindle speed variation. To ensure that the sliding gear smoothly meshes in the correct position, after the machine tool receives a shifting command, the electrical design instructs the main motor to drive the spindle to perform a slow reciprocating swing motion. Analysis indicated a fault in the solenoid valve (valve core stuck or solenoid failed), causing the oil circuit to be unable to switch, and the hydraulic cylinder did not act; or the hydraulic cylinder acted, but the contactless switch sending the feedback signal failed, and the feedback signal could not be sent after the sliding gear shifted into place, either of which would interrupt the machine tool's cycle action. After replacing the new hydraulic valve or the failed contactless switch, the fault was eliminated.

Spindle bearings are also an important part of the spindle component, and their type, structure, configuration, accuracy, installation, adjustment, lubrication, and cooling directly affect the working performance of the spindle assembly. In the spindle transmission structure, different spindle bearing models are selected according to the specifications and accuracy of the CNC machine tool. Generally, the spindle components of small and medium-sized CNC machine tools mostly use groups of high-precision rolling bearings, while heavy-duty CNC machine tools use hydrostatic bearings, and high-speed spindles often use silicon nitride ceramic rolling bearings or magnetic levitation bearings. Rolling bearings have low frictional resistance, can be preloaded, are simple to lubricate and maintain, and can work stably under a certain speed range and load variation range. Rolling bearings are produced by specialized factories, making purchase and maintenance convenient, and are widely used in CNC machine tools. However, compared with sliding bearings, rolling bearings have higher noise, a limited number of rolling elements, variable rigidity, slightly poorer vibration resistance, and significant speed limitations. Under possible conditions, the spindle assemblies of CNC machine tools try to use rolling bearings, especially most vertical spindles and spindles installed in sleeves that can move axially. In this case, rolling bearings can be lubricated with grease to avoid oil leakage. Rolling bearings are divided into three categories based on the structure of the rolling elements: ball bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, and tapered roller bearings. Spindle supports are divided into radial and axial (thrust) supports, and angular contact bearings (including angular contact ball bearings and tapered roller bearings) serve both radial and axial support functions. The axial support should be located inside the front support because the coordinate origin of a CNC machine tool is usually set at the front end of the spindle. To reduce the coordinate origin displacement caused by thermal expansion, the distance between the coordinate origin and the axial support should be shortened as much as possible. For spindle bearings, cylindrical roller bearings, tapered roller bearings, or angular contact ball bearings can be selected. Since tapered roller bearings have sliding friction between the large end face of the roller and the inner ring rib, generating more heat, their speed is limited. 1) Configuration forms of spindle bearings. The machine tool spindle drives the tool or workpiece to perform rotary motion in the support, and it should be able to transmit cutting torque, withstand cutting resistance, and ensure the necessary rotation accuracy. Currently, there are mainly three support configuration forms for CNC machine tool spindles, as shown in Figure 8-5. ① As shown in Figure 8-5a, the spindle front support uses a combination of double-row cylindrical roller bearings and a 60° angular contact double-row radial-axial ball bearing, and the rear support uses a pair of angular contact ball bearings. This configuration greatly improves the comprehensive rigidity of the spindle and can meet the requirements of heavy-duty cutting, so it is widely applied in spindles of various CNC machine tools. ② As shown in Figure 8-5b, the spindle front bearing uses high-precision double-row angular contact ball bearings, and the rear bearing uses single-row (or double-row) angular contact ball bearings. This configuration has good high-speed performance, and the maximum spindle speed can reach 4000r/min, but its load-bearing capacity is small, so it is suitable for high-speed, light-load, and precision CNC machine tool spindles. In the spindles of machining centers, to improve the load-bearing capacity, a front bearing composed of 3 to 4 angular contact ball bearings is sometimes used, and preload is achieved with a spacer. ③ As shown in Figure 8-5c, the spindle front and rear bearings use double-row and single-row tapered bearings. This type of bearing has high radial and axial rigidity, can bear heavy loads, especially strong dynamic loads, and has good installation and adjustment performance. However, this configuration limits the maximum speed and accuracy of the spindle, so it is suitable for medium-precision, low-speed, and heavy-load CNC machine tool spindles. 2) Preloading methods for spindle bearings. Bearing preloading refers to making a certain amount of interference between the bearing raceway and the rolling elements. When a rolling bearing works with clearance, it will cause the load to be concentrated on a few rolling elements in the direction of force, producing huge contact stress and contact deformation between these rolling elements and the raceway. If there is slight interference, the number of load-bearing rolling elements can be increased, the rolling elements are stressed evenly, and errors can also be homogenized. Therefore, appropriate preloading can improve the rigidity and life of the bearing, but excessive preloading will cause too much deformation of the rolling elements and the raceway, which will lead to a higher temperature rise and reduce the bearing life

Figure 8-11 shows the spindle of a certain model of CNC lathe. Its rotation accuracy includes two items: radial runout and axial movement. Radial runout is guaranteed by a double-row radial short cylindrical roller bearing at the front end of the spindle and a radial thrust ball bearing at the rear end; axial movement is guaranteed by the radial thrust bearing at the rear end of the spindle. Normally, this accuracy is adjusted before leaving the factory and generally requires no adjustment. If tool holder collision with the workpiece or other reasons affect the spindle's accuracy, spindle accuracy adjustment must be performed. During adjustment, loosen the lock screw on nut 1 or nut 2 for adjustment. After adjustment, retighten the lock screw. If requirements are still not met, repeat the above steps. After adjustment, perform an idling test for a certain period of time (usually about 1 hour). 3. Other Auxiliary Components of the Spindle. (1) Hydraulic power chuck. In CNC lathes, the hydraulic power chuck is the most commonly used workpiece fixture. It is the connecting interface between the machine tool spindle and the workpiece; the speed, torque, and rotation accuracy of the machine tool spindle are transmitted to the workpiece through the power chuck. Hydraulic power chucks are very widely used in CNC machine tools and have become indispensable fundamental functional components for mid-to-high-speed CNC lathes, CNC grinders, and CNC turn-mill centers. Hydraulic power chucks mainly include self-centering chucks, floating chucks, crankshaft chucks, and indexing chucks. Among them, the linearly driven self-centering hydraulic power chuck shown in Figure 8-12a is highly versatile and widely used. The hydraulic power chuck is fixedly mounted on the front end of the spindle. The rotary hydraulic cylinder 1 is connected to the connector 5 with screws 7, and the connector 5 is connected to the rear end face of the spindle with screws, causing the rotary hydraulic cylinder to rotate together with the spindle. The clamping and unclamping of the chuck are driven by the rotary hydraulic cylinder through a hollow draw tube 2. The rear end of the draw tube is threaded to the piston 6 inside the hydraulic cylinder, and the threads on both ends of the connection sleeve 3 are connected to the draw tube 2 and the slide sleeve 4 respectively. Figure 8-12b shows a schematic diagram of the wedge mechanism inside the chuck. When the pressure oil in the hydraulic cylinder pushes piston 6 and draw tube 2 towards the chuck, slide sleeve 4 moves to the right. Due to the action of the wedge groove on the slide sleeve and the chuck body, jaw base 11 moves radially outwards with jaw 12, thereby loosening the chuck; conversely, when the pressure oil in the hydraulic cylinder pushes the piston and draw tube towards the rear end of the spindle, the chuck clamps the workpiece through the wedge mechanism. Chuck body 9 is fixed with screws 10 and installed on the front end of the spindle. Item 8 is the box body of the rotary hydraulic cylinder. The distribution plate of the rotary hydraulic cylinder is shown in Figure 8-13. Oil is supplied to the hydraulic cylinder 3 via distribution plate 2 and piston rod 4. The distribution plate is supported by rolling bearing 1. Hydraulic cylinder 3 and piston rod 4 rotate synchronously with the machine tool spindle, while distribution plate 2 remains stationary. The distribution plate uses an axial annular clearance seal. If the oil path is improved to supply oil from the hydraulic cylinder body to the pressure cavity, the distribution plate can avoid axial movement. The piston rod of the hollow rotary hydraulic cylinder has a center hole, while other aspects are the same as the solid hydraulic cylinder. High-speed distribution pairs generate serious heat; therefore, heat dissipation fins are often designed outside the distribution plate to cool it and improve the cooling effect. To improve the reliability of clamping and ensure that the workpiece can still be clamped if a fault occurs in the oil supply line, a hydraulic lock is usually integrated into the rotary hydraulic cylinder to realize cylinder self-locking. In addition, based on different transmission mechanisms, linearly driven power chuck bodies can also be divided into wedge-type power chucks, lever-type power chucks, helical rack power chucks, and wedge-lever power chucks. (2) Automatic tool clamping and chip removal device inside the spindle of the machining center. On machining centers, to achieve automatic loading and unloading of tools on the spindle, their spindles are often designed with automatic tool clamping mechanisms. Figure 8-14 shows the structural diagram of the spindle component of the JCS-018 machining center, with an automatic tool clamping mechanism installed inside and at the rear of the spindle. Tool holder 1 uses a steep taper shank of 7:24, which is conducive to centering and brings convenience for clamping and releasing. While the tail journal of the taper shank is tensioned, the tool bar is clamped at the end of the spindle through the centering and frictional action of the taper shank. Under the action of Belleville spring 5, drawbar 4 constantly maintains a tension of about 10000N, and tightens the tail journal of tool holder 1 through steel ball 12 at the right end of the drawbar. When changing tools, first feed pressure oil into the left cavity of hydraulic cylinder 7 at the tail of the spindle, and hydraulic cylinder piston 6 pushes drawbar 4 to the right. This loosens the tool shank while compressing Belleville spring 5. The rightward movement of drawbar 4 places steel ball 12 at the right end into the flared opening of the sleeve, eliminating the tension on the tool holder. When drawbar 4 continues to move right, the end of the air nozzle pushes the tool loose, allowing the manipulator to easily extract tool holder 1. After the manipulator inserts the replacement tool, the solenoid directional valve acts to feed pressure oil into the right cavity of hydraulic cylinder 7, piston 6 returns leftward to its original position, Belleville spring 5 recovers, and pulls tool holder 1 tight again. When there is no pressure in the right cavity of hydraulic cylinder 7, helical spring 11 makes piston 6 retreat to the leftmost end. When piston 6 is at the left and right limit positions, the corresponding limit travel switches 8 and 10 send unclamping and clamping signals. To keep the spindle taper hole clean, the commonly used method is to blow chips away with compressed air. In Figure 8-14, when the spindle component is in the unclamped tool state, the hydraulic cylinder at the top of the spindle is in tight contact with the drawbar. At this time, compressed air passes through the through hole in the middle of piston 6 and drawbar 4 and is sprayed out from compressed air pipe connector 9 to blow away dust, chips, and other dirt on the spindle taper hole, ensuring the cleanliness of the spindle hole, preventing chips and dust from falling into the spindle taper hole to scratch the spindle hole surface and the tool shank's taper shank, and guaranteeing the correct position of the tool. (3) Spindle orientation device. On CNC boring machines, CNC milling machines, and machining centers primarily used for boring and milling, to achieve automatic tool changing and enable the manipulator to accurately insert the tool into the spindle hole, the keyway of the tool must be circumferentially aligned with the key position on the spindle; when retracting the tool during boring, the tool is required to move a certain distance radially in the opposite direction of the tool tip before retracting to avoid scratching the workpiece, all of which require the spindle to have a circumferential positioning function. This situation may be caused by the screw shoulder being too deep, too shallow, or the bearing not being installed in place. ② If the perpendicularity between the positioning shoulder surface for installing the bearing on the screw and the axis of the locking thread profile is out of tolerance, or the parallelism between the lock nut surface and the bearing mounting surface is out of tolerance, it will cause the bearing to tilt. Therefore, the lock thread profile on the screw used to install the bearing must be processed simultaneously with the bearing positioning shoulder surface to ensure perpendicularity; grinding is even better, and precision specialized lock nuts should be selected. ③ If the perpendicularity of the internal cavity positioning surface of the bearing housing and the gland installation surface to the axis of the bearing hole is out of tolerance, it will also cause the bearing to tilt, and the internal cavity positioning surface is difficult to process and measure. 5) Parallelism or flatness of the support housing surface is out of tolerance Whether the mating component surface is ground or scraped, as long as its parallelism or flatness exceeds the tolerance range, it will affect the positioning accuracy when the worktable moves. Usually, adjusting can be achieved by adding shims between the support housing and the base body. (2) Unsmooth Movement 1) Foreign matter entering the steel ball track If the ball screw is not equipped with a wiper or has poor protection, the accumulation of debris or dust generated during assembly and processing enters the steel ball track, causing unsmooth movement, reduced accuracy, and reduced service life. 2) Overtravel Limit switch failure, overshooting, misoperation, or collision will cause damage, dents, or even fracture of the return pipe, resulting in unsmooth operation of the steel balls, or even complete failure to rotate. 3) Eccentricity If the nut housing and the bearing housing are not concentric, radial loads will be generated. When the eccentricity is too large, the screw will bend or even become eccentric; even if it does not cause obvious bending, abnormal wear will continue to occur and rapidly reduce the accuracy of the screw. The higher the pre-tension set for the nut, the higher the requirement for eccentric accuracy. (3) Temperature Rise Problems 1) The influence of lubrication The choice of lubricating oil directly affects the temperature rise of the ball screw. Poor lubrication of the ball screw will produce a larger temperature rise, which may cause steel balls to crack or be damaged, thereby damaging the nut or screw ball grooves. Therefore, the timely replenishment of lubricating oil must be considered during the design process. If an automatic lubrication system cannot be used, the replenishment cycle of lubricating oil (grease) must be included in the maintenance manual. Generally, it is recommended to use bearing lubricating oil for ball screw oil lubrication, and lithium-soap-based grease for grease lubrication. The viscosity of the oil should be selected based on operating speed, working temperature, and load conditions. For high speed and low load conditions, it is best to use low viscosity oil; for low speed and high load, high viscosity oil is recommended. When applied in high-speed, heavy-load situations, forced cooling must be used to lower the temperature, and hollow screws should be used to introduce cooling oil to achieve the cooling effect. 2) The influence of pre-tension Generally, ball screws require certain pre-tension to achieve the purposes of improving accuracy and rigidity, but applying pre-tensioning force to the nut will increase the friction torque and resistance of the raceway, raising the temperature during work. It is recommended that the pre-tension should not exceed 8% of the screw's dynamic load. 3) The influence of pre-stretching When the temperature of the ball screw rises, the thermal stress effect will cause a slight elongation of the screw, so the length of the screw becomes unstable. Pre-compensation measures are often used to make up for this. The target value for pre-stretching compensation is to give a negative compensation value in advance. It is generally recommended that the compensation value per 1000mm is 0.02~0.03mm. Excessive pre-stretching will burn out the support bearings. Therefore, it is recommended to use a pre-stretching value corresponding to less than 5°C. However, if the screw diameter exceeds 50mm, it is not suitable for pre-stretching. A large screw diameter requires a large pre-stretching force, which leads to overheating and burning of support bearings. It is recommended to use a temperature rise of about 3°C as the compensation value. 4) The influence of the dn value The dn value is the product of the screw pitch circle diameter and the maximum rotational speed. For example, if the pitch circle diameter is Φ40mm and the maximum speed is 2000r/min, its dn value is 80000. The dn value has a significant impact on the noise, working temperature, circulation system, and service life of the screw. It is generally recommended that the dn value not exceed 70000. The dn value can be controlled by increasing the lead or decreasing the rotational speed. If the dn value exceeds the normal range, the manufacturer should be contacted for

The so-called axial clearance refers to the maximum axial movement between the screw and the nut when there is no relative rotation between them. In addition to the structural clearance itself, it also includes the movement caused by elastic deformation after an axial load is applied. Therefore, it is difficult to completely eliminate the axial clearance. The double-nut pre-tensioning method is usually used to control the elastic deformation to a minimum. Currently, there are three common structural forms for double-nut pre-tensioning: 1) Pre-tensioning with a lock nut Figure 8-28 shows a thread-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair. The left and right nuts of the ball screw are connected to the outer sleeve with flat keys. The extended end of the right nut has no flange and is threaded. Using two round nuts 1 and 2, the right nut can be moved axially relative to the screw, and then locked after eliminating the clearance. This adjustment method has the advantages of a compact structure and convenient adjustment, so it is widely used, but the displacement amount is not easily controlled precisely. Figure 8-28 Thread-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair 1—Round nut 2—Lock nut 2) Adjusting clearance by grinding a spacer As shown in Figure 8-29, by grinding and adjusting the thickness of the spacer, the left and right nuts of the ball screw generate axial displacement to achieve pre-tensioning. This method has a simple structure and good rigidity. When adjusting the clearance, the adjusting spacer needs to be removed for grinding. For the convenience of assembly and disassembly, it is best to make the adjusting spacer into a half-ring structure. Figure 8-29 Spacer-adjusted clearance ball screw and nut pair 3) Differential tooth adjustment Figure 8-30 shows a differential tooth clearance-adjusting ball screw and nut pair. External gears are machined on the ends of the left and right nuts, with the number of teeth being Z1 and Z2 respectively, and Z1 and Z2 differ by one tooth. The two gears mesh with the corresponding internal ring gears at both ends respectively. The internal ring gears are fastened to the nut housing. During pre-tensioning, the two internal ring gears are disengaged, allowing the two nuts to rotate the same number of teeth in the same direction; then the internal ring gears are re-engaged, and the relative axial position of the two nuts changes, thereby achieving the adjustment of the clearance and the application of the pre-tensioning force. Figure 8-30 Differential tooth clearance-adjusting ball screw and nut pair When both gears rotate by one tooth in the same direction, their axial displacement is: s=1/(Z1×Z2) This method allows the relative axial displacement of the two nuts to be as small as 1mm. Its adjustment accuracy is high, accurate, and reliable, but the structure is complex. Figure 8-21 is a schematic diagram of the spindle structure of the XH754 horizontal machining center, which achieves speed variation through single-stage belt transmission. 8.1.2 Common Faults and Diagnostics of Spindle Components. 1. Spindle heating. (1) Front and rear spindle bearings are damaged or bearings are not clean. Elimination method: Replace bad bearings, clean out dirt. (2) Spindle bearing preload is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the preload. (3) Lubricating oil is dirty or contains impurities. Elimination method: Clean the spindle box, replace the lubricating oil. (4) The spindle front end cover and the spindle box body gland are galled. Elimination method: Grind the spindle box front end cover so that it presses tightly against the spindle front bearing, leaving a clearance of 0.02-0.05mm between the bearing and the cover. (5) Bearing lubricating grease is depleted or there is too much lubricating grease. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. 2. The spindle stops during heavy cutting. (1) The belt connecting the motor and the spindle is too loose. Elimination method: Move the motor base, tension the belt, and then retighten the motor base. (2) There is oil on the surface of the belt. Elimination method: Wash with gasoline and wipe clean before reinstalling. (3) The friction clutch is adjusted too loosely or is worn. Elimination method: Adjust the clutch, grind or replace the friction plates. (4) The belt has been used for too long and failed. Elimination method: Replace with a new belt. 3. Spindle noise. (1) Lack of lubrication. Elimination method: Apply lubricating grease, 3mL per bearing. (2) Poor transmission balance between the small pulley and the large pulley. Elimination method: The balance weight on the pulley has fallen off; perform dynamic balancing again. (3) Bearings are scored or damaged. Elimination method: Replace the bearings. (4) Poor balance of parts at the end of the shaft. Elimination method: Redo dynamic balancing. (5) Gear meshing clearance is uneven or gears are damaged. Elimination method: Adjust the meshing clearance or replace with new gears. (6) The transmission bearing is damaged or the transmission shaft is bent. Elimination method: Repair or replace the bearing, straighten the transmission shaft. 4. Spindle has no lubricating oil circulation or insufficient lubrication. (1) The hydraulic pump rotation direction is incorrect, or the clearance is too large. Elimination method: Change the hydraulic pump rotation direction, repair the hydraulic pump. (2) The suction pipe is not inserted below the oil level of the oil tank. Elimination method: Insert the suction pipe 2/3 below the oil level. (3) Oil pipes or filters are blocked. Elimination method: Eliminate the blockage. (4) Lubricating oil pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply pressure. 5. Lubricating oil leakage. (1) The amount of lubricating oil is too large. Elimination method: Adjust the oil supply amount. (2) Check whether seals in various places are damaged. Elimination method: Replace seals. (3) Pipe fittings are damaged. Elimination method: Replace pipe fittings. 6. Tool cannot be clamped. (1) Belleville spring displacement is small. Elimination method: Adjust the stroke length of the Belleville spring. (2) Spring collet is damaged. Elimination method: Replace the spring collet. (3) Belleville spring failure. Elimination method: Replace the Belleville spring. (4) The pull stud on the tool holder is too large. Elimination method: Replace the pull stud and install it correctly. (5) Check whether the nut on the tool unclamp/clamp spring is loose. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the clamp spring clockwise so that its maximum working load is 13kN. 7. Tool cannot be unclamped after being clamped. (1) Unclamp spring is compressed too tightly. Elimination method: Turn the nut on the unclamp spring counterclockwise so that its maximum working load does not exceed 13kN. (2) Hydraulic cylinder pressure and stroke are insufficient. Elimination method: Adjust hydraulic pressure and piston stroke switch. 8. Spindle fails to change speeds. (1) Shifting hydraulic cylinder pressure is insufficient. Elimination method: Detect working pressure; if lower than rated pressure, adjust it. (2) Shifting hydraulic cylinder is worn or stuck. Elimination method: Remove burrs or galling, clean and reassemble. (3) Shifting hydraulic cylinder fork has fallen off. Elimination method: Repair or replace. (4) Shifting hydraulic cylinder bypasses oil or leaks internally. Elimination method: Replace seal ring. (5) Shifting solenoid valve is stuck. Elimination method: Repair the solenoid valve and clean it. (6) Shifting composite switch has failed. Elimination method: Replace the switch. 8.1.3 Spindle Component Fault Maintenance Examples. (6) Protection and Lubrication of Ball Screw Pairs 1) Protection of ball screw pairs Like other rolling friction transmission devices, the ball screw pair should avoid the entry of hard dust or chip dirt, so a protective device must be installed. If the ball screw pair is exposed on the machine tool, a closed protective cover should be used, such as a spiral spring steel strip sleeve, a telescopic sleeve, and a folding sleeve. During installation, one end of the protective cover is connected to the side of the ball nut, and the other end is fixed to the support housing of the ball screw. If the ball screw pair is in a hidden position, sealing rings can be used for protection. Sealing rings are installed at both ends of the nut. The contact elastic sealing ring is made of oil-resistant rubber or nylon, and its inner hole is shaped to match the screw thread raceway; the contact sealing ring has a good dust-proof effect, but due to contact pressure, the friction torque slightly increases. The non-contact sealing ring, also known as a labyrinth sealing ring, is made of hard plastic. The shape of its inner hole is opposite to the screw thread raceway, with a slight gap, which avoids friction torque but has a poor dust-proof effect. Avoid hitting the protective device during work. If the protective device is damaged, it should be replaced in time. 2) Lubrication of ball screw pairs Lubricants can improve wear resistance and transmission efficiency, and are divided into two main categories: lubricating oils and lubricating greases. Lubricating oil is generally oil for total loss systems, and lithium-based grease can be used as lubricating grease. Lubricating grease is generally added to the thread raceway and the housing space where the nut is installed, while lubricating oil is injected into the nut space through the oil hole on the housing. The lubricating grease on the ball screw should be replaced every six months. Clean the old grease on the screw and apply new grease. For ball screw pairs lubricated with oil, oil can be added once before the machine tool starts working each time. 2. Example 3: Poor protection caused synchronous belt aging and deformation, resulting in feed deviation. Fault Cause Analysis and Elimination: During automatic operation of a CNC lathe, the actual machining size occasionally differed from the program-specified size when the X-axis was feeding, with a difference of about 0.5~2mm. Because this phenomenon occurred occasionally rather than continuously, and the CNC system did not display an alarm number when it occurred, the fault was very unclear. During work, operators could not guarantee whether the machining size of the next workpiece would be qualified, and scrap products continued to appear. First, the control system output signals were checked and found to be normal; then, after resetting the system, the X-axis feed speed was tested, and the data displayed by the system was consistent with the settings; after adjusting the system parameters and re-testing, the fault remained. Therefore, it was suspected that the speed of the X-axis drive stepper motor was unstable, and there might be a "missing step" phenomenon. Opening the protective cover of the X-axis drive stepper motor of the machine tool, the input phase voltage and speed of the motor were measured, and both were within normal ranges. Using an adjustable wrench to test-rotate the X-axis drive screw, it felt alternately tight and loose. Opening the screw cover, it was found that the synchronous timing belt connecting the stepper motor and the screw was severely aged, deformed, and even missing teeth. The reason was that the fastening screws of the protective cover at the connection part were loose, and cutting fluid seeped into the synchronous belt during machine operation. After soaking, it became severely aged and deformed, making it impossible for the stepper motor to synchronize with the screw speed, causing the above fault. After replacing the synchronous belt and re-running the test program, the command size was consistent with the actual measured size, and the fault was eliminated. Example 4: Coupling connection screws were loose, causing excessive position deviation in the feed direction. Fault Cause Analysis and Elimination: During the operation of a horizontal machining center, an alarm message indicating that the Y-axis position deviation exceeded the set value appeared. This machining center uses a FANUC 0iM system and adopts a closed-loop control format. Grating scales installed on the guide rail side and the column serve as position measurement components, and the system control takes the position loop as the outer loop; a rotary encoder installed at the end of the servo motor serves as the angle measurement component, and the speed loop is the inner loop of the system control. The servo motor and the ball screw are directly connected by a coupling. Based on the machine tool control principles and the machine tool transmission connection method, it was preliminarily judged that the cause of the alarm was a poor connection of the Y-axis coupling. A check of the Y-axis transmission system revealed that the coupling connection screws were loose. After tightening all the fastening screws in the Y-axis transmission system, the fault was eliminated. Example 5: System overload alarm. Fault Cause Analysis and Elimination: For the XH716 CNC vertical machining center, the system is a FANUC OM system. This machine tool frequently experienced overload alarms during machining, with alarm number 434, manifesting as excessive Z-axis motor current and motor heating. The alarm disappeared after stopping for about 40 minutes, but after resuming work for a while, the same type of alarm appeared again. After inspection and analysis, it was believed that the electrical servo system had no faults, and it was estimated that it was caused by the load being too heavy to pull. In order to distinguish whether it was an electrical fault or a mechanical fault, the Z-axis motor was removed and disconnected from the mechanism. When running again, the fault no longer occurred, thus confirming that it was caused by the mechanical screw or moving parts being too tight. After adjusting the anti-loosening nut of the Z-axis screw, the effect was not obvious. Later, the Z-axis guide rail taper jib was adjusted, the machine load was significantly reduced, and the fault was eliminated.
